Unlike static text or isolated audio clips, videos require synchronized processing of heterogeneous data streams to capture the interplay between verbal and non-verbal communication. Furthermore, ethical considerations around privacy and consent demand careful handling of user-generated content, ensuring compliance with platform policies and data protection regulations.  

This study introduces a novel framework for depression detection in YouTube videos by integrating computer vision, natural language processing, and audio analysis techniques. By training machine learning models on labeled datasets of individuals diagnosed with depression, we aim to identify multimodal biomarkers that correlate with clinical assessments. The research also evaluates the generalizability of these models across diverse demographics and content genres, addressing potential biases in training data. Ultimately, this work seeks to bridge gaps in mental health research by demonstrating how digital footprints can serve as proxies for psychological well-being, fostering early intervention and reducing barriers to care in an increasingly online world.

title: Computation of single-cell metabolite distributions using mixture models
text:
We applied mixture models to compute metabolite distributions across 1,200 single cells from three experimental conditions (Control, Drug A, Drug B). Each model comprised two Gaussian components, validated by Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) scores (Control: BIC = 452 ± 18; Drug A: BIC = 427 ± 15; Drug B: BIC = 439 ± 22), indicating superior fit over single-Gaussian alternatives.  

In Control cells, metabolite concentrations exhibited a bimodal distribution (μ₁ = 12.4 ± 0.3 μM, σ₁ = 2.1 ± 0.2 μM; μ₂ = 28.7 ± 0.5 μM, σ₂ = 3.4 ± 0.3 μM), suggesting two distinct subpopulations. Drug A treatment shifted the lower peak to μ₁ = 8.9 ± 0.4 μM (p < 0.001, Welch’s t-test) and increased its proportion from 38% to 62%, while the higher peak remained stable (μ₂ = 29.1 ± 0.6 μM). Conversely, Drug B reduced the higher peak’s amplitude by 40% (p < 0.01) and broadened its variance (σ₂ = 5.2 ± 0.4 μM), indicating disrupted metabolic homeostasis.  

Clustering accuracy, assessed via silhouette scores, averaged 0.72 across conditions, with Drug A showing the highest coherence (0.78). Parameter correlations revealed a strong inverse relationship between μ₁ and cell volume in Drug A-treated cells (r = -0.65, p < 0.001), suggesting size-dependent metabolite sequestration.  

These results demonstrate that mixture models effectively resolve heterogeneous metabolite distributions, uncovering condition-specific subpopulations invisible to bulk averaging. The stability of μ₂ under Drug A implies a resilient metabolic compartment, whereas Drug B’s impact on variance highlights its role in destabilizing cellular regulation. Future work will integrate temporal data to resolve dynamic shifts in subpopulation structure.

title: Heterogeneity Learning for SIRS model: an Application to the COVID-19
text:
In conclusion, this study introduces a novel heterogeneity - learning framework for the Susceptible - Infectious - Recovered - Susceptible (SIRS) model and applies it to the COVID - 19 pandemic. By incorporating individual - level heterogeneity factors such as age, comorbidities, and social behavior patterns into the SIRS model, we are able to more accurately capture the complex dynamics of the disease spread.

Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model with heterogeneity learning outperforms the traditional homogeneous SIRS model in terms of prediction accuracy. It can better estimate key epidemic parameters like the basic reproduction number and the recovery rate, which are crucial for formulating effective public health policies.

Moreover, the identified heterogeneous subgroups provide valuable insights into the different risk levels among the population. This allows for targeted interventions, such as prioritizing vaccination for high - risk groups or implementing more stringent social distancing measures in areas with a higher proportion of vulnerable individuals.

However, there are still limitations. Data availability and quality remain challenges, and the model's performance could be further improved with more comprehensive and detailed datasets. Future research could explore the integration of real - time data streams and the extension of the model to consider other heterogeneity factors. Overall, our work offers a promising approach for epidemic modeling and control, especially in the face of complex and evolving infectious diseases like COVID - 19.

title: Landmark detection in Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging Using A Convolutional Neural Network
text: This study introduces a robust framework for landmark detection in cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) to enhance the precision and efficiency of cardiovascular image analysis. Accurate identification of anatomical landmarks in cardiac MRI is crucial for diagnosing heart conditions, guiding surgical interventions, and monitoring disease progression. However, manual annotation is time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability, while traditional automated methods often struggle with the complex anatomical structures and varying imaging conditions inherent in cardiac MRI. The proposed CNN-based approach leverages a multi-scale feature extraction strategy to capture both global and local contextual information, enabling precise localization of key cardiac landmarks such as the apex, mitral valve annulus, and aortic root. The model is trained on a large, diverse dataset of cardiac MRI scans, incorporating data augmentation techniques to improve generalization across different imaging protocols and patient populations. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves high detection accuracy with significant improvements in robustness compared to conventional techniques, particularly in challenging cases with low image quality or anatomical abnormalities. This automated landmark detection system has the potential to streamline clinical workflows, reduce manual labor, and support the development of advanced diagnostic and therapeutic tools in cardiology.

title: Influence of Absolute Humidity, Temperature and Population Density on COVID-19 Spread and Decay Durations: Multi-prefecture Study in Japan
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the critical importance of understanding the environmental and socio-demographic factors influencing the transmission dynamics of respiratory viruses. While numerous studies have investigated the impact of meteorological variables—such as temperature and humidity—on COVID-19 incidence, the relationship between these factors and the duration of viral spread remains underexplored, particularly in diverse geographical settings. Japan, characterized by its distinct seasonal climate variations and varying population densities across prefectures, provides a unique context for examining how absolute humidity, temperature, and demographic factors collectively shape the temporal patterns of COVID-19 transmission and decline. Absolute humidity, which reflects the total water vapor content in the air, has been hypothesized to influence viral stability and survival, potentially affecting both the onset and duration of outbreaks. Similarly, temperature may modulate transmission efficiency through its effects on host immune responses and viral persistence in the environment. Population density, as a key socio-demographic determinant, could exacerbate or mitigate these effects by altering contact rates and the potential for community spread. Despite these plausible interactions, few studies have systematically analyzed how these factors jointly influence the duration of COVID-19 waves across multiple regions. This study aims to fill this gap by examining the associations between absolute humidity, temperature, population density, and the spread and decay durations of COVID-19 across Japanese prefectures, offering insights that could inform public health strategies in similar climatic and demographic contexts worldwide.

title: GPU-Accelerated Drug Discovery with Docking on the Summit Supercomputer: Porting, Optimization, and Application to COVID-19 Research
text: The urgent need for rapid drug discovery during pandemics, such as COVID-19, demands leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to accelerate molecular docking simulations, which are critical for identifying potential therapeutic compounds. This study presents a comprehensive framework for GPU-accelerated drug discovery by porting and optimizing the AutoDock-GPU molecular docking software to the Summit supercomputer, the world’s second-most powerful HPC system. We detail the challenges and solutions in adapting AutoDock-GPU to Summit’s heterogeneous architecture, which combines IBM POWER9 CPUs with NVIDIA Volta GPUs, including optimizations for memory management, thread synchronization, and load balancing across thousands of nodes. By employing mixed-precision arithmetic, kernel fusion, and dynamic task scheduling, we achieve a 15-fold speedup over the original CPU implementation and a 3.2-fold improvement over a baseline GPU port, enabling whole-library screening of over 1 billion compounds in under 24 hours. We validate the framework’s accuracy and reproducibility through benchmarking against established docking datasets and demonstrate its application to COVID-19 research by screening a library of 1.3 billion small molecules against the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro). Our results identify 23 high-affinity candidates, including 8 novel compounds with predicted binding energies comparable to known inhibitors, highlighting the potential of GPU-accelerated docking for rapid therapeutic discovery. This work establishes a scalable, open-source pipeline for pandemic-scale virtual screening, bridging the gap between computational efficiency and biological relevance in drug discovery.

title: Is Factor Momentum More than Stock Momentum?
text:
The debate over the persistence and predictability of financial returns has long centered on identifying robust sources of momentum across asset classes. While stock momentum—the tendency of past winners to continue outperforming past losers—is well-documented in empirical asset pricing, its extension to factor portfolios remains underexplored. Factor momentum refers to the phenomenon where factors themselves (eg., value, size, or momentum) exhibit time-series continuation in their returns, suggesting that strategies betting on recent factor performance may generate excess returns. This distinction raises critical questions: Is factor momentum merely an aggregation of individual stock momentum effects, or does it represent a distinct, factor-specific phenomenon with independent predictive power? Clarifying this relationship is essential for portfolio construction, risk management, and theoretical models of asset pricing, as it challenges assumptions about the universality of momentum across market dimensions.  

Recent studies have highlighted factor momentum’s ability to deliver significant returns even after controlling for traditional risk factors, yet its underlying mechanisms remain debated. Some argue that factor momentum is a byproduct of stock-level momentum, as factors are constructed from individual securities whose past returns already exhibit persistence. Others contend that factor momentum captures unique, macroeconomic or behavioral drivers, such as slow-moving capital flows or investor overreaction to factor cycles. This tension underscores the need for rigorous empirical analysis to disentangle these effects. For instance, if factor momentum’s returns are subsumed by stock momentum, it may lack incremental value for practitioners. Conversely, if factor momentum operates independently, it could offer diversification benefits and enhance portfolio efficiency beyond what stock-level strategies provide.  

This paper investigates whether factor momentum is a distinct phenomenon or a reflection of stock momentum by analyzing its performance across global equity markets from 1990 to 2023. Using a multifactor framework, we decompose factor returns into stock-specific and cross-sectional components to isolate the contribution of each. We further test whether factor momentum’s predictability holds during periods of economic stress, such as recessions or market crashes, where stock momentum often falters. Our findings suggest that factor momentum retains explanatory power even after accounting for stock-level effects, pointing to its role as a complementary signal. These results have implications for both academic theories of return predictability and practical applications in factor-based investing, where understanding the hierarchy of momentum sources is critical for optimizing strategy design.

title: Robustness to Spurious Correlations in Text Classification via Automatically Generated Counterfactuals
text:
Our experiments demonstrate that counterfactual data augmentation (CDA) significantly improves model robustness to spurious correlations compared to baseline models trained solely on original data. On the synthetic SpuriousNews dataset, where 80% of articles with the word "bank" are finance-related (spurious correlation), a BERT-base model trained without CDA achieved 92% accuracy on the original test set but only 58% on a counterfactual-shifted test set (where "bank" articles were randomly assigned to non-finance categories). After augmenting the training set with 2,000 automatically generated counterfactual examples (e.g., replacing "bank" with "river" in finance articles), the same model’s accuracy on the shifted test set improved to 79%, a 36% relative increase (*p* < 0.01).  

On the real-world IMDb sentiment dataset, where spurious correlations exist between exclamation marks and positive sentiment, CDA reduced the performance gap between original and counterfactual-shifted test sets by 42%. For instance, a RoBERTa model trained without augmentation scored 94% on original reviews but 67% on reviews with inverted sentiment labels and preserved punctuation; with CDA, scores on the shifted set rose to 82% (*p* < 0.05).  

Qualitative analysis revealed that CDA encouraged models to rely less on superficial features. For example, attention weights for the word "bank" in finance articles decreased by 31% post-augmentation, while weights for context-rich terms like "interest rates" increased. However, CDA’s effectiveness depended on counterfactual quality: poorly generated examples (e.g., nonsensical word replacements) reduced accuracy by 5–8% in preliminary tests, underscoring the need for controlled generation methods. These results suggest that CDA is a scalable approach to mitigating spurious correlations, though further work is needed to optimize counterfactual fidelity for complex domains like medical text.

title: Migration and Refugee Crisis: a Critical Analysis of Online Public Perception
text: In conclusion, this critical analysis of online public perception regarding the migration and refugee crisis reveals a complex, often polarized discourse shaped by media narratives, political agendas, and socio-cultural biases. Our findings demonstrate that digital platforms amplify both empathy and hostility, with sentiment frequently influenced by the framing of news sources and the proliferation of misinformation. While some online communities advocate for humanitarian responses and solidarity, others perpetuate xenophobic stereotypes, underscoring the role of echo chambers in reinforcing divisive ideologies. The study also highlights the tension between global humanitarian obligations and nationalist sentiments, reflecting broader debates about sovereignty, security, and cultural identity. Importantly, the analysis underscores the need for nuanced, evidence-based discourse to counteract sensationalism and foster informed public engagement. Future research should explore longitudinal shifts in online sentiment, the impact of algorithmic curation on perception, and strategies to promote constructive dialogue across ideological divides. Ultimately, addressing the refugee crisis demands not only policy solutions but also a concerted effort to cultivate empathy and critical media literacy, ensuring that digital spaces contribute to a more equitable and compassionate global response.

title: Towards Traffic Bisimulation of Linear Periodic Event-Triggered Controllers
text: This paper introduces a novel framework for achieving traffic bisimulation in linear periodic event-triggered control (LPETC) systems, addressing the challenge of preserving behavioral equivalence between abstract and concrete models under resource-constrained networked environments. Traffic bisimulation, a refined variant of traditional bisimulation, focuses on capturing equivalence in communication patterns and control signal transmissions rather than solely on state trajectories, making it particularly relevant for event-triggered systems where data exchange is intermittent and state-dependent. We formalize the notion of traffic bisimulation for LPETC by extending existing hybrid system theories to incorporate periodic sampling and event-triggered conditions, ensuring that abstract models accurately reflect the timing and frequency of control updates in their concrete counterparts. A key contribution is the development of sufficient conditions under which traffic bisimulation can be established, leveraging Lyapunov stability analysis and periodic event-triggering mechanisms to guarantee both functional correctness and communication efficiency. We also propose a constructive algorithm for deriving abstract models that are traffic-bisimilar to given LPETC implementations, enabling formal verification of networked control systems against timing and resource constraints. The theoretical results are validated through a case study on a vehicle platooning system, demonstrating that traffic bisimulation facilitates rigorous analysis of trade-offs between control performance and communication overhead. This work bridges the gap between control theory and formal methods, offering a systematic approach to designing and verifying event-triggered systems in cyber-physical applications where predictable traffic behavior is critical.

title: An Accelerated-Decomposition Approach for Security-Constrained Unit Commitment with Corrective Network Reconfiguration- Part II: Results and Discussion
text:
The security-constrained unit commitment (SCUC) problem stands as a cornerstone in power system operation, ensuring that generation resources are optimally scheduled to meet demand while adhering to operational constraints under both normal and contingency conditions. However, traditional SCUC formulations often overlook the potential benefits of corrective network reconfiguration (CNR), which involves adjusting the topology of the power grid through switching operations to enhance system security and operational flexibility. By integrating CNR into SCUC, operators can dynamically modify network configurations in response to contingencies, thereby mitigating the impact of outages and reducing the need for costly reserve allocations. Despite its promise, the incorporation of CNR introduces significant computational challenges due to the combinatorial nature of switching decisions and their interactions with unit commitment variables. This complexity is further exacerbated by the need to evaluate a vast number of contingency scenarios, making conventional solution approaches computationally intractable for large-scale systems.  
To address these challenges, this paper introduces an accelerated-decomposition approach tailored for SCUC with CNR, building upon the theoretical framework established in Part I. The proposed methodology leverages a hybrid decomposition strategy that combines Benders decomposition with advanced cutting-plane techniques to efficiently handle the interdependencies between unit commitment, network topology, and contingency constraints. By strategically partitioning the problem into manageable subproblems and exploiting problem structure, the approach achieves substantial computational speedups while maintaining solution optimality.  
This part of the study presents a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method using real-world power system benchmarks, including the IEEE 118-bus and Polish 2383-bus systems. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the accelerated-decomposition approach in reducing solution times by up to 70% compared to state-of-the-art alternatives, enabling its application to large-scale systems with minimal computational overhead. Furthermore, the analysis reveals how CNR-enhanced SCUC improves system resilience by reducing load shedding and operational costs under contingencies, highlighting the practical value of the proposed framework. The discussion also explores trade-offs between computational efficiency and solution quality, providing insights into the scalability and robustness of the approach. These findings underscore the potential of integrating CNR into SCUC to advance grid security and operational flexibility in the face of evolving challenges.

title: Vision as an Energy-Driven Process
text: The traditional view of vision as a passive, information-processing system has been challenged by emerging evidence suggesting that visual perception is fundamentally shaped by energetic constraints and active resource management. This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework that reconceptualizes vision as an energy-driven process, integrating principles from thermodynamics, neurobiology, and ecological psychology. We argue that visual systems have evolved to optimize energy efficiency, balancing the metabolic costs of neural computation with the adaptive benefits of acquiring and interpreting visual information. Drawing on empirical studies across species, we demonstrate how energy considerations influence key aspects of vision, including photoreceptor sensitivity, retinal circuitry, cortical processing, and attentional mechanisms. For instance, we show that the distribution of photoreceptors in the retina correlates with ecological demands for energy-efficient sampling of visual scenes, while neural suppression mechanisms minimize redundant processing to conserve metabolic resources. Furthermore, we explore how perceptual phenomena, such as visual illusions and change blindness, may reflect adaptive strategies for managing energy expenditure under uncertainty. By reframing vision through an energetic lens, our framework provides a unifying explanation for diverse observations in visual neuroscience and offers new directions for research into the interplay between biological constraints and perceptual experience. This perspective underscores the importance of considering energy dynamics in understanding the evolution, development, and function of visual systems.

title: The Wage Premium of Communist Party Membership: Evidence from China
text:
The wage premium associated with Communist Party of China (CPC) membership has long been a subject of debate, reflecting broader discussions about the interplay between political affiliation and economic outcomes in authoritarian regimes. In China, where the CPC maintains a dominant role in governance and societal organization, membership is often perceived as a gateway to career advancement, resource access, and social networks. Empirical studies in political economy and labor markets have increasingly sought to quantify this premium, yet results remain mixed. While some scholars argue that Party membership signals loyalty, competence, or access to elite networks—all of which may enhance productivity and earnings—others contend that observed wage gaps reflect institutional biases or unobserved heterogeneity, such as differences in education, industry, or regional opportunities. This paper contributes to this debate by providing rigorous evidence on the magnitude and mechanisms of the CPC membership wage premium in contemporary China, leveraging a combination of nationally representative household surveys and quasi-experimental methods to address endogeneity concerns.  

China’s unique institutional context offers a compelling case study. Since the 1980s, economic reforms have transformed the labor market, yet the CPC’s influence persists through formal and informal channels. Membership is not automatically granted; it requires nomination, vetting, and ideological commitment, suggesting that affiliated individuals may possess distinct traits or advantages. However, the Party’s role in allocating promotions, training opportunities, and state-sector jobs complicates causal inference. Prior studies using cross-sectional data have struggled to disentangle whether higher wages stem from selection (e.g., more ambitious individuals seeking membership) or treatment effects (e.g., membership directly boosting earnings). By contrast, this study employs panel data and instrumental variable techniques to isolate the causal impact of Party membership, focusing on transitions into membership and subsequent wage trajectories.  

Our findings challenge simplistic narratives. While a statistically significant wage premium exists, its size varies across sectors and time periods, with the largest effects observed in state-owned enterprises and among younger cohorts. We further demonstrate that the premium is partly explained by differences in job stability, promotion rates, and access to non-wage benefits, rather than purely productivity-related factors. These results underscore the importance of institutional structures in shaping labor market inequalities in China and provide insights into how political capital interacts with economic reforms. The study also raises questions about the broader implications of Party membership for social mobility and meritocracy in an era of rising inequality.

title: Dependencies and systemic risk in the European insurance sector: Some new evidence based on copula-DCC-GARCH model and selected clustering methods
text:
Our empirical analysis reveals significant interdependencies among European insurers, with systemic risk concentrated in specific clusters. Using the copula-DCC-GARCH model, we estimate time-varying conditional correlations between 25 major insurers from 2010–2022. Average pairwise correlations range from 0.32 (UK-Germany) to 0.78 (France-Italy), with heightened co-movements during the 2020 COVID-19 crisis (peak correlation: 0.89 for France-Italy). Tail dependence coefficients, derived from Clayton copulas, indicate asymmetric risk spillovers: lower tail dependence averages 0.45 during crises versus 0.18 in stable periods, suggesting heightened contagion in downturns.  

Hierarchical clustering identifies three distinct groups: (1) Core EU (Germany, France, Netherlands), (2) Peripheral EU (Italy, Spain, Portugal), and (3) Nordic-Baltic (Sweden, Denmark, Finland). The Core EU cluster exhibits the highest average correlation (0.65) and systemic risk contribution, measured via ΔCoVaR, with French insurers driving 32% of cluster-wide risk. K-means clustering confirms these groupings, with silhouette scores >0.7 indicating robust separation.  

Network analysis reveals that 60% of systemic risk flows originate from the Core EU cluster, particularly via reinsurance linkages. During stress periods, the Core’s connectedness index rises from 0.45 to 0.72, underscoring its vulnerability to shocks. These findings highlight the need for targeted macroprudential policies focusing on interconnected Core EU insurers to mitigate systemic risk.

title: Transient Stability of Power Systems Integrated With Inverter-Based Generation
text: The transient stability of power systems integrated with inverter-based generation (IBG) remains a critical challenge as the global energy landscape shifts toward renewable-dominated grids. This study has demonstrated that IBG introduces unique dynamics, such as fast response times and limited inertia, which significantly influence system stability during disturbances. Unlike synchronous generators, inverter-controlled resources rely on advanced control strategies to emulate inertial and primary frequency responses, yet their performance under high-penetration scenarios remains constrained by communication delays, parameter sensitivity, and grid-forming capability limitations. Through time-domain simulations and eigenvalue analysis, we confirmed that improper coordination between grid-following and grid-forming inverters can exacerbate frequency deviations and voltage instability, particularly in weak grid conditions. However, adaptive control frameworks incorporating virtual inertia and synthetic damping show promise in mitigating these risks, provided they are tailored to local grid characteristics and disturbance types. Future research must prioritize the development of standardized stability criteria for IBG-dominated systems, alongside real-time monitoring tools to assess dynamic interactions between inverters and conventional generators. Additionally, advancements in cyber-physical security protocols are essential to prevent malicious disruptions of control algorithms. As power systems evolve, interdisciplinary collaboration among engineers, policymakers, and stakeholders will be vital to ensuring resilient integration of IBG while maintaining transient stability thresholds. By addressing these gaps, the transition to a sustainable, low-carbon grid can proceed without compromising reliability, ultimately enabling a more flexible and robust energy infrastructure for the future.

title: Sum Throughput Maximization in Multi-Tag Backscattering to Multiantenna Reader
text: This paper addresses the problem of sum throughput maximization in a multi-tag backscattering communication system where multiple backscatter tags transmit data to a multiantenna reader. The core challenge lies in optimizing the resource allocation and reflection coefficients of the tags to enhance overall system performance while mitigating interference among tags. We propose a joint optimization framework that integrates power allocation at the reader and reflection coefficient design at the tags, aiming to maximize the sum throughput of the system under practical constraints, including individual tag power limitations and channel conditions. The optimization problem is formulated as a non-convex problem, which is computationally complex to solve directly. To address this, we decompose the problem into two subproblems: power allocation and reflection coefficient optimization. For power allocation, we employ a water-filling-inspired algorithm to efficiently distribute power among tags based on their channel gains. For reflection coefficient optimization, we utilize semidefinite relaxation techniques to transform the non-convex problem into a convex one, enabling the use of standard convex optimization solvers. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly improves the sum throughput compared to baseline schemes, particularly in scenarios with a large number of tags or varying channel conditions. The findings provide valuable insights into the design of efficient multi-tag backscattering systems for future Internet of Things applications.

title: The structure of multiplex networks predicts play in economic games and real-world cooperation
text: Understanding the mechanisms underlying human cooperation remains a central challenge across social and biological sciences, particularly in contexts involving repeated interactions and strategic decision-making. While traditional models often focus on isolated pairwise relationships, real-world cooperative systems—from economic networks to global supply chains—are inherently multiplex, comprising interdependent layers of social, economic, and institutional ties. Recent advances in network science have highlighted how multiplexity (i.e., the coexistence of multiple relationship types within a single system) reshapes information flow, trust dynamics, and collective behavior. However, few studies have systematically examined whether the structural properties of multiplex networks—such as layer overlap, interlayer coupling, and cross-layer redundancy—can predict cooperative outcomes in both controlled experimental settings and large-scale real-world systems. This paper bridges this gap by integrating computational modeling of multiplex networks with behavioral experiments and empirical data on global cooperation. We hypothesize that specific structural configurations of multiplex networks enhance cooperation by reducing uncertainty, facilitating reputation tracking, and aligning incentives across layers, thereby addressing fundamental puzzles about the evolution of cooperation in complex societies.

title: OER Recommendations to Support Career Development
text: Open Educational Resources (OER) have emerged as a transformative tool in education, offering accessible, adaptable, and cost-effective learning materials. This paper explores the potential of OER to support career development by providing personalized, skill-focused learning pathways aligned with evolving labor market demands. Drawing on a systematic review of existing OER initiatives and empirical data from learner engagement studies, the research identifies key challenges in integrating OER into career development frameworks, including gaps in content quality, discoverability, and alignment with industry competencies. The paper proposes a set of evidence-based recommendations to enhance OER utility for career advancement, such as developing dynamic OER repositories curated by subject-matter experts, embedding career-relevant assessments and micro-credentials, and fostering partnerships between educational institutions and industry stakeholders. Additionally, it highlights the importance of leveraging artificial intelligence to personalize OER recommendations and track skill progression. By addressing these gaps, OER can empower learners to navigate career transitions more effectively, reduce barriers to lifelong learning, and bridge the divide between education and employment. The findings underscore the need for collaborative efforts among policymakers, educators, and employers to maximize OER’s impact on global workforce readiness.

title: Energy Scheduling for Residential Distributed Energy Resources with Uncertainties Using Model-based Predictive Control
text:
The global transition toward decentralized energy systems has accelerated the integration of residential distributed energy resources (DERs), including rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) panels, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and electric vehicles (EVs). These technologies empower households to generate, store, and consume energy locally, reducing reliance on centralized grids and enabling participation in demand response programs. However, the stochastic nature of renewable generation (e.g., solar irradiance variability) and unpredictable household load patterns introduce significant uncertainties, posing challenges for optimal energy scheduling. Effective coordination of DERs under such conditions is critical to enhancing grid resilience, minimizing energy costs, and achieving carbon neutrality goals. Traditional rule-based or heuristic control methods often struggle to balance conflicting objectives—such as cost minimization, self-sufficiency, and grid stability—while accounting for real-time uncertainties. This gap underscores the need for advanced control strategies capable of dynamically adapting to evolving conditions.  

Model-based predictive control (MPC) has emerged as a promising framework for addressing these challenges by leveraging system models to predict future states and optimize control actions over a receding horizon. Unlike reactive approaches, MPC explicitly incorporates uncertainty through stochastic or robust formulations, enabling proactive decision-making. For residential DERs, MPC can optimize charging/discharging schedules for BESS, modulate EV charging, and manage PV surplus or deficit by interacting with the grid or neighboring prosumers. By integrating weather forecasts, historical load data, and real-time market prices, MPC reduces reliance on conservative assumptions, improving both economic and technical performance.  

This study proposes an MPC-based energy scheduling framework tailored to residential DERs, explicitly addressing uncertainties in renewable generation and load demand. The approach combines a high-fidelity system model with scenario-based stochastic optimization to hedge against forecast errors, ensuring robustness while maintaining computational tractability. Simulation results demonstrate the framework’s ability to reduce electricity costs by up to 22% and improve renewable utilization by 18% compared to conventional methods, validating its potential for real-world deployment.

title: A Bayesian method for inference of effective connectivity in brain networks for detecting the Mozart effect
text: The Bayesian effective connectivity analysis revealed significant network-level alterations during the Mozart listening condition compared to baseline. Posterior probability distributions indicated a 32% increase (95% HDI: [24%, 40%]) in directed connectivity from the right auditory cortex (RA) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), suggesting enhanced top-down modulation of auditory processing. Conversely, connectivity from the DLPFC to the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) decreased by 19% ([12%, 26%]), potentially reflecting reduced cognitive control demands. A 27% ([18%, 36%]) enhancement in RA-to-ventral striatum (VS) connectivity aligned with prior fMRI studies linking music to reward processing. Model comparison via Bayes factors strongly favored the proposed network architecture (BF₁₀ = 48.2) over null models. Post-hoc analysis showed these effects persisted across 89% of participants (n=42/47), with weaker responses in non-musicians (β=0.61, p=0.02). The results demonstrate that Bayesian inference robustly captures dynamic reconfiguration of auditory-executive-reward loops during music perception, providing quantitative evidence for the Mozart effect’s neurobiological basis through directed connectivity patterns rather than regional activation alone.

title: Roadmap to a Roadmap: How Could We Tell When AGI is a 'Manhattan Project' Away?
text:
In conclusion, determining when AGI development reaches a "Manhattan Project" scale—characterized by concentrated, high-stakes effort with transformative potential—requires a nuanced, multi-dimensional framework. This paper has outlined key indicators across technical, organizational, and societal dimensions. Technical milestones, such as breakthroughs in recursive self-improvement or cross-domain generalization, could signal a paradigm shift in capabilities, necessitating urgent collective action. Organizational shifts, including unprecedented resource mobilization, centralized coordination, and global talent convergence, would further indicate a critical inflection point. Meanwhile, societal indicators—such as heightened public awareness, policy urgency, and ethical debates—would reflect the broader stakes of AGI’s imminent arrival.  

Crucially, these indicators are interdependent and context-dependent. A surge in funding alone does not equate to a Manhattan Project if technical progress remains incremental, just as theoretical breakthroughs may lack impact without institutional alignment. Moreover, the path to AGI may not follow a linear trajectory; discontinuous jumps in capability could outpace preparedness efforts. This underscores the need for adaptive monitoring frameworks that integrate real-time data from research, policy, and public discourse.  

Ultimately, the question of whether AGI is a "Manhattan Project" away is not purely empirical but also normative. It hinges on societal choices about risk tolerance, resource allocation, and ethical priorities. Proactive engagement from policymakers, researchers, and civil society is essential to shape these dynamics. By establishing clear benchmarks and fostering interdisciplinary dialogue, we can better anticipate critical junctures and mitigate existential risks. The roadmap to AGI remains uncertain, but with vigilance and collaboration, humanity can navigate it with foresight rather than reaction. The time to refine our indicators and institutions is now—before the project’s scale becomes undeniable.

title: On forward invariance in Lyapunov stability theorem for local stability
text: This paper delves into the nuanced relationship between forward invariance and the Lyapunov stability theorem concerning local stability analysis. Traditional interpretations of Lyapunov's direct method often emphasize the role of a continuously differentiable Lyapunov function in establishing local asymptotic stability by demonstrating its negative definiteness along trajectories. However, the intrinsic connection between forward invariance—the property where trajectories remain confined within a specified set—and the stability criteria remains underexplored in classical literature. We systematically analyze how forward invariance of a sublevel set of the Lyapunov function facilitates a more intuitive understanding of local stability, particularly in non-smooth or constrained dynamical systems. By integrating forward invariance principles, we derive refined sufficient conditions for local stability that accommodate broader classes of systems, including those with discontinuous dynamics or state-dependent constraints. Theoretical results are illustrated through examples, such as switched systems and piecewise-defined models, where forward invariance provides a unifying framework to verify stability without requiring global differentiability of the Lyapunov function. This work bridges gaps between geometric invariance theory and classical stability analysis, offering practical tools for stability verification in complex dynamical systems.

title: Summer vacation and COVID-19: effects of metropolitan people going to summer provinces
text: The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly disrupted global mobility patterns, reshaping not only international travel but also domestic movements, particularly during peak vacation periods. Among these, summer vacations represent a critical phase, characterized by heightened population flows from metropolitan areas to less densely populated summer provinces, driven by the pursuit of leisure, cooler climates, and temporary relief from urban stressors. However, during the pandemic, such movements have introduced complex challenges for public health management, as metropolitan populations—often originating from regions with higher infection rates—migrated to areas with potentially limited healthcare infrastructure and lower prior exposure to the virus. This paper examines the interplay between summer vacation-related migration and COVID-19 transmission dynamics, focusing on the movement of people from major metropolitan centers to summer provinces in China. By analyzing mobility data, infection trends, and public health responses, we aim to elucidate how these seasonal shifts influenced pandemic trajectories and to provide insights for managing future health crises amid evolving travel behaviors.

title: Using Multiple Imputation to Classify Potential Outcomes Subgroups
text:
Classifying subgroups based on potential outcomes is essential in causal inference and personalized medicine, yet missing data often undermines the reliability of such classifications. This paper introduces a novel framework that leverages multiple imputation (MI) to enhance subgroup identification under missing covariate or outcome data. By generating multiple imputed datasets and applying a consistent classification algorithm across each, we aggregate results using Rubin’s rules to account for imputation uncertainty, yielding robust subgroup assignments. We demonstrate the method’s validity through simulations comparing it to complete-case analysis and single imputation, showing improved coverage and reduced bias in subgroup-specific effect estimates. An application to clinical trial data reveals clinically meaningful subgroups that would be obscured by conventional methods. The approach is particularly advantageous when missingness patterns differ across subgroups or when missing data are non-ignorable. We provide practical guidance for selecting MI parameters and integrating classification models, such as decision trees or cluster analysis, within the framework. This work bridges gaps between missing data techniques and subgroup analysis, offering a scalable solution for observational and experimental studies seeking to identify heterogeneous treatment effects or risk profiles.  
(Word count: 198)

title: The Snowball Earth transition in a climate model with drifting parameters
text:
The Snowball Earth hypothesis posits that during the Neoproterozoic era, between 720 and 635 million years ago, Earth experienced episodes of extreme glaciation where ice sheets extended to the equator, plunging the planet into a globally frozen state. These events, marked by abrupt transitions into and out of deep freeze conditions, represent some of the most dramatic climate shifts in Earth’s history. Understanding the mechanisms driving these transitions remains a critical challenge in paleoclimatology, as they provide insights into planetary habitability, ice-albedo feedback processes, and the stability of Earth’s climate system under extreme conditions. While previous studies have explored Snowball Earth dynamics using general circulation models (GCMs) with fixed parameters, these approaches often struggle to capture the full range of uncertainties inherent in ancient climate reconstructions. This paper introduces a novel framework by employing a climate model with drifting parameters—a method that allows key variables, such as atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, solar luminosity, and ice-sheet dynamics, to evolve stochastically within plausible bounds. By integrating parameter uncertainty directly into the modeling process, this approach offers a more robust representation of the complex interplay between forcing factors and feedback mechanisms during Snowball Earth episodes.  

Traditional GCMs typically rely on static parameter values derived from geological proxies or theoretical assumptions, which may oversimplify the chaotic nature of Earth’s climate system. For instance, uncertainties in Proterozoic CO₂ levels, estimated to range from 10 to 1,000 times pre-industrial values, can profoundly influence the onset and termination of glaciation. Similarly, variations in solar output or land-ice albedo thresholds introduce additional layers of complexity. The drifting-parameter methodology addresses these limitations by treating parameters as probabilistic variables, enabling the exploration of multiple climate trajectories under varying conditions. This study applies this approach to simulate the transition from a temperate climate to a Snowball state and subsequent deglaciation, focusing on the role of stochastic parameter interactions in triggering abrupt shifts. Preliminary results suggest that even minor fluctuations in CO₂ or albedo can destabilize the climate system, leading to bistable states—a finding with implications for both ancient climate reconstructions and modern projections of tipping points.  

By embracing parameter uncertainty, this research bridges a critical gap between deterministic modeling and the inherent variability of Earth’s climatic past. The drifting-parameter framework not only enhances the fidelity of Snowball Earth simulations but also provides a template for studying other periods of rapid climate change. Ultimately, this work underscores the importance of accounting for stochasticity in climate models, particularly when investigating systems poised near critical thresholds. The findings challenge conventional assumptions about the predictability of ancient climate transitions and highlight the need for probabilistic approaches in both paleoclimate studies and future climate projections.

title: Exploring the Endogenous Nature of Meme Stocks Using the Log-Periodic Power Law Model and Confidence Indicator
text:
The log-periodic power law (LPPL) model was applied to daily price data of GameStop (GME) and AMC Entertainment (AMC) from January 2020 to December 2022 to test for endogenous bubble dynamics. For GME, the model identified a critical time (\(t_c\)) of January 28, 2021 (\(\pm 2\) days), coinciding with its peak price of \$483.00, with estimated parameters \(\omega = 6.2 \pm 0.5\) (angular frequency), \(\beta = 0.78 \pm 0.09\) (power-law exponent), and \(\phi = 1.2 \pm 0.3\) (phase shift). The adjusted \(R^2\) was 0.92, indicating strong fit. Similarly, AMC exhibited a critical time (\(t_c\)) of June 2, 2021 (\(\pm 3\) days), peaking at \$72.62, with \(\omega = 5.8 \pm 0.6\), \(\beta = 0.65 \pm 0.11\), and \(\phi = 0.9 \pm 0.4\) (\(R^2 = 0.89\)). These parameters align with theoretical expectations for speculative bubbles (\(0 < \beta < 1\)), supporting endogenous growth driven by investor herding.  
The confidence indicator (CI), derived from social media sentiment and trading volume, correlated strongly with price acceleration in both stocks. For GME, CI reached 92/100 three days before \(t_c\), dropping to 35/100 post-crash. AMC’s CI peaked at 88/100 two days prior to \(t_c\), then declined to 40/100. Granger causality tests confirmed CI Granger-caused price changes (\(p < 0.01\)), while the reverse was insignificant (\(p > 0.1\)), reinforcing the predictive role of collective behavior.  
These findings suggest meme stock surges are primarily endogenous, fueled by self-reinforcing feedback loops between retail investor sentiment and price dynamics. The LPPL model’s accuracy in predicting crash timing (\(\pm 3\) days) underscores its utility for identifying speculative phases, while the CI provides a real-time metric for market exuberance. Limitations include potential exogenous shocks (e.g., regulatory changes) not captured in the model.

title: IAN: Combining Generative Adversarial Networks for Imaginative Face Generation
text: In conclusion, this paper introduces IAN, a novel framework that integrates multiple generative adversarial networks to achieve imaginative face generation with unprecedented realism and diversity. By leveraging a hierarchical architecture that combines coarse-to-fine generation strategies with dynamic style modulation, IAN demonstrates superior capability in synthesizing faces that transcend conventional datasets, capturing intricate attributes and creative variations. Experimental results on both qualitative and quantitative metrics confirm that IAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of visual fidelity, diversity, and user preference, while maintaining stability during training. Furthermore, the framework’s flexibility allows for easy adaptation to various generative tasks, opening avenues for future research in imaginative content creation. This work represents a significant step toward bridging the gap between realistic and imaginative synthesis, offering potential applications in entertainment, design, and beyond. Future directions include exploring more sophisticated style control mechanisms and expanding the framework to other domains of creative generation.

title: The impact of small changes in thoroughfare connectivity on the potential for student walking
text: This study investigates the impact of minor adjustments in thoroughfare connectivity on the likelihood of students walking to school, addressing a critical gap in understanding how urban design influences active transportation among youth. Using a mixed-methods approach, we analyze spatial data from 30 urban neighborhoods, incorporating measures of street network density, intersection complexity, and pedestrian infrastructure quality alongside survey responses from 1,200 students aged 10–18. A quasi-experimental design evaluates connectivity changes, such as adding crosswalks, shortening block lengths, or improving sidewalk continuity, within a 1-kilometer radius of schools. Results indicate that even modest enhancements in connectivity—like introducing one additional controlled crossing per block or reducing average block size by 10%—can increase the probability of students walking by 8–12%, with stronger effects in low-income areas. Qualitative findings highlight perceived safety and convenience as key mediators. The study contributes by demonstrating that targeted, small-scale interventions, rather than large-scale redevelopment, can effectively promote walking behavior. These insights support policymakers and urban planners in optimizing neighborhood designs to encourage healthier, more sustainable commuting habits among students, with implications for reducing traffic congestion and improving public health outcomes.

title: Economics of disagreement -- financial intuition for the Rényi divergence
text:
Disagreement is an intrinsic feature of human interaction, permeating fields as diverse as politics, social sciences, and economics. In economic and financial contexts, disagreement manifests itself through differing beliefs, expectations, and assessments of risk among market participants. These divergences are not merely academic curiosities; they have profound implications for asset pricing, market efficiency, and the dynamics of financial markets. Understanding the economic consequences of disagreement is thus crucial for both theoretical advancements and practical applications in finance.

This paper introduces a novel financial intuition for the Rényi divergence, a measure originating from information theory that generalizes the concept of relative entropy or Kullback-Leibler divergence. The Rényi divergence provides a flexible framework for quantifying the difference between two probability distributions, capturing not only the degree of disagreement but also the nuances in how disagreements manifest across different states of the world. By exploring the economic interpretations of the Rényi divergence, we aim to bridge the gap between information-theoretic concepts and financial economics, offering new insights into how disagreement influences market behavior and outcomes.

Our investigation is structured around the application of Rényi divergence to model disagreement among rational agents in financial markets. We demonstrate how this measure can elucidate phenomena such as speculative bubbles, trading volume, and the dispersion of beliefs, providing a unified theoretical foundation for understanding diverse market behaviors.

title: Differentiating the Value Function by using Convex Duality
text: This paper introduces a novel approach to differentiating the value function in stochastic optimization problems by leveraging convex duality theory. Traditional methods for computing gradients of value functions often rely on direct perturbation analysis or implicit function theorems, which can be computationally intensive or intractable in high-dimensional or non-smooth settings. We propose an alternative framework that reformulates the primal optimization problem using its convex dual, enabling gradient computation through the dual variables. By exploiting the strong duality property and smoothness conditions in the dual space, we derive explicit expressions for the gradient of the value function with respect to problem parameters, such as initial conditions or cost coefficients. This method circumvents the need for solving auxiliary optimization problems at each parameter value, offering significant computational advantages. We demonstrate the theoretical validity of the approach under standard convexity and regularity assumptions and provide convergence guarantees for the gradient estimates. Numerical experiments on portfolio optimization and inventory control problems illustrate the efficiency and accuracy of the dual-based differentiation method compared to finite-difference approximations and adjoint state techniques. The results suggest that convex duality provides a robust and scalable alternative for gradient-based optimization in dynamic decision-making models.

title: Generalised linear models for prognosis and intervention: Theory, practice, and implications for machine learning
text:
Generalised linear models (GLMs) have long served as a cornerstone of statistical inference, providing a flexible framework for modeling relationships between variables when the outcome follows a distribution from the exponential family. Unlike ordinary linear regression, GLMs accommodate non-normal response variables—such as binary, count, or proportional data—through a link function, enabling robust analysis of diverse datasets. Their interpretability, computational efficiency, and theoretical guarantees have cemented their role in fields ranging from epidemiology to economics, where understanding risk factors and predicting outcomes are critical. However, as data complexity grows and machine learning (ML) methods dominate predictive analytics, the relevance of GLMs is increasingly debated. Critics argue that their rigid assumptions and limited capacity to capture nonlinear interactions render them obsolete in the era of deep learning and ensemble methods. Yet, GLMs persist in practice due to their transparency, ease of implementation, and ability to quantify uncertainty—qualities often sacrificed by black-box ML models.  

This paper bridges the gap between traditional statistical modeling and modern ML by examining GLMs through three lenses: theoretical foundations, practical applications, and implications for interpretable machine learning. We revisit the mathematical underpinnings of GLMs, emphasizing their adaptability to varying data structures and their role in causal inference. Through case studies in healthcare and public policy, we demonstrate how GLMs remain indispensable for prognosis and intervention design, particularly when explainability and stakeholder trust are prioritized. Finally, we explore how GLMs inspire advancements in ML, such as regularized regression and generalized additive models, while highlighting scenarios where hybrid approaches—combining GLMs with neural networks or tree-based methods—outperform pure ML alternatives. By situating GLMs within the broader ML ecosystem, this work challenges the narrative of their obsolescence and advocates for their continued relevance in an era of data-driven decision-making.

title: No data? No problem! A Search-based Recommendation System with Cold Starts
text:
Our experiments evaluated the proposed search-based recommendation system (SBRS) against traditional collaborative filtering (CF) and content-based (CB) methods under cold-start conditions. Using a synthetic dataset of 10,000 users and 5,000 items (with 20% cold-start items), SBRS demonstrated a 32% improvement in precision@10 (0.68 vs. CF’s 0.51 and CB’s 0.54) and a 25% higher recall@10 (0.72 vs. 0.58 and 0.60, respectively). Notably, SBRS reduced the mean absolute error (MAE) for cold-start item ratings by 41% (MAE = 0.82) compared to CF (MAE = 1.39) and CB (MAE = 1.12), leveraging semantic embeddings from item descriptions to infer preferences.  

Ablation studies revealed that hybrid scoring (combining search relevance and user-item affinity) contributed 58% of the precision gain, while dynamic query expansion accounted for 31%. For instance, when 10% of user history was withheld, SBRS maintained 92% of its baseline performance, whereas CF and CB dropped to 67% and 74%, respectively. Statistical significance (p < 0.01) was confirmed via t-tests on 10-fold cross-validation.  

Qualitative analysis showed SBRS effectively handled niche items (e.g., “vegan keto recipes”) by matching latent semantic patterns in queries, whereas CF struggled with sparse interaction data. However, SBRS’s reliance on text quality introduced occasional mismatches (e.g., “sci-fi” confused with “scientific journals”), highlighting a trade-off between coverage and interpretability. These results underscore SBRS’s robustness in cold-start scenarios, though challenges remain in balancing semantic richness with computational efficiency.

title: Multi-layered Network Structure: Relationship Between Financial and Macroeconomic Dynamics
text: In conclusion, this study illuminates the intricate, multi-layered interdependencies between financial and macroeconomic dynamics, revealing a complex web of interactions that transcend traditional sectoral boundaries. Our findings demonstrate that financial networks exhibit distinct structural properties—such as scale-free topology and modular organization—that amplify both resilience and systemic risk, depending on the nature of external shocks. Macroeconomic variables, including interest rates and inflation, act as pivotal nodes within this structure, shaping the propagation of financial stress across sectors. Conversely, financial innovations and liquidity fluctuations significantly influence macroeconomic stability, highlighting bidirectional causality. These insights underscore the necessity of adopting a holistic, network-based approach to policymaking, where regulatory frameworks account for cross-sectoral linkages and systemic vulnerabilities. Future research should explore the role of technological advancements and geopolitical shifts in reshaping these networks, ensuring that models remain adaptive to evolving global dynamics. Ultimately, this work reinforces the imperative for interdisciplinary collaboration to safeguard economic resilience in an interconnected world.

title: Stuttering Speech Disfluency Prediction using Explainable Attribution Vectors of Facial Muscle Movements
text:
This paper introduces a novel framework for stuttering speech disfluency prediction by leveraging explainable attribution vectors derived from facial muscle movements. Stuttering, a complex speech disorder characterized by involuntary disruptions in fluency, is often accompanied by distinct facial muscle activations that precede or coincide with disfluent events. Traditional prediction models rely heavily on acoustic features, overlooking the rich nonverbal cues embedded in facial dynamics. To address this gap, we propose a multimodal approach that integrates facial movement analysis with machine learning to enhance prediction accuracy while maintaining interpretability.  
Our method begins with high-resolution facial landmark tracking to capture subtle muscle movements, followed by the generation of spatiotemporal attribution vectors using gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM). These vectors quantify the contribution of specific facial regions (e.g., jaw, eyebrows, lips) to disfluency predictions, providing clinically meaningful explanations for model decisions. A hybrid deep learning architecture, combining convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for spatial feature extraction and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks for temporal modeling, is employed to classify speech segments as fluent or disfluent.  
Experimental results on a dataset of 50 individuals with persistent stuttering demonstrate that incorporating facial attribution vectors improves prediction accuracy by 12.7% compared to acoustic-only models, achieving an F1-score of 0.89. Furthermore, the explainable vectors reveal that exaggerated lip tightening and eyebrow raises are strongly predictive of block-type disfluencies, while asymmetric jaw movements correlate with prolongations. Clinicians can utilize these insights to design targeted behavioral interventions. By bridging computational rigor with clinical interpretability, this work advances the development of transparent, patient-centered assistive technologies for stuttering management, offering a promising pathway toward personalized therapy and real-time disfluency monitoring.

title: Neural document expansion for ad-hoc information retrieval
text:
Ad-hoc information retrieval (IR) systems play a pivotal role in enabling users to efficiently locate relevant information within large document collections. Traditional IR models primarily rely on exact keyword matching between a user’s query and the content of documents, often facing challenges in capturing semantic nuances and contextual relevance. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced when dealing with short or ambiguous queries, where the lack of contextual information hinders the retrieval of truly pertinent documents. To address this gap, document expansion techniques have emerged as a promising approach to enrich document representations by incorporating additional terms or phrases that are likely to match user intent. 

Recent advancements in neural networks, particularly in natural language processing (NLP), have provided powerful tools for learning latent semantic representations of text. Neural document expansion leverages these advancements to generate supplementary content that enhances the original document’s visibility to retrieval systems. By utilizing deep learning models such as transformers, these methods can capture complex linguistic patterns and generate contextually coherent expansions, thereby improving the alignment between queries and documents. 

Despite the potential of neural document expansion, existing research has primarily focused on generic retrieval scenarios, with limited exploration of its effectiveness in ad-hoc IR settings. This paper aims to bridge this gap by proposing a novel neural document expansion framework tailored for ad-hoc retrieval tasks. Our approach integrates contextualized embeddings and attention mechanisms to dynamically generate expansions that are both semantically relevant and query-aware. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our method significantly enhances retrieval performance, particularly for short and ambiguous queries, thereby advancing the state-of-the-art in ad-hoc IR.

title: Can Insider Trading Be Committed Without Trading?
text: The traditional legal framework defines insider trading as the illicit trading of securities based on material nonpublic information (MNPI). However, emerging financial practices and technological advancements challenge this conventional understanding, prompting a reevaluation of whether insider trading can occur absent actual securities transactions. This paper examines the concept of "non-trading insider misconduct," analyzing scenarios where individuals misuse MNPI to influence market behavior, manipulate perceptions, or extract economic advantages without directly buying or selling securities. Through case studies of pre-announcement market signaling, strategic information leaks, and derivative-based strategies that decouple trading from traditional equity positions, the study reveals gaps in existing regulatory paradigms. The analysis integrates legal, economic, and ethical perspectives to argue that non-trading actions exploiting MNPI may inflict comparable harm to classical insider trading, undermining market integrity and investor trust. The paper concludes by proposing a redefinition of insider trading liability to encompass non-transactional misconduct, advocating for regulatory updates that address modern financial complexities and ensure equitable enforcement across global markets.

title: Learning Opinion Dynamics From Social Traces
text:
The proliferation of digital social platforms has transformed how individuals express opinions, interact with peers, and shape collective beliefs. From Twitter threads to Reddit discussions, these platforms generate vast, time-stamped datasets—termed *social traces*—that capture the evolution of public sentiment in unprecedented detail. Unlike traditional surveys or controlled experiments, social traces reflect spontaneous, real-world interactions, offering a unique lens to study opinion dynamics at scale. However, extracting meaningful patterns from this deluge of data remains challenging due to its high dimensionality, noise, and the interplay of latent factors such as social influence, cognitive biases, and external events.  

Opinion dynamics, a multidisciplinary field spanning sociology, physics, and computer science, seeks to model how individual attitudes emerge, propagate, and converge within networks. Classical approaches, such as the voter model or bounded confidence theory, rely on simplified assumptions about human behavior and homogeneous interactions. Yet real-world opinions are shaped by complex, heterogeneous processes, including echo chambers, viral memes, and counter-narratives. This gap highlights the need for data-driven methods that leverage social traces to uncover nuanced mechanisms of opinion change.  

This paper introduces a computational framework to infer opinion dynamics directly from observable social traces, bypassing the need for explicit surveys or synthetic assumptions. By integrating techniques from network science, natural language processing, and temporal point processes, we analyze how linguistic cues, interaction patterns, and structural network properties collectively influence opinion trajectories. Our approach not only advances theoretical understanding but also provides actionable insights for applications like misinformation mitigation, public health communication, and social movement analysis.

title: A deep network approach to multitemporal cloud detection
text:
The proposed deep network model for multitemporal cloud detection was evaluated on a test dataset comprising 5,000 multitemporal image patches (each 256 × 256 pixels) spanning 12 months across three distinct climatic zones. The model achieved an overall accuracy of 92.3%, with a precision of 91.5% and recall of 90.8% for cloud detection, significantly outperforming the baseline single-image U-Net (84.7% accuracy, p < 0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). Temporal consistency analysis revealed that incorporating multitemporal data reduced false positives by 18.2% compared to single-date predictions, particularly in regions with persistent cloud cover (e.g., tropical zones). 

Quantitative results demonstrated robust performance across seasons: accuracy remained above 90% in both dry (91.8%) and wet seasons (90.1%), with a slight dip (88.5%) during transitional periods due to rapid atmospheric changes. The model’s attention mechanism highlighted temporal features most critical for discrimination, such as cloud motion vectors and diurnal temperature variations, with 82% of attention weights focusing on temporal differences in adjacent time steps. 

Error analysis identified challenges in detecting optically thin cirrus clouds (recall: 78.4%), which exhibited minimal spectral and temporal contrast. However, combining thermal infrared bands with visible-near infrared data improved thin-cloud detection by 12.6%. Ablation studies confirmed that the 3D convolutional layers capturing spatiotemporal dependencies contributed 7.3% to the overall accuracy gain. These findings underscore the value of leveraging temporal context for cloud masking, particularly in dynamic environments, while highlighting avenues for improving thin-cloud detection through hybrid spectral-temporal feature fusion.

title: Constraints in Random Effects Age-Period-Cohort Models
text: In conclusion, this paper has systematically explored the critical role of constraints in random effects age-period-cohort (APC) models, addressing both theoretical and practical challenges inherent in disentangling the intertwined effects of age, period, and cohort. We demonstrated that constraints are not merely technical adjustments but are foundational to model identifiability, ensuring that estimates reflect meaningful temporal patterns rather than arbitrary parameterizations. Through simulations and empirical analyses, we illustrated how poorly chosen constraints can distort inference, while well-specified constraints—whether through linear restrictions, nonparametric priors, or hierarchical structures—can enhance both the robustness and interpretability of APC models. Our findings underscore the importance of aligning constraints with substantive knowledge or empirical evidence, particularly when dealing with complex, multidimensional data. Future research should focus on developing adaptive constraint frameworks that leverage external information or data-driven methods to select optimal restrictions, thereby reducing reliance on arbitrary assumptions. Additionally, extending these approaches to non-Gaussian outcomes and dynamic APC models could further broaden their applicability. Ultimately, a nuanced understanding of constraints is essential for advancing APC methodology, enabling researchers to draw more reliable insights from temporal data across diverse fields, from epidemiology to social science.

title: Twin Estimates of the Effects of Prenatal Environment, Child Biology, and Parental Bias on Sex Differences in Early Age Mortality
text: This study employs twin data to disentangle the effects of prenatal environment, child biology, and parental bias on sex differences in early-age mortality. Utilizing a co-twin control design, we analyze mortality patterns among male-female twin pairs, comparing outcomes within monozygotic (MZ) and dizygotic (DZ) twins to isolate genetic and environmental influences. Our findings reveal that male infants face higher mortality risks than females, driven primarily by biological vulnerabilities rather than differential parental investment. While prenatal conditions and shared environmental factors contribute to mortality disparities, parental behaviors show minimal sex-based bias in early life. Notably, the male excess mortality is more pronounced in MZ twins, suggesting a stronger biological component. These results challenge assumptions about parental discrimination as a primary driver of sex differentials in early survival, highlighting the need for interventions targeting biological and prenatal determinants to reduce early-life sex disparities.

title: Towards Smart Sustainable Cities: Addressing semantic heterogeneity in building management systems using discriminative models
text: The rapid global trend of urbanization has underscored the imperative for smart sustainable cities, where building management systems (BMS) play a pivotal role in optimizing energy efficiency, enhancing occupant comfort, and reducing environmental impact. However, the integration of diverse BMS components, often developed by different vendors using proprietary protocols and data formats, introduces significant challenges in achieving seamless interoperability and holistic system optimization. Semantic heterogeneity—the discrepancy in meaning and interpretation of data across various subsystems—emerges as a critical barrier to effective data integration and intelligent decision-making within BMS. Addressing this issue requires innovative approaches that can reconcile diverse semantic representations while preserving the integrity and contextual relevance of the data. Discriminative models, known for their proficiency in pattern recognition and classification tasks, offer promising solutions to detect and resolve semantic inconsistencies. This paper explores the application of discriminative models to mitigate semantic heterogeneity in BMS, thereby facilitating the development of smart sustainable cities that are both efficient and resilient.

title: The Mechanism of the Origin and Development of Lightning from Initiating Event to Initial Breakdown Pulses (v.2)
text: This study explores the intricate mechanism underlying the origin and development of lightning, focusing on the transition from initiating events to initial breakdown pulses (IBPs). By integrating high-speed imaging, radio-frequency measurements, and three-dimensional electric field modeling, we analyze the role of cosmic ray-induced ionization, hydrometeor collisions, and corona discharge in triggering electrical activity within thunderstorms. Our findings reveal that IBPs emerge from localized charge separation processes, driven by turbulent airflow and particle interactions, which generate precursor ionization channels. These channels facilitate the propagation of stepped leaders, with IBPs serving as early markers of charge imbalance resolution. The research also highlights the influence of cloud microphysics and environmental electric fields on IBP morphology and timing. By advancing the understanding of these early-stage dynamics, this work provides critical insights into lightning initiation, offering implications for improved forecasting models and hazard mitigation strategies.

title: Key Borrowers Detection by Long-Range Interactions
text:
Our experiments evaluated the proposed LRI-Net model against baseline methods—Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), and a Graph Neural Network (GNN) without long-range interactions—across three key metrics: precision, recall, and F1-score. On a dataset of 50,000 borrowers (10% labeled as key borrowers), LRI-Net achieved a precision of 92.3%, recall of 89.7%, and F1-score of 91.0%, outperforming LR (78.5%, 72.1%, 75.2%), RF (84.1%, 80.3%, 82.1%), and the baseline GNN (88.9%, 85.2%, 87.0%). Notably, LRI-Net’s recall improved by 5.3% over the GNN baseline, indicating its superior ability to identify true key borrowers missed by shorter-range models.  
Ablation studies revealed that removing long-range attention reduced F1-score by 6.8%, confirming the critical role of distant transactional interactions. For instance, in a case study of a mid-sized manufacturing firm, LRI-Net flagged it as a key borrower due to sparse but high-value transactions with geographically distant suppliers—a pattern invisible to shorter-range models. However, LRI-Net’s precision dipped slightly (2.1%) in sectors with homogeneous transaction patterns (e.g., retail), suggesting room for sector-specific tuning.  
Statistical significance was validated via paired t-tests (p < 0.01), and runtime analysis showed LRI-Net processed 1,000 borrowers in 12.4 seconds, comparable to the GNN baseline. These results underscore LRI-Net’s efficacy in leveraging long-range dependencies for accurate key borrower detection.

title: GARCH(1,1) model of the financial market with the Minkowski metric
text: The integration of the Minkowski metric into the GARCH(1,1) framework offers a compelling alternative to traditional Euclidean-based volatility modeling, addressing limitations in capturing asymmetric and non-linear dependencies inherent in financial time series. By extending the conditional variance equation to incorporate a generalized distance metric, this study demonstrates that the Minkowski-GARCH(1,1) model enhances volatility forecasting accuracy, particularly during periods of market stress, as evidenced by lower RMSE and MAE values compared to the standard GARCH(1,1) and GJR-GARCH benchmarks. The parameter \( p \) in the Minkowski metric emerges as a critical tuning mechanism, allowing the model to adapt to varying degrees of asymmetry in return distributions, with empirical results favoring values between 1.5 and 2.0 for major equity indices. These findings underscore the potential of geometric generalizations in econometric modeling, challenging the dominance of Euclidean assumptions in risk management practices.
