Future research could explore the Minkowski metric’s applicability to multivariate GARCH frameworks or high-frequency data, where non-linear effects may be more pronounced. Ultimately, this study contributes to a growing literature on metric-space approaches to financial volatility, advocating for greater flexibility in modeling assumptions to better reflect the complex dynamics of modern markets.

title: Evaluating Semantic Interaction on Word Embeddings via Simulation
text: This paper introduces a novel simulation-based framework for evaluating semantic interactions in word embeddings, addressing the challenge of quantifying how embeddings capture nuanced linguistic relationships. Unlike traditional evaluation methods relying on static benchmarks, our approach dynamically simulates semantic interactions by generating controlled perturbations in word contexts and measuring corresponding embedding shifts. We design a series of experiments that manipulate lexical relationships (e.g., synonymy, antonymy, and hypernymy) and contextual variations to observe how embeddings adapt. By comparing pre- and post-perturbation embeddings using cosine similarity and clustering analysis, we assess their sensitivity to semantic changes. Results demonstrate that popular models like GloVe and BERT exhibit varying degrees of robustness in capturing direct semantic interactions but struggle with complex, context-dependent relationships. Our framework provides a scalable, interpretable method for diagnosing embedding limitations and guiding improvements, offering insights into how word representations encode meaning dynamically across different linguistic scenarios.

title: Learning-based Prediction and Uplink Retransmission for Wireless Virtual Reality (VR) Network
text:
The rapid proliferation of wireless virtual reality (VR) applications has introduced unprecedented demands for ultra-low latency and high-reliability communication in next-generation wireless networks. Wireless VR systems require seamless real-time interaction between users and virtual environments, where even millisecond-level delays or packet losses can significantly degrade user experience by causing motion sickness or visual artifacts. To meet these stringent requirements, traditional communication protocols relying solely on reactive retransmission mechanisms face inherent limitations, as they struggle to proactively mitigate transmission failures under dynamic wireless channel conditions. This challenge becomes more pronounced in crowded scenarios with limited bandwidth resources, where frequent retransmissions exacerbate network congestion and increase end-to-end latency.

Recent advancements in machine learning (ML) have opened new avenues for optimizing wireless network performance through data-driven predictive modeling. By leveraging historical transmission patterns, channel state information, and user mobility trajectories, ML algorithms can proactively identify potential transmission failures before they occur, enabling preemptive resource allocation and intelligent retransmission strategies. Such predictive approaches not only reduce latency but also enhance spectral efficiency by minimizing unnecessary retransmissions. However, existing studies predominantly focus on isolated aspects of VR traffic prediction or retransmission optimization, overlooking the interdependence between these two critical components. A holistic framework that integrates learning-based prediction with adaptive retransmission mechanisms remains underexplored, particularly in the context of wireless VR networks characterized by highly correlated spatiotemporal traffic patterns.

This paper proposes a novel learning-based prediction and uplink retransmission framework tailored for wireless VR networks, aiming to achieve a fundamental trade-off between latency and reliability. By combining deep reinforcement learning with edge computing, our approach dynamically predicts VR frame transmission failures and adjusts retransmission parameters in real time, ensuring robust performance under varying network conditions.

title: Economics of carbon-dioxide abatement under an exogenous constraint on cumulative emissions
text: This paper examines the economic implications of achieving carbon-dioxide (CO₂) abatement under an exogenous constraint on cumulative emissions, a framework increasingly relevant for global climate policy aiming to limit temperature rise. We integrate an intertemporal optimization model with a cumulative emissions cap to analyze the optimal allocation of abatement efforts across time and sectors, accounting for technological progress, abatement costs, and economic growth. Our findings demonstrate that an exogenous cumulative cap induces a "front-loading" of abatement investments compared to scenarios without such a constraint, driven by the urgency of staying within the carbon budget. The model highlights trade-offs between short-term economic costs and long-term climate benefits, emphasizing the role of innovation in lowering abatement costs over time. We also explore the distributional impacts across sectors and regions, showing that early-moving industries and regions with low-cost abatement options benefit most. These results provide insights for policymakers designing carbon budgets and abatement strategies to balance economic efficiency with climate goals.

title: Human brain activity for machine attention
text:
The human brain operates as a dynamic network of neural processes, continuously filtering and prioritizing sensory information to guide behavior. This selective attention—the ability to focus on specific stimuli while suppressing irrelevant distractions—has long been a cornerstone of cognitive neuroscience. However, as artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly interact with humans in real-world environments, from autonomous vehicles to healthcare assistants, the need to align machine perception with human attentional priorities has become critical. Traditional AI models, particularly those relying on deep learning, often process data in ways that diverge from human cognitive mechanisms, leading to mismatches in how machines interpret and respond to complex scenes. Bridging this gap requires a deeper understanding of the neural signatures underlying human attention and their translation into computational frameworks.  

Recent advances in neuroimaging and machine learning have opened new avenues for decoding brain activity patterns associated with attentional selection. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalography (EEG) studies have revealed that attention modulates neural responses in visual, parietal, and frontal cortices, reflecting both bottom-up salience and top-down goals. Yet, translating these biological insights into machine attention models remains challenging due to differences in temporal resolution, spatial specificity, and the abstract nature of neural coding. Moreover, most AI systems prioritize efficiency over biological plausibility, often sacrificing interpretability for performance.  

This research explores the intersection of human neuroscience and machine attention by investigating whether neural activity patterns can directly inform the design of attention mechanisms in AI. By leveraging high-density EEG recordings and deep learning techniques, we aim to decode the temporal dynamics of attentional allocation in humans and map these processes to computational attention models. Our approach seeks to answer a fundamental question: Can machine attention systems achieve human-like prioritization by emulating the neural mechanisms that govern selective perception? The implications extend beyond theoretical neuroscience, offering pathways to enhance AI safety, human-AI collaboration, and neuroprosthetic technologies that align with natural cognitive processes.

title: The Life and Death of SSDs and HDDs: Similarities, Differences, and Prediction Models
text:
Our analysis of 5,000 SSDs and HDDs revealed distinct failure patterns and lifespans. SSDs exhibited a mean time to failure (MTTF) of 4.8 years (95% CI: 4.5–5.1), with 68% failing due to write cycle exhaustion (median write cycles: 2,300) and 22% from controller malfunctions. HDDs showed a longer MTTF of 6.2 years (95% CI: 5.9–6.5), but 54% failed due to mechanical issues (e.g., motor/head failure), while 31% resulted from logical errors. Temperature significantly impacted both: SSDs operating above 50°C had a 32% higher failure rate (HR = 1.32, *p* < 0.01), whereas HDDs above 45°C showed a 19% increase (HR = 1.19, *p* = 0.02).  

Usage intensity also diverged: SSDs in high-write environments (≥50GB/day) failed 2.1 years faster than low-usage counterparts (*p* < 0.001), while HDDs in similar conditions degraded 1.7 years sooner (*p* = 0.003). Survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards) confirmed that workload type (sequential vs. random) had a stronger effect on SSDs (HR = 1.45) than HDDs (HR = 1.12).  

Our predictive models demonstrated high accuracy: a random forest classifier for SSDs achieved 89% precision (AUC = 0.92) using write cycles, temperature, and workload as features, while HDDs’ logistic regression model reached 84% precision (AUC = 0.87) with spindle speed and power-on hours. These results underscore that while SSDs are more vulnerable to write-related wear, HDDs remain susceptible to mechanical stress. Both benefit from temperature control, but SSDs demand stricter workload management. Future work will explore emerging technologies like HAMR HDDs and QLC SSDs to refine longevity forecasts.

title: Quantifying Volatility Reduction in German Day-ahead Spot Market in the Period 2006 through 2016
text: This study provides a comprehensive analysis of volatility reduction in the German day-ahead spot market from 2006 to 2016, utilizing a range of econometric models and robustness checks. Our findings indicate a significant decline in price volatility over the observed period, driven primarily by increased renewable energy integration, regulatory reforms, and enhanced market liquidity. The transition to a more decentralized energy system, coupled with the introduction of market coupling mechanisms, has contributed to greater price stability by reducing dependency on conventional fossil fuels and mitigating supply-side uncertainties. These results underscore the effectiveness of policy interventions aimed at fostering competitive and sustainable electricity markets. However, the persistent influence of external factors, such as geopolitical tensions and fuel price fluctuations, highlights the need for continued monitoring and adaptive regulatory frameworks. Future research should explore the impact of emerging technologies, such as energy storage and demand response, on long-term volatility trends, ensuring the resilience of the German energy market in an evolving global context.

title: Loss Rate Forecasting Framework Based on Macroeconomic Changes: Application to US Credit Card Industry
text: This study introduces a comprehensive Loss Rate Forecasting Framework designed to enhance predictive accuracy in dynamic macroeconomic environments, with a specific focus on the US credit card industry. Traditional loss forecasting models often rely on historical default data and static risk metrics, which can lead to significant forecasting errors during periods of economic volatility. To address this limitation, our framework integrates real-time macroeconomic indicators—such as GDP growth, unemployment rates, inflation, and consumer confidence indices—into a machine learning-driven predictive model. By leveraging advanced feature engineering techniques, including lagged variables and interaction terms, the model captures the nonlinear relationships between macroeconomic shifts and credit card loss rates. We employ a hybrid approach that combines gradient boosting machines (GBM) for initial feature selection and a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network to model temporal dependencies, ensuring robustness against overfitting and improving generalization across economic cycles. Empirical validation using quarterly data from 2000 to 2023 demonstrates that the proposed framework outperforms conventional methods, reducing mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) by 18–25% in out-of-sample tests. Notably, the model accurately anticipated elevated loss rates during the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting its utility for proactive risk management. The framework’s modular design allows for easy adaptation to other lending sectors or geographic markets by incorporating relevant macroeconomic variables. These findings provide actionable insights for financial institutions seeking to align credit risk strategies with macroeconomic trends, ultimately enhancing portfolio resilience and regulatory compliance.

title: A Nonparametric Bayesian Item Response Modeling Approach for Clustering Items and Individuals Simultaneously
text: Item response theory (IRT) models have become a cornerstone in educational and psychological measurement, providing a robust framework for analyzing the relationship between latent traits and observed responses. Traditional IRT approaches typically focus on estimating individual ability parameters or item characteristics independently, often overlooking the inherent structure within both items and respondents. Recent advancements have highlighted the potential of clustering methods to uncover latent groupings among items and individuals, enhancing interpretability and enabling more nuanced insights into data. However, existing parametric models impose strict distributional assumptions, which may not hold in real-world scenarios, limiting their flexibility and applicability. To address these limitations, we propose a nonparametric Bayesian IRT modeling approach that simultaneously clusters items and individuals without relying on predefined distributional forms. This innovative framework leverages the strengths of Bayesian nonparametrics to capture complex data structures, offering a more adaptive and comprehensive solution for educational and psychological assessments.

title: What Factors Drive Individual Misperceptions of the Returns to Schooling in Tanzania? Some Lessons for Education Policy
text: This paper examines the factors contributing to individual misperceptions of the returns to schooling in Tanzania, a context where educational investments are critical for economic development yet often hindered by inaccurate beliefs about potential earnings. Using nationally representative household survey data combined with a novel survey module measuring subjective expectations of returns to education, we explore the extent and sources of misperceptions among youth and adults. We find significant discrepancies between perceived and actual returns, with many individuals underestimating the financial benefits of additional schooling, particularly at higher education levels. Key drivers of these misperceptions include limited access to reliable information, socio-cultural norms, and regional disparities in labor market outcomes. Additionally, we identify differences by gender, with young women more likely to underestimate returns due to entrenched gender biases and occupational stereotypes. Our analysis underscores the importance of targeted information campaigns and policy interventions that address information gaps and challenge social norms, providing actionable insights for education policymakers aiming to encourage greater educational attainment and reduce inequality in Tanzania.

title: Considerations for Eye Tracking Experiments in Information Retrieval
text:
Eye tracking technology has emerged as a pivotal tool in information retrieval (IR) research, offering granular insights into user interactions with search interfaces, documents, and query formulations. By capturing gaze patterns, fixations, and saccades, researchers can infer cognitive processes such as attention allocation, comprehension, and decision-making during search tasks. These metrics provide a window into user behavior beyond traditional performance indicators like click-through rates or query reformulations, enabling a deeper understanding of how users process and evaluate information. However, the integration of eye tracking into IR experiments introduces unique methodological and practical challenges, ranging from hardware limitations to participant variability and data interpretation complexities. Addressing these considerations is critical to ensuring the validity, reliability, and generalizability of findings in this rapidly evolving field.  

The adoption of eye tracking in IR has been driven by its ability to quantify visual attention, a key component of user engagement. For instance, fixation durations and heatmaps reveal which elements of a search results page—such as snippets, titles, or advertisements—attract the most focus, while scanpaths illustrate how users navigate between results. Such data can inform the design of more intuitive interfaces, optimize content placement, and identify usability bottlenecks. Yet, the technology’s sensitivity to environmental factors—such as lighting, screen resolution, or participant head movements—poses significant experimental control challenges. Additionally, individual differences in reading speed, cognitive load, and familiarity with search systems can introduce noise, complicating cross-study comparisons.  

This paper systematically explores the methodological, technical, and ethical considerations essential for conducting rigorous eye tracking experiments in IR. We discuss the selection of appropriate eye tracking hardware and software, calibration protocols, and task design to balance ecological validity with experimental precision. We also address data preprocessing challenges, such as artifact removal and the integration of gaze data with traditional IR metrics. Finally, we examine ethical concerns, including participant privacy and informed consent, particularly when analyzing sensitive search behaviors. By synthesizing best practices and emerging trends, this work aims to equip researchers with practical guidelines to enhance the robustness and impact of eye tracking studies in IR.

title: Markovian And Non-Markovian Processes with Active Decision Making Strategies For Addressing The COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Our simulations revealed distinct outcomes for Markovian and non-Markovian models under active decision-making strategies. In the Markovian framework, a reactive strategy (e.g., lockdowns triggered by threshold infection rates) reduced peak daily infections by 42% (from 12,500 to 7,250 cases) but extended the epidemic duration by 30 days compared to passive mitigation. Conversely, a proactive strategy (e.g., preemptive lockdowns based on predictive modeling) lowered peak infections by 58% (to 5,200 cases) and shortened the epidemic by 15 days, though it incurred a 20% higher economic cost due to prolonged restrictions.  
Non-Markovian models, incorporating memory effects (e.g., delayed compliance with social distancing), showed slower initial infection spread but higher long-term variability. Under reactive policies, peak infections decreased by only 28% (to 8,900 cases), with a 25% increase in hospitalization rates due to delayed interventions. Proactive strategies in this context reduced peak infections by 45% (to 6,875 cases) but required 35% stricter enforcement to counteract behavioral lag.  
Comparatively, non-Markovian systems under active decision-making exhibited 18% greater sensitivity to policy timing than Markovian counterparts, emphasizing the role of human behavior in shaping outcomes. Economic costs across both models correlated strongly with restriction duration (r = 0.89), while healthcare burden inversely related to intervention speed (r = -0.92). These findings underscore the trade-offs between epidemiological efficacy and socioeconomic impact, highlighting non-Markovian dynamics as critical for modeling real-world policy scenarios where human behavior introduces delays and feedback loops.

title: Gamification of Enterprise Systems: A Synthesis of Mechanics, Dynamics, and Risks
text: In conclusion, the gamification of enterprise systems represents a transformative approach to enhancing user engagement, motivation, and performance within organizational contexts. By integrating carefully designed mechanics—such as points, badges, and leaderboards—and leveraging dynamics like feedback loops and social interaction, organizations can create more immersive and rewarding experiences that align with strategic objectives. However, the successful implementation of gamification requires a nuanced understanding of both its potential and its risks. Overemphasis on competition, misalignment with organizational culture, and ethical concerns related to data privacy and manipulation can undermine its effectiveness. Future research should focus on developing robust frameworks for evaluating gamification’s long-term impact, exploring adaptive designs that cater to diverse user needs, and addressing ethical considerations through transparent, user-centric approaches. As enterprises continue to navigate digital transformation, gamification offers a promising yet complex tool whose value hinges on thoughtful design, continuous evaluation, and alignment with broader organizational goals.

title: Adaptive Precision Training for Resource Constrained Devices
text: This paper introduces Adaptive Precision Training (APT), a novel framework designed to optimize deep learning model training for resource-constrained devices, such as edge computing platforms and mobile devices. Traditional deep learning models often demand significant computational resources, making deployment on low-power devices challenging. APT addresses this issue by dynamically adjusting the numerical precision of model parameters and activations during training, enabling efficient resource utilization without substantial sacrifices in model accuracy. The core innovation of APT lies in its adaptive precision selection mechanism, which evaluates the impact of different precision levels on gradient propagation and model convergence in real-time. By leveraging a lightweight precision controller, APT can allocate varying bit-widths to different layers or operations based on their sensitivity to quantization errors. This layer-wise adaptive precision strategy ensures that critical components of the model maintain higher precision to preserve accuracy, while less sensitive components operate at lower precision to reduce computational overhead and memory footprint. Furthermore, APT incorporates a progressive precision refinement technique that gradually increases precision during the later stages of training to fine-tune the model for optimal performance. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that APT achieves comparable accuracy to full-precision training while significantly reducing energy consumption and training time. For instance, on a Raspberry Pi 4, APT reduces energy usage by up to 60% and speeds up training by 40% compared to conventional quantization methods, with minimal accuracy loss. These findings highlight the potential of APT to enable efficient on-device training, facilitating the deployment of advanced deep learning models in resource-limited environments.

title: Urban volumetrics: spatial complexity and wayfinding, extending space syntax to three dimensional space
text:
The built environment of contemporary cities has evolved into increasingly complex three-dimensional (3D) spatial configurations, driven by rapid urbanization, vertical expansion, and the integration of multi-layered transportation networks. Traditional methods of analyzing urban form, such as space syntax, have primarily focused on two-dimensional (2D) planar relationships, offering valuable insights into pedestrian movement, accessibility, and social interaction within street networks. However, the growing prevalence of elevated walkways, underground corridors, mixed-use developments, and sky bridges in modern cities necessitates a shift toward 3D spatial analysis to better understand how vertical dimensions influence human navigation and spatial behavior.  
Urban volumetrics, as an emerging interdisciplinary framework, seeks to extend space syntax theory into 3D space by incorporating vertical stratification, volumetric connectivity, and multi-level visibility. This approach addresses a critical gap in existing research: while 2D space syntax effectively explains horizontal movement patterns, it fails to account for the vertical displacements and layered interactions that characterize contemporary urban environments. For instance, the presence of atriums, mezzanines, and vertical circulation systems (e.g., stairs, escalators, elevators) introduces new challenges for wayfinding, particularly in dense urban settings where spatial hierarchy and visual guidance are disrupted by fragmented 3D layouts.  
This paper argues that integrating volumetric analysis into space syntax can enhance our understanding of spatial complexity and its impact on navigation efficiency, cognitive mapping, and social cohesion. By examining case studies of mixed-use developments and transit-oriented districts, we demonstrate how 3D spatial metrics—such as volumetric integration, depth, and visual permeability—provide a more nuanced assessment of urban form compared to conventional 2D measures. Ultimately, this research contributes to a paradigm shift in urban design and planning, advocating for 3D-aware strategies to improve wayfinding, reduce disorientation, and foster inclusive, legible urban spaces.

title: Relative utility bounds for empirically optimal portfolios
text: This paper establishes theoretical bounds on the relative utility of empirically optimal portfolios compared to their theoretically optimal counterparts, addressing a critical gap in portfolio optimization literature. While classical mean-variance frameworks assume perfect knowledge of asset return distributions, practical implementations rely on finite historical data, leading to estimation errors that degrade out-of-sample performance. We derive explicit upper and lower bounds for the expected utility loss incurred when using sample-based optimal portfolios, quantified in terms of data size, dimensionality, and risk preferences. Our analysis leverages concentration inequalities and high-dimensional statistics to characterize the worst-case divergence between empirical and true optimal portfolios under general utility functions. The results reveal that utility losses decay polynomially with sample size but may deterioriate exponentially in asset dimension, highlighting fundamental limits to data-driven optimization in high-dimensional settings. We further propose corrected estimators that asymptotically achieve the theoretical utility bound under mild regularity conditions. Numerical simulations with synthetic and empirical financial data validate the tightness of our bounds and demonstrate their practical relevance for asset allocation strategies. These findings provide rigorous guidelines for balancing model complexity and data requirements in portfolio construction, with implications for both academic research and industry practice.

title: A general solution to the preferential selection model
text:
The preferential selection model, a cornerstone of network science, evolutionary biology, and social dynamics, describes systems where entities (e.g., nodes, species, or individuals) are chosen with probability proportional to their intrinsic fitness or accumulated advantage. First formalized by Herbert Simon in 1955 and later popularized by Price’s cumulative advantage theory and Barabási-Albert’s scale-free networks, this framework explains phenomena as diverse as citation networks, wealth inequality, and protein interaction networks. Despite its broad applicability, existing solutions to the preferential selection model often rely on domain-specific assumptions or approximations, limiting their generality. For instance, discrete-time formulations dominate, while continuous-time analogs remain underexplored. Moreover, most derivations assume linear preferential attachment—where selection probability scales directly with fitness—despite empirical evidence of nonlinear relationships in real-world systems. These gaps hinder a unified understanding of preferential processes across disciplines.  

This paper addresses these limitations by presenting a general solution to the preferential selection model, valid for both linear and nonlinear attachment rules and arbitrary initial conditions. By leveraging stochastic calculus and generating functions, we derive closed-form expressions for the time-dependent distribution of selected entities, revealing how nonlinearity and system size influence emergent behavior. Unlike prior work, our approach accommodates heterogeneous fitness landscapes and dynamic selection thresholds, enabling analysis of systems with time-varying parameters.  

The implications of this solution are far-reaching. In social networks, it clarifies how early adopters amplify their influence under nonlinear attachment, while in evolutionary biology, it quantifies the role of fitness variability in species diversification. Furthermore, the framework provides a foundation for optimizing preferential selection mechanisms in algorithmic design, such as recommendation systems or resource allocation. By unifying disparate treatments of preferential dynamics, this work advances theoretical understanding and offers practical tools for modeling complex systems.

title: Distributed Computation for Solving the Sylvester Equation Based on Optimization
text:
The proposed distributed optimization framework for solving the Sylvester equation \(AX + XB = C\) was evaluated using synthetic matrices of sizes \(n = m = 100\) and \(n = m = 500\), with 4 and 8 computing nodes. For \(n = 100\), the centralized solver achieved a residual norm \(\|AX + XB - C\|_F = 2.1 \times 10^{-14}\) in 0.82 seconds, while the distributed method with 4 nodes reached \(\|AX + XB - C\|_F = 3.5 \times 10^{-14}\) in 1.24 seconds (1.51× speedup per node). With 8 nodes, the residual increased slightly to \(5.8 \times 10^{-14}\), but computation time dropped to 0.98 seconds (6.57× speedup per node), demonstrating scalability despite marginal accuracy loss.  
For \(n = 500\), the centralized solver required 127.3 seconds (\(\|AX + XB - C\|_F = 1.9 \times 10^{-13}\)), whereas the distributed approach with 4 nodes took 45.2 seconds (\(\|AX + XB - C\|_F = 2.7 \times 10^{-13}\)) and with 8 nodes took 28.6 seconds (\(\|AX + XB - C\|_F = 3.1 \times 10^{-13}\)), achieving 4.50× and 4.45× speedups per node, respectively. Convergence analysis revealed that increasing nodes reduced iteration count by 12–18% but required 15–20% more communication rounds, balancing speed and overhead.  
Error metrics remained below \(10^{-12}\) across tests, validating numerical stability. The trade-off between speedup and residual growth was attributed to consensus rounding in distributed updates. These results confirm the framework’s efficiency for large-scale problems, with 8-node setups reducing time by 77–78% compared to centralized methods while maintaining acceptable error thresholds. Future work will optimize communication protocols to further minimize overhead.

title: Learning abstract structure for drawing by efficient motor program induction
text:
In this work, we have presented a computational framework for learning abstract structural representations that enable efficient motor program induction for drawing tasks. By integrating a hierarchical generative model with a motor control architecture, our approach demonstrates how abstract structure—such as geometric relationships and compositional rules—can be inferred from sparse visual demonstrations and subsequently generalized to produce novel drawings. Unlike end-to-end systems that rely on pixel-level imitation, our method explicitly encodes structural invariants, allowing it to adapt to variations in object pose, scale, and configuration while maintaining drawing accuracy. This structural abstraction not only reduces the dimensionality of the motor control problem but also facilitates rapid generalization, as evidenced by our experiments showing successful reproduction of unseen characters and objects after observing only a handful of examples.  

Crucially, our framework bridges the gap between perceptual abstraction and motor execution by learning a shared latent space where structural relationships are decoupled from low-level motor commands. This enables the system to reuse learned primitives across different tasks, a hallmark of human-like efficiency. The Bayesian optimization component further enhances sample efficiency by focusing exploration on plausible motor programs, minimizing the need for exhaustive search.  

While our results are promising, future work will explore scaling the approach to more complex domains, such as three-dimensional drawings or dynamic interactions with objects. Additionally, integrating perceptual feedback mechanisms could enable online correction of motor programs, improving robustness to environmental variability. By advancing our understanding of how abstract structure guides motor learning, this research contributes to both cognitive science and artificial intelligence, offering insights into the computational principles underlying human skill acquisition and paving the way for more adaptive, general-purpose robotic systems.

title: Modeling and simulating the spatial spread of an epidemic through multiscale kinetic transport equations
text:
This paper introduces a novel multiscale modeling framework for simulating the spatial spread of infectious diseases using kinetic transport equations. Traditional compartmental models often overlook spatial heterogeneity and individual mobility patterns, limiting their accuracy in capturing real-world epidemic dynamics. To address this, we propose a kinetic approach that integrates microscopic agent-based interactions with macroscopic population-level transport processes. The model incorporates heterogeneous movement behaviors, such as random walks and directed travel, while accounting for disease transmission dynamics through collision-like terms derived from kinetic theory. By coupling these mechanisms, we capture both local contagion and long-range dissemination across geographic scales.  

The framework is formulated as a system of multiscale kinetic transport equations, where the phase space distribution describes the density of susceptible, infected, and recovered individuals in space, velocity, and disease state. A hybrid numerical method combining discrete velocity approximations for the kinetic component and finite volume schemes for spatial transport ensures computational efficiency. We validate the model using synthetic and empirical data, demonstrating its ability to reproduce observed patterns of spatial clustering and wave-like propagation. Sensitivity analyses reveal critical roles of mobility parameters and contact rates in shaping epidemic trajectories.  

Applications to hypothetical and historical outbreaks highlight the model’s utility in evaluating intervention strategies, such as travel restrictions and localized lockdowns. By bridging scales from individual movements to regional spread, this approach provides a robust tool for public health planning and real-time epidemic forecasting.

title: Social networks, confirmation bias and shock elections
text: The advent of social networks has fundamentally transformed the landscape of political communication, enabling unprecedented connectivity and information dissemination while simultaneously fostering echo chambers that reinforce ideological homogeneity. Confirmation bias—the tendency to favor information aligning with preexisting beliefs and dismiss contradictory evidence—has long been recognized as a critical psychological mechanism shaping individual decision-making. However, its interaction with social networks in the context of electoral politics remains underexplored, particularly in scenarios involving "shock elections," where unexpected outcomes defy conventional polling and expert predictions. These elections, such as the 2016 U.S. presidential race or the 2016 Brexit referendum, reveal a paradox: despite access to diverse information sources, voters increasingly cluster within ideologically segregated online communities, amplifying partisan narratives and reducing exposure to opposing viewpoints. This paper examines how social networks exacerbate confirmation bias through algorithmic filtering, selective sharing, and peer reinforcement, creating feedback loops that distort collective perceptions of candidate viability and policy issues. By integrating theories of cognitive bias, network science, and electoral behavior, we argue that the structural properties of social networks—not merely individual psychological traits—play a pivotal role in driving electoral surprises. Understanding this dynamic is crucial for interpreting modern democratic processes and mitigating risks to electoral integrity.

title: Modelling Covid-19 epidemic in Mexico, Finland and Iceland
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has posed significant challenges to global health systems, necessitating robust epidemiological models to guide public health interventions. This study develops and compares compartmental models tailored to the distinct demographic, social, and healthcare contexts of Mexico, Finland, and Iceland to analyze transmission dynamics and evaluate control strategies. Using publicly available data on confirmed cases, hospitalizations, and mortality, we calibrate susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) frameworks incorporating age-structured contact patterns, mobility trends, and non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). Our findings reveal that Mexico’s epidemic was driven by high community transmission in densely populated regions, with NPIs reducing peak infections by 40% but insufficient to prevent healthcare system strain. Finland’s earlier implementation of targeted lockdowns and high testing rates flattened the curve effectively, while Iceland’s small population and aggressive contact tracing minimized outbreak severity despite early border openings. Sensitivity analyses highlight the critical role of compliance with social distancing and mask mandates in all three countries. The models underscore the importance of context-specific parameters in epidemic forecasting and provide actionable insights for optimizing mitigation strategies in resource-varied settings. This work contributes to the global understanding of COVID-19 dynamics by emphasizing adaptive modeling approaches for heterogeneous populations.

title: Event Prediction in the Big Data Era: A Systematic Survey
text:
The proliferation of big data has revolutionized decision-making across industries, enabling organizations to extract actionable insights from vast, heterogeneous datasets. Among its transformative applications, event prediction—the process of forecasting future occurrences based on historical and real-time data—has emerged as a critical tool for mitigating risks, optimizing operations, and enhancing strategic planning. From financial markets and healthcare systems to smart cities and cybersecurity, the ability to anticipate events such as stock market fluctuations, disease outbreaks, or infrastructure failures holds immense potential to improve societal resilience and economic efficiency. However, the complexity and scale of big data, characterized by high velocity, volume, and variety, present unique challenges for traditional prediction models, necessitating innovative methodologies that leverage advanced computational techniques and interdisciplinary approaches.  

Recent advancements in machine learning, artificial intelligence, and data analytics have reshaped event prediction by addressing these challenges through scalable, adaptive frameworks. Techniques such as deep learning, graph neural networks, and ensemble methods now dominate the landscape, enabling models to process unstructured data, capture dynamic temporal patterns, and integrate multimodal information sources. Despite these strides, gaps persist in understanding the trade-offs between model interpretability and accuracy, the ethical implications of predictive analytics, and the robustness of systems in noisy, evolving environments. Furthermore, the lack of standardized benchmarks and reproducibility frameworks complicates cross-domain comparisons and real-world deployment.  

This systematic survey synthesizes the current state of event prediction research in the big data era, evaluating methodologies, applications, and open challenges. By analyzing over 200 peer-reviewed studies spanning 2015–2023, we categorize approaches by data type, algorithmic design, and use case, highlighting trends such as the integration of real-time streaming data and explainable AI. Our findings underscore the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration to address ethical, computational, and scalability barriers, while providing a roadmap for researchers and practitioners seeking to harness big data for predictive analytics. This work aims to bridge theoretical advancements with practical implementation, fostering innovation in an era where timely, accurate event prediction is indispensable.

title: Addressing the Privacy Implications of Mixed Reality: A Regulatory Approach
text:
Our survey of 1,200 mixed reality (MR) users revealed that 78% (n=936) expressed concerns about unintended data collection, particularly regarding biometric (65%) and location data (59%). Despite these concerns, only 32% (n=384) reported reading privacy policies before using MR devices, highlighting a significant gap between awareness and proactive behavior. When informed about GDPR-inspired regulatory frameworks, support for mandatory data anonymization rose from 41% to 67%, suggesting that regulatory clarity enhances user trust.  

A comparative analysis of three MR platforms demonstrated varying compliance with proposed regulations. Platform A, which implemented real-time consent prompts and data minimization protocols, reduced unwanted data collection by 42% compared to Platform B, which lacked such measures. However, Platform C, despite adhering to strict data encryption standards, still faced criticism for opaque third-party data sharing practices, underscoring the need for transparency beyond technical safeguards.  

Our legal review identified key jurisdictional gaps: only 28% of countries currently have MR-specific privacy laws, while 63% rely on generalized data protection regulations. In simulated enforcement scenarios, introducing mandatory privacy impact assessments (PIAs) for MR applications reduced reported privacy violations by 31% in the EU, but only 12% in regions without such requirements. This disparity highlights the uneven global implementation of privacy protections.  

Quantitative data from user interviews (n=50) revealed that 84% prioritized “control over data sharing” as their top privacy concern, yet only 29% felt MR devices provided adequate tools to manage permissions. These findings align with our regression analysis, which showed a strong correlation (r=0.76, p<0.01) between regulatory transparency and user satisfaction. Collectively, the results emphasize that technical solutions alone are insufficient; holistic regulatory frameworks addressing consent, transparency, and cross-border enforcement are critical to mitigating privacy risks in MR ecosystems.

title: Exact Combinatorial Optimization with Graph Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
In this work, we have introduced a novel framework for exact combinatorial optimization leveraging graph convolutional neural networks (GCNs), bridging the gap between heuristic-driven approximation methods and provably optimal solutions. By integrating GCNs with a branch-and-bound search strategy, we demonstrated that neural networks can effectively guide the exploration of combinatorial solution spaces, achieving exact optimality while significantly reducing computational overhead compared to traditional solvers. Our approach capitalizes on the inductive biases of GCNs to learn problem-specific patterns and symmetries, enabling intelligent pruning of the search tree and prioritization of promising branches. This synergy between machine learning and combinatorial optimization not only preserves theoretical guarantees but also enhances scalability for structured problems like the traveling salesman and maximum cut.

Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that our method matches the optimality of state-of-the-art solvers while requiring fewer computational resources in many cases. Notably, the GCN’s ability to generalize across problem instances of varying sizes and structures highlights its potential for transfer learning, reducing the need for problem-specific tuning. However, challenges remain in scaling to extremely large instances, where the exponential growth of the solution space tests the limits of even hybrid approaches. Future work will explore adaptive network architectures and reinforcement learning techniques to dynamically refine search strategies, as well as extensions to stochastic and dynamic optimization settings.

Our framework represents a paradigm shift in combinatorial optimization, proving that learned heuristics can coexist with exact methods without sacrificing correctness. By embedding structural knowledge into neural architectures, we open avenues for solving previously intractable problems in logistics, circuit design, and network analysis. This work underscores the transformative potential of integrating deep learning with classical algorithms, paving the way for a new generation of efficient, interpretable, and generalizable optimization tools.

title: Multiple Sclerosis disease: a computational approach for investigating its drug interactions
text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder affecting the central nervous system, characterized by complex pathogenesis and diverse clinical manifestations. Effective management often involves polypharmacy, increasing the risk of adverse drug interactions (ADIs) that may compromise therapeutic outcomes or exacerbate disease progression. This study introduces a computational framework to systematically investigate drug interactions in MS treatment by integrating multi-omics data, pharmacological networks, and machine learning algorithms. We curated a comprehensive dataset encompassing FDA-approved and off-label MS medications, their metabolic pathways, protein targets, and reported ADIs from clinical databases. Using network analysis, we constructed a drug-drug interaction (DDI) network to identify high-risk combinations based on shared metabolic enzymes (e.g., CYP3A4, CYP2D6) and transporters. Machine learning models, including random forest and gradient boosting, were trained on pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic features to predict clinically significant DDIs with 89% accuracy. The framework highlighted critical interactions, such as interferon-beta with immunosuppressants increasing infection risk, and antispasmodics altering cytochrome P450 activity. Validation against electronic health records demonstrated its potential to reduce unanticipated ADIs by 34%. This computational approach offers a scalable tool for clinicians and researchers to optimize MS pharmacotherapy, minimize iatrogenic harm, and guide personalized treatment strategies through data-driven insights into drug interaction mechanisms.

title: Future Smart Connected Communities to Fight COVID-19 Outbreak
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has posed unprecedented challenges to global public health, economies, and social systems, exposing vulnerabilities in traditional community management and crisis response mechanisms. As the world grapples with recurring waves of infections, the urgent need for resilient, adaptive, and technologically integrated solutions has become evident. Smart connected communities (SCCs), characterized by the seamless integration of digital technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), big data analytics, and 5G networks, offer a transformative framework to enhance pandemic preparedness and response. By leveraging real-time data collection, predictive modeling, and automated decision-making, SCCs enable proactive identification of outbreak hotspots, optimized resource allocation, and dynamic adjustments to public health policies. Furthermore, these communities facilitate remote healthcare delivery, contact tracing, and public communication, addressing critical gaps in conventional strategies. This paper explores the potential of future SCCs to combat COVID-19 and similar pandemics by examining their technical foundations, governance models, and socio-ethical implications. Through a multidisciplinary lens, we analyze how SCCs can empower individuals, institutions, and governments to collaborate effectively, fostering a culture of resilience and innovation in the face of global health crises.

title: Synthetic Data Generation for Economists
text: The growing complexity of economic models and data-driven decision-making has amplified the demand for high-quality datasets, yet real-world economic data often face limitations due to privacy concerns, accessibility barriers, and sampling biases. Synthetic data generation (SDG) has emerged as a transformative solution, enabling economists to create artificial datasets that replicate the statistical properties of real data while preserving confidentiality and addressing gaps in empirical research. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of SDG methodologies tailored for economic applications, emphasizing their potential to enhance causal inference, policy evaluation, and predictive modeling. We review generative techniques, including statistical resampling, probabilistic models, and deep learning-based approaches like generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs), highlighting their strengths and limitations in capturing economic relationships. Through case studies on labor markets, consumer behavior, and macroeconomic indicators, we demonstrate how SDG can mitigate data scarcity, enable counterfactual analysis, and facilitate robustness checks. We also address critical challenges, such as ensuring representativeness, avoiding model misspecification, and validating synthetic datasets against real-world benchmarks. Finally, we discuss ethical considerations, including the risk of reinforcing biases in training data and the implications for reproducibility. By bridging gaps between computational methods and economic theory, this paper advocates for SDG as a vital tool to expand the frontier of empirical research while upholding data governance standards.

title: Towards Social & Engaging Peer Learning: Predicting Backchanneling and Disengagement in Children
text:
Peer learning, where children collaborate and learn from one another, is a cornerstone of modern educational theory, fostering critical thinking, social skills, and deeper conceptual understanding. However, its effectiveness hinges on active participation and sustained engagement from all learners. In group settings, subtle cues such as backchanneling (brief verbal or nonverbal responses like nodding or saying “uh-huh”) and disengagement (e.g., inattention, withdrawal, or off-task behavior) significantly influence the dynamics of interaction and learning outcomes. While backchanneling can signal attentiveness and encourage dialogue, disengagement disrupts knowledge transfer and diminishes collective progress. Understanding and predicting these behaviors in real time remains a challenge, particularly in children, whose social and cognitive development introduces variability in communication patterns.  

Traditional methods of assessing engagement often rely on post-hoc observations or self-reports, which fail to capture the fluidity of peer interactions. Recent advances in multimodal learning analytics, including computer vision, audio processing, and machine learning, offer tools to decode these behaviors automatically. By analyzing facial expressions, gaze patterns, speech prosody, and body language, researchers can now infer engagement levels and predict shifts in participation. This study explores the feasibility of using such technologies to identify backchanneling and disengagement in children aged 8–12 during collaborative tasks.  

We propose a framework that leverages temporal and contextual features from multimodal data streams to model these behaviors, addressing gaps in existing literature that focus primarily on adult populations or isolated modalities. Our work aims to empower educators with real-time feedback mechanisms, enabling timely interventions to sustain engagement and promote equitable participation. By bridging computational methods with pedagogical goals, this research contributes to the design of adaptive, socially intelligent learning environments tailored to children’s developmental needs.

title: I like fish, especially dolphins: Addressing Contradictions in Dialogue Modeling
text:
Our experiments evaluated three dialogue models—BERT-Base, GPT-3.5, and a fine-tuned T5 variant—on their ability to resolve contradictions in user-generated dialogue, focusing on the nuanced example: *“I like fish, especially dolphins.”* We measured contradiction detection accuracy (CDA) and resolution quality (RQ) via human evaluations (1–5 Likert scale) on 500 test cases.  
BERT-Base achieved 68% CDA but scored low in RQ (2.1/5), often flagging non-contradictory statements due to lexical overlap (e.g., misclassifying *“I dislike trout but love salmon”*). GPT-3.5 improved to 82% CDA and 3.4/5 RQ, generating coherent resolutions like *“Dolphins are mammals, so you likely meant ‘marine animals’ instead of ‘fish’”* in 74% of cases. However, it struggled with sarcasm (e.g., *“Sure, fish are *so* intelligent like dolphins!”*), resolving only 52% of such cases correctly.  
The fine-tuned T5 outperformed both (91% CDA, 4.1/5 RQ), leveraging a contrastive loss function to distinguish literal from metaphorical language. For the original example, it generated: *“Your statement contains a factual contradiction—dolphins are mammals. Did you mean to express admiration for their intelligence?”* in 89% of trials. Human evaluators noted its resolutions were *“context-aware”* and *“less robotic”* than GPT-3.5’s.  
Error analysis revealed residual challenges: all models failed on culturally contextual contradictions (e.g., *“I hate sushi but love raw fish”*), underscoring the need for grounded world knowledge. These results suggest that combining contrastive learning with commonsense reasoning modules could further improve contradiction handling in dialogue systems.

title: Corona-Warn-App: Tracing the Start of the Official COVID-19 Exposure Notification App for Germany
text:
The Corona-Warn-App marked a pivotal moment in Germany’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, serving as the first large-scale implementation of a decentralized, privacy-preserving exposure notification system. By leveraging Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) technology and the Exposure Notification Framework co-developed by Apple and Google, the app prioritized user autonomy and data protection, aligning with Germany’s stringent privacy laws and fostering public trust. Its launch in June 2020 addressed critical gaps in manual contact tracing, enabling rapid, anonymous alerts to users exposed to potential infections. Despite initial challenges—including technical glitches, fragmented adoption across federal states, and public skepticism—the app demonstrated resilience through iterative updates and transparent communication. By the end of 2020, over 26 million downloads underscored its societal relevance, even as debates persisted about its effectiveness in reducing transmission rates.  

The app’s legacy extends beyond its technical achievements. It highlighted the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration, involving epidemiologists, software engineers, and policymakers, and set a precedent for ethical digital health tools. However, its reliance on voluntary participation and smartphone penetration revealed limitations in addressing equity gaps, particularly among older populations and low-income communities. Future iterations could integrate additional features, such as vaccine certificates or symptom tracking, while maintaining core privacy principles.  

Ultimately, the Corona-Warn-App exemplifies how digital innovation can complement public health infrastructure during crises. While its direct impact on pandemic outcomes remains subject to ongoing research, its role in normalizing exposure notification systems and inspiring global adaptations is undeniable. As societies prepare for future health emergencies, the app’s development offers valuable lessons in balancing efficacy, ethics, and public engagement.

title: Principles to Practices for Responsible AI: Closing the Gap
text: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has underscored the urgent need to translate ethical principles into actionable practices to ensure responsible AI development and deployment. While global frameworks and guidelines for responsible AI have proliferated, a persistent gap remains between high-level principles and their concrete implementation in real-world systems. This paper examines the key challenges hindering the effective operationalization of responsible AI principles, including ambiguous terminology, conflicting stakeholder interests, and the lack of standardized evaluation metrics. By analyzing case studies across diverse sectors—such as healthcare, finance, and criminal justice—we identify common barriers to implementation, including organizational silos, insufficient technical tools, and regulatory fragmentation. To bridge this gap, we propose a multi-stakeholder approach centered on three pillars: (1) developing clear, context-specific guidelines with measurable indicators; (2) fostering interdisciplinary collaboration among technologists, ethicists, policymakers, and affected communities; and (3) integrating accountability mechanisms throughout the AI lifecycle, from design to deployment. We also emphasize the role of adaptive governance frameworks that balance innovation with risk mitigation. By synthesizing insights from academia, industry, and civil society, this paper provides actionable recommendations for closing the principle-practice divide in responsible AI. Our findings suggest that proactive engagement with diverse stakeholders, coupled with robust evaluation protocols, can enable more equitable, transparent, and trustworthy AI systems. Ultimately, bridging this gap requires not only technical solutions but also systemic shifts in how AI governance is conceptualized and enforced globally.

title: Towards Earnings Call and Stock Price Movement
text:
The relationship between corporate earnings calls and stock price movements has long been a focal point in financial research, owing to its profound implications for market efficiency, investor behavior, and corporate communication strategies. Earnings calls, as structured events where management discusses financial performance with analysts and investors, serve as critical channels for disseminating firm-specific information and shaping market expectations. These interactions not only reflect a company’s operational outcomes but also convey forward-looking insights, managerial confidence, and strategic priorities, all of which influence investor sentiment and decision-making. Prior studies have extensively documented the immediate stock price reactions to earnings announcements, highlighting the role of information asymmetry and surprise elements in driving short-term volatility. However, the nuanced dynamics of earnings calls—including linguistic tone, question-and-answer sessions, and non-verbal cues—remain underexplored, particularly in their long-term impact on stock performance.  
Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and sentiment analysis have enabled researchers to quantify qualitative aspects of corporate disclosures, revealing that linguistic features such as optimism, uncertainty, and complexity can systematically affect market responses. Despite these insights, gaps persist in understanding how contextual factors, such as industry competition, macroeconomic conditions, or institutional frameworks, moderate the efficacy of earnings call communication. Moreover, the increasing prevalence of virtual earnings calls post-pandemic has introduced new variables, including technological mediation and audience engagement patterns, that may alter information transmission mechanisms.  
This study aims to bridge these gaps by examining the interplay between earnings call characteristics and stock price movements through a multi-dimensional lens, integrating linguistic, contextual, and behavioral perspectives. By analyzing a large-scale dataset of U.S. firms, we investigate how managerial communication strategies during earnings calls influence both immediate and delayed stock returns, while accounting for firm heterogeneity and market states. Our findings contribute to the literature by offering a holistic framework for evaluating the informational value of earnings calls and providing actionable insights for investors and policymakers.

title: Neural Joint Entropy Estimation
text: Estimating joint entropy from high-dimensional data is a fundamental challenge in information theory and machine learning, with applications ranging from feature selection to causal inference. Traditional methods, such as histogram-based estimators and k-nearest neighbors approaches, suffer from the curse of dimensionality and computational inefficiency in large-scale settings. This paper introduces a novel framework for neural joint entropy estimation that leverages deep neural networks to learn flexible, data-driven representations of probability distributions. By optimizing a differentiable entropy surrogate objective, our model implicitly captures the underlying structure of the data while avoiding explicit density estimation. We demonstrate theoretically that our approach provides consistent estimates under mild assumptions and empirically show its effectiveness on synthetic and real-world datasets, including multivariate Gaussian distributions and neural spike train recordings. Our method achieves significant improvements in accuracy and scalability compared to state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in high-dimensional regimes, opening new avenues for entropy-based analysis in complex systems.

title: Personalized fall detection monitoring system based on learning from the user movements
text:
Falls among older adults and individuals with mobility impairments represent a critical public health challenge, with over 37 million falls requiring medical attention annually worldwide. Beyond immediate physical injuries, falls often trigger a cascade of long-term consequences, including reduced mobility, loss of independence, and heightened fear of future incidents, which collectively exacerbate healthcare costs and diminish quality of life. Traditional fall detection systems, such as wearable sensors or ambient devices, have sought to address this issue by identifying fall events through predefined motion thresholds or environmental cues. However, these methods frequently suffer from high false-positive rates, limited adaptability to individual movement patterns, and discomfort during prolonged use, reducing user compliance and overall effectiveness.  

Recent advancements in machine learning and ubiquitous computing have opened new avenues for developing more intelligent, user-centric solutions. By leveraging data-driven approaches, modern systems can learn from an individual’s unique gait, posture, and daily activity rhythms to distinguish between normal movements and potentially hazardous events. This personalization not only enhances detection accuracy but also minimizes unnecessary alarms, fostering trust and long-term adoption. Yet, challenges persist in balancing model complexity with real-time performance, ensuring robustness across diverse user demographics, and addressing privacy concerns related to continuous motion data collection.  

This paper introduces a novel personalized fall detection framework that integrates adaptive machine learning models with lightweight sensor fusion techniques. The system dynamically refines its detection criteria by analyzing user-specific movement signatures over time, enabling it to adapt to changes in health status or mobility aids. By prioritizing user comfort and contextual awareness, the proposed approach aims to bridge the gap between technical innovation and practical usability, offering a scalable solution for both clinical and home-based care settings.

title: Initialization of a Disease Transmission Model
text:
The Results and Analysis section evaluates the performance of three initialization strategies—random, cluster-based, and data-informed—for a compartmental disease transmission model simulating influenza spread in a synthetic population of 100,000 individuals. Simulations ran over 90 days with a basic reproduction number (R₀) of 2.5, recovery rate of 0.1 days⁻¹, and initial infectious count of 10.  

The random initialization strategy produced significant variability in epidemic trajectories. Across 50 replicates, peak infection rates ranged from 12.3% to 18.7% of the population (mean: 15.2%), with peak timing varying by ±8 days (mean: Day 42). This variability arose from uneven spatial distribution of initial cases, leading to localized outbreaks that either fizzled or merged unpredictably.  

Cluster-based initialization, which grouped initial cases into 5 geographic clusters, reduced variability but introduced bias. Peak infection rates averaged 16.8% (range: 16.1–17.5%), occurring consistently around Day 38. However, this method overestimated early transmission in densely populated areas, underestimating rural spread by 22% compared to empirical data from similar regions.  

The data-informed strategy, using mobility patterns and demographic data to seed cases proportionally, yielded the most stable and realistic outcomes. Peak infections averaged 15.9% (range: 15.5–16.3%) at Day 40, closely matching the 16.2% peak observed in historical influenza data. Early growth rates (r = 0.12 day⁻¹) aligned with estimates from contact tracing studies, while spatial distribution errors were reduced by 34% versus cluster-based initialization.  

These results demonstrate that initialization methods significantly impact model robustness. Random approaches are unsuitable for precise forecasting, while cluster-based methods risk spatial bias. Data-informed initialization, despite requiring more input data, provides the most reliable foundation for predicting epidemic dynamics, particularly when validating against real-world patterns. Future work should explore hybrid methods to balance computational efficiency with accuracy in low-data settings.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Deep Convolutional Candlestick Learner
text:
The exploration of adversarial robustness in the Deep Convolutional Candlestick Learner (DCCL) reveals critical insights into the resilience of financial deep learning models against carefully crafted perturbations. Our experiments demonstrate that while the DCCL achieves strong baseline performance on clean candlestick data, its susceptibility to adversarial attacks—particularly those targeting temporal patterns and price volatility representations—poses significant risks for real-world deployment. White-box attacks, leveraging gradient-based optimization, consistently degraded prediction accuracy by up to 32% across multiple asset classes, underscoring the model’s reliance on superficial features rather than robust market fundamentals. Black-box transfer attacks, though less effective, still achieved notable success rates, highlighting vulnerabilities even when attackers lack full model knowledge.  

Notably, adversarial training and input transformations (e.g., JPEG compression, noise injection) improved robustness but at the cost of reduced clean-data performance, reflecting a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and security. Certified defenses, while theoretically promising, proved computationally infeasible for high-frequency trading timelines, suggesting a need for scalable alternatives. Furthermore, our analysis of attack transferability revealed that perturbations optimized for one asset often harmed performance on others, implying that adversarial examples exploit shared vulnerabilities in feature extraction pipelines rather than asset-specific dynamics.  

These findings emphasize the urgency of integrating adversarial robustness into the design of financial AI systems. Future work should prioritize developing defense mechanisms tailored to sequential data, such as temporal smoothing or attention-based anomaly detection, while advancing interpretability tools to identify model blind spots. Additionally, industry-academia collaborations could establish standardized benchmarks for adversarial threats in algorithmic trading, fostering more secure ecosystems. Ultimately, the DCCL’s vulnerabilities serve as a cautionary tale: as financial models grow in complexity, so too must our efforts to safeguard them against both intentional manipulation and unintended distributional shifts.

title: Competitive pricing despite search costs if lower price signals quality
text: This paper explores the paradox of competitive pricing in markets with search costs, where lower prices may paradoxically signal higher quality rather than cost leadership. Traditional economic models suggest that search costs deter price competition by increasing consumer inertia, enabling firms to maintain higher margins. However, we argue that when consumers infer quality from price—perceiving lower prices as indicative of superior efficiency or value—firms face strategic incentives to reduce prices to signal quality, even amid search costs. Using a theoretical framework integrating signaling theory and search cost literature, we demonstrate that under specific conditions (e.g., asymmetric information, credible cost structures), price cuts can enhance perceived quality, expand market share, and offset reduced margins through volume gains. Empirical evidence from e-commerce and service industries supports these findings, highlighting the role of consumer heuristics in shaping competitive dynamics. The study contributes to understanding pricing strategies in digitally driven markets where search costs persist but quality signaling remains pivotal.

title: Can Testing Ease Social Distancing Measures? Future Evolution of COVID-19 in NYC
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has reshaped global public health strategies, compelling policymakers to balance infection control with socioeconomic sustainability. Among U.S. metropolitan areas, New York City (NYC) emerged as an epicenter during the early phases, experiencing catastrophic strain on healthcare systems and necessitating stringent social distancing measures (SDMs), including lockdowns, mask mandates, and capacity restrictions. While these interventions effectively curbed transmission, their prolonged implementation risks exacerbating economic disparities, mental health crises, and public fatigue. As vaccination campaigns progressed, attention shifted toward testing as a potential tool to relax SDMs while maintaining epidemiological safety. Mass testing, particularly through rapid antigen and PCR-based surveillance, has been proposed to identify asymptomatic cases, isolate infected individuals promptly, and enable targeted interventions rather than blanket restrictions. However, the interplay between testing efficacy, population compliance, and viral variant dynamics remains poorly understood, especially in densely populated urban settings like NYC. This study examines whether scalable testing strategies could safely reduce reliance on SDMs by analyzing NYC’s epidemiological trajectory from 2020 to 2023, incorporating data on testing coverage, case detection rates, and mobility patterns. We employ a compartmental model calibrated to NYC’s demographics and variant-specific transmission parameters to simulate scenarios under varying testing intensities and SDM relaxation timelines. Our findings aim to inform evidence-based policies for post-pandemic resilience, addressing critical questions about the feasibility of transitioning from reactive containment to sustainable coexistence with endemic respiratory pathogens.

title: Corporate Governance and Firms Financial Performance in the United Kingdom
text: This study examines the relationship between corporate governance mechanisms and the financial performance of firms in the United Kingdom, utilizing a comprehensive dataset of publicly listed companies spanning the period 2010 to 2022. Employing a mixed-methods approach, we analyze both quantitative financial indicators—including return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and Tobin’s Q—and qualitative governance features such as board composition, independence, ownership structure, and executive compensation practices. Our findings reveal a statistically significant and positive correlation between robust corporate governance practices and enhanced financial performance. Specifically, firms with a higher proportion of independent directors, greater board diversity, and effective oversight mechanisms tend to exhibit superior profitability and market valuation. Additionally, the study identifies that ownership concentration, particularly institutional ownership, plays a pivotal role in aligning managerial interests with shareholder objectives, thereby improving operational efficiency and reducing agency costs. However, the impact of executive compensation on financial performance is nuanced, showing a threshold effect where excessive compensation packages may dilute the positive governance outcomes. The research also highlights the moderating influence of external regulatory frameworks, such as the UK Corporate Governance Code, in strengthening the governance-performance nexus. These insights contribute to the broader literature on corporate governance by providing empirical evidence specific to the UK context, suggesting that adherence to high governance standards is instrumental in fostering sustainable financial success. The study concludes with policy recommendations aimed at enhancing governance transparency and accountability to further optimize firm performance in the UK market.

title: Learning Undirected Graphs in Financial Markets
text:
Financial markets are complex systems characterized by intricate interdependencies among diverse assets, institutions, and economic variables. These relationships, often nonlinear and dynamic, underpin market efficiency, risk propagation, and systemic stability. Understanding the structure of these interactions is crucial for portfolio optimization, risk management, and regulatory oversight, yet traditional models frequently oversimplify or ignore the underlying network topology. Undirected graphs, which represent pairwise relationships without assuming directional causality, offer a powerful framework to model these latent connections. By capturing co-movements, correlations, or shared latent factors, graph-based approaches can reveal hidden patterns in asset returns, liquidity flows, or credit linkages that are obscured in conventional analyses.  

Recent advances in machine learning and statistical inference have enabled more robust estimation of undirected graphs from high-dimensional financial data. However, challenges persist, including non-stationarity, sparsity, and the presence of latent confounders such as macroeconomic shocks or investor sentiment. Existing methods, ranging from Gaussian graphical models to sparse inverse covariance estimation, often struggle to balance model flexibility with interpretability while accounting for these real-world complexities. This paper addresses these gaps by proposing a novel framework for learning undirected graphs in financial markets, integrating time-varying dependencies, structural constraints, and domain-specific priors. We demonstrate its applicability across asset classes, highlighting how inferred graphs can improve portfolio diversification, stress-testing scenarios, and systemic risk assessment.

title: Why are Developers Struggling to Put GDPR into Practice when Developing Privacy-Preserving Software Systems?
text:
Our survey of 215 software developers revealed that 78% encountered significant challenges implementing GDPR-compliant features, with 62% citing "ambiguous legal requirements" as the primary barrier. Despite 89% reporting familiarity with GDPR’s core principles (e.g., data minimization, consent management), only 34% felt confident in their implementations’ legal robustness. This gap underscores a disconnect between theoretical knowledge and practical application, particularly in interpreting vague terms like "legitimate interest" (cited by 56% of respondents).  

Quantitative analysis of 12 open-source projects showed inconsistent adoption of GDPR-mandated features. Only 42% implemented user data deletion workflows, while 29% included mechanisms for data portability. Automated consent management tools were present in 51% of projects but often lacked granularity (e.g., opt-in/opt-out controls for specific data types). Interviews with 15 developers revealed that 73% prioritized functional requirements over compliance due to tight deadlines, and 60% relied on third-party libraries for cryptographic operations, raising concerns about dependency risks.  

A chi-square test revealed a statistically significant correlation (p < 0.01) between project size and compliance completeness: larger teams (≥10 members) achieved 68% higher adherence to GDPR’s technical safeguards compared to solo developers. However, even in large teams, 45% struggled with cross-border data transfer mechanisms, highlighting persistent gaps in understanding international data flow regulations.  

These findings suggest three root causes: (1) fragmented guidance on translating legal obligations into code, (2) resource constraints forcing trade-offs between compliance and delivery timelines, and (3) overreliance on external tools without verifying their GDPR alignment. For instance, 82% of developers using open-source libraries for encryption admitted they rarely audited these tools for compliance, creating latent vulnerabilities. Addressing these challenges requires clearer technical guidelines, integrated compliance checklists in development frameworks, and targeted training on balancing legal and engineering priorities.

title: Uncovering the structure of clinical EEG signals with self-supervised learning
text: In conclusion, this study demonstrates the potential of self-supervised learning (SSL) to uncover meaningful structure in clinical EEG signals without relying on extensive labeled datasets.
