By leveraging contrastive and predictive SSL frameworks, we successfully extracted representations that capture both spatial and temporal patterns inherent in EEG data, achieving competitive performance on downstream tasks such as seizure detection and sleep stage classification. Importantly, our approach outperformed traditional supervised baselines when labeled data were scarce, highlighting its practical value in clinical settings where annotation is costly and time-consuming. The learned embeddings revealed interpretable clusters corresponding to distinct neurophysiological states, suggesting that SSL can identify clinically relevant features even in the absence of explicit labels. Furthermore, our experiments indicated that SSL models trained on diverse EEG datasets generalize well across patients and recording conditions, addressing a key challenge in real-world EEG analysis. These findings pave the way for scalable, data-efficient tools in clinical neuroscience, enabling deeper insights into brain dynamics while reducing reliance on expert annotations. Future work will explore integrating multimodal data and refining SSL objectives to further enhance representation quality and robustness, ultimately advancing the translation of EEG-based diagnostics into routine clinical practice.

title: Digital image processing to detect subtle motion in stony coral
text: This study introduces an advanced digital image processing framework designed to detect subtle motion in stony corals, a critical yet under-explored indicator of coral health and environmental stress responses. Traditional methods for monitoring coral behavior, such as visual observation or manual tracking, are limited by subjectivity and low temporal resolution, particularly for micro-scale movements linked to physiological processes like polyp expansion, contraction, or mucus secretion. To address these challenges, we propose a computational pipeline integrating optical flow estimation, spatiotemporal filtering, and machine learning-based anomaly detection. First, high-resolution video sequences of coral colonies are processed using dense optical flow algorithms to quantify pixel-level displacement fields, capturing even minimal motion patterns. A temporal Gaussian filter is then applied to suppress noise while preserving dynamic features, followed by a spatial convolutional layer to enhance localized motion contrasts. Next, an unsupervised autoencoder model identifies deviations from baseline motion behavior, enabling the detection of subtle, stress-induced movements without requiring labeled training data. Experimental validation on controlled aquarium datasets demonstrates the framework’s ability to distinguish between normal polyp activity and stress-related motions (e.g., due to thermal or chemical stressors) with 92% accuracy. Furthermore, field trials in natural reef environments confirm robustness against varying lighting conditions and water turbulence. This approach provides a non-invasive, scalable tool for real-time coral health monitoring, offering early warnings of environmental stressors and supporting marine conservation efforts. Future work will explore integration with underwater robotic platforms for large-scale deployment.

title: Inference of a universal social scale and segregation measures using social connectivity kernels
text:
The study of social networks has long been a cornerstone of sociological and computational research, providing profound insights into the structure and dynamics of human interactions. Central to this domain is the concept of social scale—a framework that categorizes individuals or groups based on their relative positions within a network, reflecting underlying patterns of connectivity, influence, and resource distribution. Despite its importance, however, a universally accepted metric for quantifying social scale remains elusive, with existing measures often tailored to specific contexts or limited by methodological constraints. This gap hinders comparative analyses across diverse social systems and impedes a nuanced understanding of how social hierarchies emerge and evolve.  
Parallel to this challenge, the phenomenon of social segregation—the tendency for groups to cluster based on shared attributes such as race, income, or ideology—has garnered significant attention due to its implications for equity, cohesion, and collective well-being. Traditional segregation indices, such as the dissimilarity index or exposure metrics, have been instrumental in quantifying spatial or demographic divisions but frequently overlook the nuanced connectivity patterns that define modern digital and hybrid social environments. The rise of online platforms and multi-layered networks further complicates this landscape, demanding tools that capture both structural and relational dimensions of segregation.  
This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for inferring a universal social scale and corresponding segregation measures using *social connectivity kernels*—mathematical constructs that encode interaction probabilities across individuals or groups. By integrating principles from network science, statistical physics, and social theory, we derive scalable metrics that generalize across diverse social contexts, from offline communities to digital ecosystems. Our approach addresses key limitations of prior work by accounting for heterogeneous interaction strengths, multi-modality, and dynamic network evolution, thereby offering a more holistic view of social stratification and division. We validate the framework through empirical analyses of real-world networks, demonstrating its utility in uncovering latent hierarchies and quantifying segregation in ways that align with qualitative observations while providing new avenues for intervention and policy design.

title: Deep Learning with Heterogeneous Graph Embeddings for Mortality Prediction from Electronic Health Records
text: Accurate mortality prediction from electronic health records (EHRs) is crucial for improving clinical decision-making and patient care. However, EHRs present a complex, heterogeneous data structure, encompassing temporal sequences of clinical events, static patient attributes, and intricate relationships among medical concepts, making traditional predictive models insufficient. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework that leverages heterogeneous graph embeddings to enhance mortality prediction from EHR data. We propose a multi-modal graph construction method that integrates structured EHR elements—such as diagnoses, procedures, medications, and laboratory results—with unstructured clinical notes, creating a comprehensive representation of patient health trajectories. By employing graph neural networks (GNNs), we capture both local and global interactions among medical entities, extracting meaningful embeddings that encode rich semantic and temporal information. These embeddings are then fused with traditional time-series features within a hybrid deep learning architecture, combining the strengths of GNNs for relational reasoning and recurrent neural networks for sequential pattern recognition. Our approach is evaluated on a large, real-world EHR dataset, demonstrating significant improvements in predictive performance over state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in capturing long-term dependencies and rare event patterns. Furthermore, we analyze the interpretability of our model through attention mechanisms and graph visualization techniques, providing clinicians with actionable insights into key risk factors. The results suggest that incorporating heterogeneous graph embeddings into deep learning models offers a promising direction for advancing mortality prediction and personalized medicine.

title: Predicting COVID-19 Pneumonia Severity on Chest X-ray with Deep Learning
text:
The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the urgent need for rapid, accurate, and scalable tools to assess disease severity, particularly in resource-constrained healthcare settings. Pneumonia, a leading complication of severe COVID-19, is often diagnosed and monitored using chest X-rays (CXRs), which provide critical insights into lung involvement. However, manual interpretation of CXRs is time-consuming, subjective, and prone to inter-observer variability, especially during surges in patient volume. Automated severity prediction using deep learning (DL) offers a promising solution to enhance diagnostic efficiency, standardize assessments, and prioritize high-risk patients for timely intervention. By leveraging advances in artificial intelligence (AI), this study explores the potential of DL models to predict COVID-19 pneumonia severity directly from CXRs, addressing a critical gap in clinical decision-making.  

Recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility of DL for detecting COVID-19-related abnormalities in CXRs, but fewer have focused on quantifying severity or predicting clinical outcomes. Traditional severity scoring systems, such as the Radiographic Assessment of Lung Edema (RALE) score, rely on manual annotation of lung opacities, limiting their scalability. In contrast, DL models can automatically extract hierarchical features from raw imaging data, potentially capturing subtle patterns indicative of disease progression. This research aims to develop and validate a DL framework that predicts pneumonia severity by integrating spatial and textural CXR features, enabling real-time risk stratification.  

Our approach addresses two key challenges: (1) the scarcity of large, annotated datasets for training robust models, and (2) the need for interpretable predictions to gain clinician trust. By using a multi-center dataset of COVID-19 CXRs labeled with clinical severity metrics, we train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify images into mild, moderate, or severe categories. We further evaluate the model’s generalizability across diverse patient populations and its alignment with ground-truth severity scores. This work contributes to the growing body of evidence supporting AI-augmented radiology, offering a tool to reduce diagnostic delays and improve resource allocation during public health emergencies.

title: Digital Currency and Economic Crises: Helping States Respond
text:
Our analysis of 12 economies that adopted digital currencies (DCs) during the 2020–2022 crisis period reveals significant impacts on fiscal responsiveness and economic stability. On average, countries with DC frameworks reduced unemployment benefit disbursement times by 47%, from 14.2 days to 7.5 days, compared to non-adopters (p < 0.01). For instance, Country A’s blockchain-based system processed 8.2 million payments in 10 days, whereas its pre-crisis legacy system required 42 days for 5.5 million transactions. Similarly, DC-enabled conditional cash transfers in Country B reached 94% of eligible households within 72 hours of crisis onset, versus 68% under traditional methods.  

Liquidity provision also improved markedly. Central banks in DC-adopting nations increased money supply by an average of 12.3% in Q2 2020, compared to 8.1% in non-adopters (p = 0.03). Country C’s DC-linked smart contracts automated 70% of small business loan approvals, boosting lending by 22% year-over-year despite a 15% contraction in GDP.  

However, adoption challenges persisted. Countries with low digital infrastructure (e.g., Country D) saw only 58% of citizens utilize DC benefits, versus 89% in tech-advanced economies. Additionally, 30% of surveyed businesses reported transaction delays due to interoperability issues between private DCs and central bank systems.  

These results suggest DCs enhance crisis response speed and financial inclusion but require robust infrastructure and regulatory coordination. The data underscores DCs’ potential to streamline fiscal policy, though equitable access remains a critical hurdle. Future research should explore long-term effects on inflation and cross-border DC integration.

title: Getting to Know One Another: Calibrating Intent, Capabilities and Trust for Human-Robot Collaboration
text: In conclusion, effective human-robot collaboration hinges on the nuanced calibration of intent, capabilities, and trust between human and robotic partners. This paper has demonstrated that misalignment in any of these dimensions can lead to suboptimal outcomes, ranging from reduced task efficiency to breakdowns in cooperation. By integrating models of human intent recognition, adaptive capability disclosure, and trust-aware decision-making, we have outlined a framework that enables robots to dynamically adjust their behavior in response to human expectations and actions. Our experimental results highlight the importance of transparency in capability communication and the role of consistent, predictable behavior in building and maintaining trust over time. However, challenges remain in scaling these approaches to more complex, real-world environments where uncertainty and variability are heightened. Future work must address the integration of multimodal sensing and learning techniques to better infer human intent in diverse contexts, as well as the development of robust metrics for evaluating trust dynamics in long-term interactions. Additionally, ethical considerations surrounding autonomy, agency, and the potential for over-reliance on robotic systems warrant careful examination. Ultimately, the success of human-robot collaboration will depend on our ability to design systems that not only perform tasks effectively but also foster a sense of shared understanding and mutual respect. By prioritizing these principles, we can pave the way for more seamless, productive, and trustworthy interactions between humans and robots.

title: Mixed-Reality Robotic Games: Design Guidelines for Effective Entertainment with Consumer Robots
text: Mixed-reality robotic games represent an emerging intersection of robotics, augmented/virtual reality (AR/VR), and interactive entertainment, offering novel opportunities to engage users through immersive, physically embodied experiences. However, designing effective and entertaining mixed-reality games that leverage consumer robots poses unique challenges, including balancing virtual and physical interactions, ensuring intuitive user engagement, and maintaining technical robustness across diverse environments. This paper presents a comprehensive set of design guidelines aimed at optimizing entertainment value in mixed-reality robotic games while addressing these challenges. Drawing on an interdisciplinary review of human-robot interaction (HRI), game design principles, and mixed-reality technologies, we identify key considerations such as seamless integration of virtual and physical elements, adaptive robot behaviors to enhance responsiveness, and intuitive control interfaces that reduce cognitive load. Additionally, we emphasize the importance of creating meaningful social interactions, either through cooperative or competitive gameplay involving multiple robots or human-robot teams. Our guidelines also address technical aspects, including robust localization, real-time synchronization, and safety mechanisms to prevent unintended robot actions. To validate these recommendations, we conducted a user study evaluating a prototype mixed-reality game featuring consumer robots, revealing significant improvements in user satisfaction, engagement, and perceived enjoyment when following our design principles. This work contributes practical insights for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop entertaining and accessible mixed-reality robotic games, advancing the potential of consumer robots as interactive entertainment platforms.

title: Teaching Economics with Interactive Browser-Based Models
text:
The landscape of economics education has undergone significant transformation in recent decades, driven by advancements in digital technology and pedagogical innovation. Traditional lecture-based methods, while foundational, often struggle to engage students in complex economic concepts that require dynamic, real-time comprehension of interconnected variables. This challenge is compounded by the abstract nature of economic modeling, where students frequently encounter barriers in translating theoretical frameworks into intuitive understanding. Interactive browser-based models (IBBMs) have emerged as a promising solution to bridge this gap, offering accessible, hands-on tools that democratize economic experimentation and visualization. By leveraging web technologies such as JavaScript, D3.js, and computational platforms like Observable or Jupyter notebooks, IBBMs enable students to manipulate parameters, observe outcomes, and iterate hypotheses in real time—all within a standard web browser without requiring specialized software. This immediacy fosters active learning, allowing students to "learn by doing" through iterative exploration rather than passive observation.

Recent studies in educational technology highlight the efficacy of interactive tools in enhancing conceptual retention and critical thinking skills across disciplines. In economics, where models like supply-demand equilibrium, game theory, or macroeconomic simulations often rely on static diagrams or complex mathematical derivations, IBBMs provide a dynamic alternative. They allow instructors to design modular, scenario-based lessons that adapt to diverse learning styles while addressing common misconceptions. For instance, a student adjusting interest rates in a browser-based IS-LM model can instantly visualize the impact on output and inflation, deepening their grasp of monetary policy trade-offs. Such interactivity aligns with constructivist learning theories, emphasizing knowledge construction through exploration and reflection.

Despite their potential, the adoption of IBBMs in economics classrooms remains uneven. Barriers include limited awareness of available tools, perceived technical complexity, and concerns about alignment with curricular standards. This paper addresses these gaps by (1) reviewing existing IBBM platforms and their pedagogical applications, (2) evaluating their impact on student engagement and learning outcomes through a meta-analysis of empirical studies, and (3) proposing a framework for integrating IBBMs into economics curricula across skill levels. By synthesizing insights from educational research and practical case studies, this work aims to empower instructors to harness IBBMs as scalable, low-cost supplements to traditional instruction, ultimately fostering a more inclusive and interactive economics education ecosystem.

title: Estimation of number of runaway electrons per avalanche in Earth's atmosphere
text: The estimation of runaway electron populations generated during relativistic electron avalanches in Earth's atmosphere is critical for understanding high-energy radiation processes linked to thunderstorms, terrestrial gamma-ray flashes (TGFs), and space weather interactions. This study presents a novel analytical framework to quantify the number of runaway electrons produced per avalanche event, integrating kinetic theory with Monte Carlo simulations of electron-molecule collisions. By modeling the propagation of seed electrons (10–100 keV) through atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen at altitudes of 15–40 km, we derive scaling laws for avalanche multiplication efficiency under varying electric field strengths (0.1–1 kV/m) and air densities. Key findings reveal that the number of runaway electrons per avalanche follows a power-law distribution dependent on the initial electron energy and the ratio of electric field to local air density (E/N), with multiplication factors exceeding 10³ under optimal conditions. Simulations incorporating relativistic feedback mechanisms—where backscattered X-rays generate secondary seed electrons—demonstrate a non-linear enhancement in avalanche growth, particularly in regions of strong electric field gradients. We validate our model against satellite observations of TGF spectra and balloon-borne radiation measurements, showing agreement within a factor of 2 for electron fluxes above 1 MeV. The results suggest that localized electric field structures, such as those in thunderstorm lightning leaders or sprite streamers, may produce avalanches with 10⁶–10⁸ runaway electrons, sufficient to explain observed TGF durations and energy distributions. This work advances quantitative understanding of relativistic runaway electron avalanches, providing constraints for global atmospheric radiation budgets and potential applications in lightning physics and radiation belt dynamics.

title: Synthesis of Supervisors Robust Against Sensor Deception Attacks
text:
The integration of advanced sensors into cyber-physical systems (CPS) has enhanced operational efficiency and autonomy across critical domains, including industrial automation, autonomous vehicles, and smart infrastructure. However, the reliance on sensor data for decision-making exposes these systems to sensor deception attacks, where adversaries manipulate measurements to induce unsafe or unstable supervisor behavior. Such attacks exploit vulnerabilities in sensor-controller feedback loops, potentially leading to catastrophic failures in safety-critical applications. Despite growing awareness of cyber-physical threats, designing supervisors resilient to sensor deception remains a pressing challenge, requiring novel approaches to reconcile real-time performance with robustness guarantees.  

Traditional supervisory control frameworks assume trusted sensor inputs, limiting their applicability in adversarial environments. While existing research has addressed fault detection and cryptographic protections, these methods often lack adaptability to dynamic attack patterns or impose prohibitive computational overhead. This paper introduces a systematic methodology for synthesizing supervisors that are inherently robust against sensor deception attacks, leveraging formal verification and optimization techniques. By modeling attacks as bounded perturbations in sensor outputs, we derive attack-resilient control policies that ensure system safety and liveness despite adversarial interference.  

Our approach integrates reachability analysis with constraint-based optimization to generate supervisors that tolerate worst-case sensor manipulations within predefined bounds. We validate the framework through case studies on a robotic manipulation system and a power grid control scenario, demonstrating its ability to thwart deception attacks while maintaining operational objectives. The results highlight the feasibility of proactively embedding robustness into supervisory design, offering a scalable solution for securing CPS against evolving cyber threats.

title: Overlapping-sample Mendelian randomisation with multiple exposures: A Bayesian approach
text:
Our Bayesian overlapping-sample Mendelian randomisation (MR) framework was applied to evaluate causal relationships between three exposures (body mass index [BMI], systolic blood pressure [SBP], and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [LDL-C]) and a single outcome (coronary artery disease [CAD]). Using data from 86,342 UK Biobank participants, we identified 127 independent SNPs associated with at least one exposure (p < 5×10⁻⁸). The Bayesian model estimated posterior causal effects while accounting for sample overlap and correlated exposures.  
For BMI, the posterior mean odds ratio (OR) for CAD was 1.42 (95% credible interval [CI]: 1.28–1.57), indicating a 42% higher risk per standard deviation (SD) increase in BMI. SBP showed a weaker association (OR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.02–1.25), while LDL-C had an OR of 1.21 (95% CI: 1.09–1.34). Notably, the model attenuated the effect of LDL-C by 18% compared to univariate MR, reflecting shared genetic instruments with BMI and SBP.  
Heterogeneity statistics revealed moderate pleiotropy (I² = 0.32 for BMI, 0.41 for SBP), which the Bayesian shrinkage prior effectively addressed. Posterior inclusion probabilities highlighted 23 SNPs driving BMI’s effect, with *FTO* and *MC4R* contributing 34% of the total signal. These results align with observational studies but provide stronger causal evidence by mitigating confounding and reverse causation. The Bayesian framework’s ability to jointly model exposures improved precision, as evidenced by narrower CIs compared to separate analyses. This approach demonstrates robustness in disentangling overlapping causal pathways in complex traits.

title: Distributed Consensus of Nonlinear Multi-Agent Systems With Mismatched Uncertainties and Unknown High-Frequency Gains (Extended Version)
text: In conclusion, this paper has addressed the challenging problem of achieving distributed consensus in nonlinear multi-agent systems subject to mismatched uncertainties and unknown high-frequency gains. By developing a novel adaptive control protocol that integrates robust control techniques with adaptive estimation mechanisms, we have successfully overcome the limitations imposed by mismatched disturbances and uncertain gain parameters. Theoretical analysis confirms the stability and convergence of the proposed approach, while simulation results demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving consensus under diverse operating conditions. Notably, the method exhibits robustness to parameter variations and external disturbances, making it suitable for practical applications where precise system modeling is difficult. Future work will explore extensions to more complex network topologies and the integration of event-triggered control strategies to reduce communication overhead while maintaining performance guarantees. This research contributes to advancing the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of distributed control in uncertain multi-agent systems.

title: Low-Cost Maximum Entropy Covariance Matrix Reconstruction Algorithm for Robust Adaptive Beamforming
text: This paper proposes a novel low-cost maximum entropy covariance matrix reconstruction algorithm tailored for robust adaptive beamforming applications. Traditional adaptive beamforming techniques often rely on accurate estimation of the covariance matrix of the received signal, which is susceptible to performance degradation in the presence of model mismatches, limited snapshot availability, or low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions. To address these challenges, the proposed algorithm leverages the principle of maximum entropy to reconstruct the covariance matrix by optimizing an entropy-based objective function, ensuring maximum uncertainty (or least commitment) beyond the available data constraints. This approach effectively mitigates the adverse effects of insufficient samples and enhances robustness against steering vector errors. The key innovation lies in its computational efficiency: by incorporating a low-rank approximation and iterative optimization framework, the algorithm significantly reduces computational complexity while preserving reconstruction accuracy. Furthermore, a diagonal loading-like regularization term is dynamically adjusted to balance noise suppression and mainlobe preservation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives, including sample covariance matrix inversion and robust Capon beamforming, in terms of output signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) and robustness under various mismatch scenarios. The algorithm’s low computational overhead makes it particularly suitable for real-time applications in large-scale antenna arrays and resource-constrained systems, such as wireless communications and radar signal processing.

title: Evolutionary dynamics of cryptocurrency transaction networks: An empirical study
text: The advent of cryptocurrencies, spearheaded by Bitcoin in 2009, has revolutionized the landscape of financial transactions by introducing decentralized, peer-to-peer networks that operate independently of traditional banking systems. Cryptocurrency transaction networks, characterized by their distributed ledger technology (DLT), have garnered significant attention from researchers, policymakers, and investors due to their potential to disrupt conventional financial infrastructures. These networks exhibit complex, dynamic behaviors shaped by interactions among diverse participants, including individual users, institutional investors, and miners, whose collective actions drive the evolution of network topology and transaction patterns over time. Despite the growing body of literature on cryptocurrency markets, empirical studies focusing on the evolutionary dynamics of transaction networks remain limited, particularly in capturing longitudinal changes and identifying underlying mechanisms influencing network growth and resilience. This study aims to fill this gap by conducting a comprehensive empirical analysis of cryptocurrency transaction networks, examining how structural properties, user behaviors, and external factors collectively shape their evolution.

title: Using detrended deconvolution foreign exchange network to identify currency status
text: The identification of currency status—whether a currency acts as a global benchmark, a regional anchor, or a peripheral player—is critical for understanding international monetary dynamics and assessing financial stability risks. Traditional methods often rely on static network centrality measures or bilateral exchange rate models, which may overlook temporal dependencies and nonlinear interactions in high-frequency foreign exchange (FX) data. This paper introduces a novel framework, the Detrended Deconvolution Foreign Exchange Network (DDFEN), to dynamically classify currency status by integrating detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) with deconvolution-based network inference. By decomposing FX rate time series into trend and fluctuation components, DDFEN isolates multiscale dependencies while mitigating nonstationarity biases inherent in raw data. A deconvolution algorithm then reconstructs a weighted, directed network where nodes represent currencies and edges capture directional influence across temporal scales. We apply this method to a dataset of 30 major currencies over 2000–2023, using rolling windows to track evolving network topologies. Our results reveal that traditional benchmarks like the USD and EUR exhibit persistent centrality, but emerging currencies (e.g., CNY, INR) demonstrate increasing interconnectedness during periods of policy intervention or market stress. A machine learning classifier trained on DDFEN-derived features achieves 89% accuracy in distinguishing currency tiers, outperforming baseline models that ignore temporal or multiscale effects. The framework also identifies early warning signals of currency regime shifts, such as the USD’s diminished dominance during the 2020 COVID-19 crisis. These findings advance monetary network analysis by providing a scalable, interpretable tool for policymakers and investors to monitor currency hierarchies in real time.

title: Sizing of Movable Energy Resources for Service Restoration and Reliability Enhancement
text:
The integration of movable energy resources (MERs), such as mobile energy storage systems and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technologies, has emerged as a promising strategy to enhance grid resilience and reliability in the face of increasing extreme weather events, aging infrastructure, and growing demand for uninterrupted power supply. Traditional approaches to service restoration following outages often rely on centralized generation and manual reconfiguration, which can be slow, costly, and insufficient for modern distributed energy systems. MERs offer a flexible, decentralized alternative by enabling rapid deployment to critical load points, reducing restoration times, and providing ancillary services to stabilize the grid during transient conditions. However, the effectiveness of MERs in improving system reliability depends heavily on their optimal sizing and strategic placement, which must account for dynamic load patterns, renewable intermittency, and network constraints.  

Accurate sizing of MERs remains a complex challenge due to the stochastic nature of both supply and demand, as well as the interdependencies between restoration objectives and long-term reliability metrics. Existing methodologies often oversimplify these interactions, leading to suboptimal resource allocation or overinvestment in capacity. This research addresses this gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for MER sizing that integrates service restoration priorities with reliability enhancement goals under uncertainty. By leveraging advanced optimization techniques and real-world data analytics, the framework evaluates trade-offs between cost, response time, and system robustness, ensuring MERs are dimensioned to meet both immediate and sustained operational needs.  

The study contributes to the body of knowledge by developing a multi-objective sizing model that explicitly incorporates spatiotemporal variability in load demand, renewable generation, and failure probabilities. Unlike previous works, which focus on isolated aspects of MER deployment, this approach provides a holistic perspective, enabling utilities and policymakers to balance economic efficiency with resilience targets. The findings offer actionable insights for designing scalable MER fleets capable of adapting to evolving grid conditions, ultimately supporting the transition toward a more resilient and sustainable energy infrastructure.

title: Custom Edge-Element FEM Solver and its Application to Eddy-Current Simulation of Realistic 2M-Element Human Brain Phantom
text:
The custom edge-element finite element method (FEM) solver demonstrated robust performance in simulating eddy-current distributions within a realistic 2-million-element human brain phantom under a 10 kHz sinusoidal excitation. Computational results revealed a peak eddy-current density of 12.3 mA/m² concentrated in the basal ganglia and thalamic regions, aligning with anatomical conductivity contrasts (white matter: 0.12 S/m; gray matter: 0.33 S/m; cerebrospinal fluid: 1.65 S/m). The solver achieved a relative error of 1.8% in total induced power (12.7 mW vs. analytical benchmarks for simplified geometries) and maintained convergence within 4 iterations using an algebraic multigrid preconditioner, reducing solution time by 62% compared to unpreconditioned runs. Memory usage peaked at 14.2 GB for the full phantom, with linear scaling observed for sub-domain decompositions.  

Spatial validation against MRI-derived conductivity maps showed 89% correlation in current density hotspots, with discrepancies attributed to simplified sulcal geometry in the phantom model. Frequency-dependent analysis revealed a 3.2-fold increase in superficial eddy currents (cortex) when frequency elevated from 1 kHz to 10 kHz, consistent with skin-effect theory. The solver’s parallel efficiency reached 87% on 16 CPU cores, though load imbalance in heterogeneous brain regions caused a 12% performance drop at 32 cores. These results confirm the solver’s suitability for large-scale biophysical simulations, though future work will address geometric fidelity and dynamic conductivity variations.

title: Analysis of Safe Ultrawideband Human-Robot Communication in Automated Collaborative Warehouse
text: In conclusion, this study has comprehensively analyzed the feasibility and safety of ultrawideband (UWB) technology for human-robot communication in automated collaborative warehouses. Through rigorous experimentation and simulation, we demonstrated that UWB systems offer high-precision localization, low latency, and robustness against multipath interference, making them well-suited for dynamic warehouse environments. Our findings confirm that UWB can effectively support safe human-robot collaboration by enabling real-time tracking of both human workers and robots, thereby reducing collision risks and enhancing operational efficiency. The integration of UWB with existing safety protocols, such as speed and separation monitoring, further strengthens its applicability in industrial settings. Additionally, our analysis of regulatory compliance and electromagnetic exposure ensures that UWB implementations adhere to international safety standards, addressing potential health concerns. Future work should focus on optimizing UWB antenna designs for wearable devices and exploring its integration with advanced AI-driven collision avoidance algorithms. Overall, UWB technology presents a promising solution for enhancing safety and productivity in next-generation collaborative warehouses, paving the way for more intelligent and human-centric automation systems.

title: Robust Transient Stability Constrained Optimal Power Flow with Power Flow Routers Considering Renewable Uncertainties
text: This paper proposes a robust transient stability constrained optimal power flow (RTS-COPF) framework integrating power flow routers (PFRs) to address renewable uncertainties in modern power systems. The approach enhances system resilience by incorporating transient stability margins into the optimization process while dynamically adjusting power flow paths through PFRs. A two-stage robust optimization model is developed, where the first stage determines baseline generator dispatch and PFR configurations, and the second stage employs affine decision rules to hedge against worst-case renewable fluctuations within predefined uncertainty sets. The transient stability constraints are formulated using time-domain simulation-based surrogate models to ensure computational tractability. Case studies on the IEEE 39-bus and 118-bus systems demonstrate that the proposed method improves stability margins by 15-20% compared to traditional deterministic approaches while reducing operational costs by 8-12% through optimal PFR placement and adaptive control. The framework exhibits strong robustness against ±20% wind power variations, validating its effectiveness for high-renewable penetration scenarios.

title: Weather regimes linked to daily precipitation anomalies in Northern Chile
text: The arid and semi-arid regions of Northern Chile, encompassing the Atacama Desert and adjacent areas, are among the driest places on Earth, with precipitation events being rare yet highly variable in both space and time. Understanding the drivers of daily precipitation anomalies in this region is crucial for improving water resource management, agricultural planning, and disaster preparedness, particularly in the context of ongoing climate change. Precipitation variability in Northern Chile is influenced by a complex interplay of large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns, local topography, and oceanic conditions. Among these, weather regimes—persistent and recurrent large-scale atmospheric configurations—play a pivotal role in modulating precipitation extremes. Previous studies have identified key weather regimes over the Southeast Pacific and adjacent South American continent, such as the Southeast Pacific Subtropical High (SPSH) and the Bolivian High, which exert significant control over moisture transport and convergence processes. However, the specific weather regimes linked to daily precipitation anomalies in Northern Chile, particularly at fine temporal scales, remain poorly understood. This study aims to address this gap by systematically identifying and characterizing the dominant weather regimes associated with anomalous precipitation events in Northern Chile, using a combination of reanalysis data and observational records. The findings will enhance our understanding of precipitation dynamics in this water-stressed region and provide a foundation for improving seasonal forecasting and climate adaptation strategies.

title: Security Analysis for Distributed IoT-Based Industrial Automation
text: The integration of distributed Internet of Things (IoT) devices in industrial automation systems has significantly enhanced operational efficiency and flexibility but has concurrently introduced complex security challenges. This paper presents a comprehensive security analysis of distributed IoT-based industrial automation environments, focusing on the identification and assessment of vulnerabilities across hardware, software, and communication layers. We examine threats such as unauthorized access, data tampering, and denial-of-service attacks, which can disrupt critical industrial processes and compromise safety. By employing a systematic approach that combines threat modeling, risk assessment, and empirical testing, we evaluate the resilience of common IoT architectures used in industrial settings. Our findings highlight specific weaknesses in authentication mechanisms, data encryption, and network segmentation that can be exploited by adversaries. Furthermore, we propose a multi-layered security framework that incorporates intrusion detection systems, anomaly-based monitoring, and adaptive access control to mitigate identified risks. The study contributes to the body of knowledge by offering practical guidelines for enhancing the security posture of distributed IoT-based industrial automation systems, ensuring both operational continuity and data integrity in the face of evolving cyber threats.

title: Clinical connectivity map for drug repurposing: using laboratory tests to bridge drugs and diseases
text:
Drug repurposing—the identification of new therapeutic uses for existing medications—has emerged as a critical strategy to accelerate the development of safe, cost-effective treatments for unmet medical needs. Traditional approaches, such as target-based screening or observational studies, often face limitations due to incomplete mechanistic understanding of diseases or the slow pace of clinical validation. However, the integration of real-world clinical data, particularly laboratory test results, offers a promising avenue to uncover hidden relationships between drugs and diseases. Laboratory tests, routinely collected in clinical practice, provide objective, quantitative measures of physiological and pathological states, serving as dynamic biomarkers of disease progression and treatment response. By systematically analyzing these data, researchers can construct a "clinical connectivity map" that links drugs to diseases through shared patterns of test abnormalities, revealing novel repurposing opportunities.  

This study introduces a computational framework that leverages large-scale electronic health records (EHRs) to identify drug-disease associations based on laboratory test dynamics. Unlike prior methods relying on gene expression or adverse event data, our approach focuses on measurable clinical phenotypes, enabling the discovery of repurposable drugs even when their molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. By analyzing millions of lab test results across diverse patient populations, we quantify how drugs influence disease-relevant biomarkers, providing evidence for therapeutic effects beyond their original indications.  

The proposed method addresses key challenges in drug repurposing, including the need for scalable, patient-centric evidence and the ability to prioritize candidates with high translational potential. Our findings demonstrate the utility of lab-driven connectivity mapping in identifying underrecognized drug-disease relationships, offering a practical tool to complement existing computational and experimental strategies. This work underscores the value of mining clinical data to bridge the gap between bench research and bedside application, accelerating the repurposing pipeline for complex and emerging diseases.

title: Modeling, Vibration Control, and Trajectory Tracking of a Kinematically Constrained Planar Hybrid Cable-Driven Parallel Robot
text: The vibration control and trajectory tracking performance of the planar hybrid cable-driven parallel robot were evaluated through simulations and experiments. For vibration suppression, a PID controller reduced residual oscillations by 62% (from 8.2 mm to 3.1 mm peak-to-peak displacement) during a step input test at 1 Hz, while a sliding mode controller (SMC) achieved an 81% reduction (to 1.5 mm) under identical conditions. The SMC demonstrated superior robustness, with oscillations decaying within 0.3 seconds versus 0.8 seconds for PID. Trajectory tracking experiments using a circular path (radius = 0.15 m, velocity = 0.2 m/s) revealed a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 2.4 mm with PID and 1.1 mm with SMC, attributed to the latter’s reduced sensitivity to cable stiffness variations (modeled as ±15% uncertainty). Frequency response analysis showed a 12% wider bandwidth (4.2 Hz vs. 3.7 Hz) for SMC, enabling faster dynamic responses. However, PID exhibited 18% lower steady-state energy consumption (12.4 W vs. 15.1 W) due to smoother control signals. These results confirm that SMC excels in vibration damping and accuracy but requires optimization to balance energy efficiency. The hybrid robot’s kinematic constraints, validated via a 0.5% maximum end-effector orientation error, ensured stable operation within the designed workspace, aligning with simulation predictions.

title: An Algorithm to find Superior Fitness on NK Landscapes under High Complexity: Muddling Through
text:
In this study, we introduced a novel algorithm designed to navigate NK landscapes under conditions of high complexity, where traditional optimization methods often falter due to ruggedness and interdependencies among variables. Our approach, termed "Muddling Through," leverages adaptive local search with stochastic perturbations to escape suboptimal fitness peaks, combined with a memory-guided mechanism that prioritizes promising regions of the landscape. Empirical evaluations across a range of NK configurations demonstrate that Muddling Through significantly outperforms established benchmarks, particularly in highly epistatic environments where the fitness landscape is most challenging. Notably, the algorithm’s ability to dynamically adjust its exploration-exploitation balance allows it to maintain robust performance even as problem complexity increases, a critical advantage in real-world applications where computational resources are limited and problem structures are unpredictable.  

These findings contribute to the broader understanding of heuristic search in complex spaces by emphasizing the value of flexibility and incremental progress over rigid, global optimization strategies. While Muddling Through does not guarantee global optima, its practical efficacy in high-dimensional, nonlinear settings underscores its potential for applications in evolutionary computation, operations research, and bioinformatics. Future work will explore hybridizations with other metaheuristics to further enhance scalability, as well as theoretical analyses of its convergence properties under varying landscape topologies. Ultimately, this research reinforces the notion that "muddling through"—a deliberate, adaptive, and opportunistic approach—can yield superior results in domains where perfection is elusive and complexity is inherent.

title: Sustainable financing of permanent CO2 disposal through a Carbon Takeback Obligation
text: This paper explores a novel policy mechanism, the Carbon Takeback Obligation (CTBO), as a means to achieve sustainable financing for permanent carbon dioxide (CO2) disposal. As global climate goals increasingly demand deep decarbonization across all sectors, including those with hard-to-abate emissions, the need for reliable and scalable negative emissions technologies becomes critical. Permanent CO2 disposal, such as through geological storage or mineral carbonation, offers a durable solution but faces significant financial barriers due to high upfront costs and long-term liability risks. The CTBO is proposed as a market-based regulatory approach that requires fossil fuel producers and importers to ensure a proportionate volume of CO2 generated from their products is captured and permanently stored. By internalizing the cost of disposal within the supply chain, this mechanism creates a stable revenue stream to support the development and deployment of carbon capture and storage (CCS) infrastructure. The study evaluates the economic viability, policy feasibility, and environmental effectiveness of CTBO through a combination of theoretical modeling and case study analysis. Key findings indicate that CTBO can incentivize private sector investment in CCS while minimizing competitive distortions and ensuring compliance through traceable carbon accounting systems. Furthermore, the mechanism aligns with existing international trade regulations and can be adapted to various national contexts. The paper concludes that CTBO presents a promising avenue for bridging the financing gap in permanent CO2 disposal, contributing to net-zero emissions targets without relying solely on public subsidies or volatile carbon markets.

title: Modeling a Nonlinear Biophysical Trend Followed by Long-Memory Equilibrium with Unknown Change Point
text: The accurate modeling of complex biophysical systems has long been a cornerstone of scientific inquiry, particularly in fields such as ecology, climate science, and neurobiology, where nonlinear dynamics and long-term memory effects are prevalent. These systems often exhibit intricate patterns characterized by nonlinear trends, where variables evolve in a non-additive manner, coupled with long-memory equilibrium processes that reflect persistent dependencies over extended timescales. A critical challenge in such modeling arises when the underlying system undergoes an abrupt structural change at an unknown point in time, known as a change point. This change point can significantly alter the system's dynamic behavior, rendering traditional stationary models inadequate. Despite the importance of capturing these features, existing methodologies frequently struggle to simultaneously account for nonlinearity, long-memory properties, and unknown change points within a unified framework. This gap in the literature motivates the current study, which aims to develop a novel statistical model that integrates these complexities. By doing so, we seek to enhance the understanding of biophysical systems that exhibit such multifaceted dynamics, providing researchers with a robust tool for analyzing time-series data in environments where change is both inevitable and poorly understood.

title: Finite-time stabilization in optimal time of homogeneous quasilinear hyperbolic systems in one dimensional space
text: This paper addresses the finite-time stabilization problem for a class of homogeneous quasilinear hyperbolic systems in one-dimensional space, focusing on achieving stabilization in optimal time. We investigate systems described by first-order partial differential equations with variable coefficients, where the nonlinearity arises from homogeneous flux functions of degree one. By employing a backstepping approach combined with a novel scaling transformation, we derive explicit feedback control laws that ensure finite-time convergence of the system state to zero. The optimality of the stabilization time is established by constructing a Lyapunov function and analyzing the decay rate of the system energy. Our results demonstrate that the minimal stabilization time is determined by the system's inherent characteristics, such as the propagation speeds and coupling structure. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical findings, illustrating rapid stabilization for both scalar and vector cases. This work provides a systematic framework for designing optimal finite-time controllers for hyperbolic PDE systems with applications in fluid flow control and traffic management.

title: Market laws
text:
The concept of “market laws” has long been central to economic theory and policy, yet its nuanced implications for modern economies remain a subject of ongoing debate. Broadly defined, market laws refer to the foundational principles and mechanisms—such as supply and demand, competition, and price signals—that govern the allocation of resources in free and regulated markets alike. These laws are not merely abstract constructs; they shape the dynamics of industries, influence consumer behavior, and determine the success or failure of businesses. While classical economists like Adam Smith and David Ricardo emphasized the self-regulating nature of markets, contemporary scholars increasingly recognize that market laws operate within complex systems influenced by technological innovation, globalization, and regulatory frameworks. This tension between theoretical ideals and real-world outcomes underscores the need to critically examine how market laws function in practice, particularly in an era marked by rapid change and systemic interconnectedness.  

Historically, market laws have been framed as universal truths, with neoclassical economics positioning them as immutable forces driven by rational actors. However, empirical evidence suggests that these laws are often contingent on contextual factors, including institutional structures, cultural norms, and power imbalances. For instance, monopolistic practices or information asymmetry can distort market outcomes, challenging the assumption of perfect competition. Similarly, the rise of digital platforms has introduced network effects and data-driven dynamics that redefine traditional notions of supply and demand. These developments raise critical questions: To what extent do market laws remain relevant in shaping economic activity, and how must they adapt to address emerging challenges such as inequality, environmental degradation, and technological disruption?  

This paper seeks to explore the evolving role of market laws in contemporary economies, analyzing their theoretical foundations, practical applications, and limitations. By integrating insights from behavioral economics, institutional theory, and case studies of industries undergoing transformation, the study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of how market laws interact with external forces to produce diverse economic outcomes. The findings have implications for policymakers, businesses, and scholars seeking to navigate the complexities of modern markets while balancing efficiency, equity, and sustainability.

title: Challenging Eukaryogenesis: The Story of the Eukaryotic Ancestor
text:
Our comparative genomic analysis of 1,250 prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes revealed key insights into the evolutionary trajectory of eukaryotic ancestry. Phylogenetic reconstruction using a concatenated dataset of 478 conserved proteins placed the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA) within a clade sharing 32% ± 4% gene homology with Asgard archaea, significantly higher than the 18% ± 3% observed in other archaeal lineages (p < 0.001). This supports the hypothesis that LECA emerged from an Asgard-like progenitor.  

Metabolic reconstruction identified 127 eukaryotic signature proteins (ESPs) in Asgard genomes, including homologs of actin (89% identity) and tubulin (76% identity), suggesting early cytoskeletal evolution. However, mitochondrial endosymbiosis markers (e.g., ATP synthase subunits) were absent in all Asgard lineages, implying endosymbiosis occurred post-LECA.  

Structural modeling of Asgard ESCRT-III proteins revealed a 68% similarity to eukaryotic homologs, indicating partial pre-adaptation for membrane remodeling. Conversely, nuclear pore complex components were entirely absent, suggesting this feature evolved de novo in eukaryotes.  

Bayesian divergence dating estimated LECA’s emergence at 1.8–2.1 billion years ago, aligning with fossil evidence of early eukaryotes. These findings collectively challenge the “prokaryote-to-eukaryote” leap model, instead proposing a mosaic origin where Asgard archaea contributed core machinery, while later innovations (e.g., mitochondria, nucleus) drove eukaryotic complexity.

title: A Horserace of Volatility Models for Cryptocurrency: Evidence from Bitcoin Spot and Option Markets
text: In this study, we conducted a comprehensive horserace of volatility models applied to Bitcoin spot and option markets, evaluating their performance in capturing the unique dynamics of cryptocurrency volatility. Our findings reveal that while traditional GARCH-type models provide a baseline for volatility estimation, they are consistently outperformed by more sophisticated approaches, particularly those incorporating realized measures or machine learning techniques. The HAR-RV model, augmented with jump components, demonstrated superior accuracy in forecasting Bitcoin’s volatility, especially during periods of heightened market stress. Meanwhile, machine learning methods, such as neural networks, exhibited remarkable adaptability to non-linear patterns but faced challenges in interpretability and overfitting risks. Option-implied volatility, derived from Bitcoin derivatives, emerged as a valuable complementary signal, offering forward-looking insights that enhance predictive power when integrated with time-series models. These results underscore the importance of model flexibility and data integration in capturing the idiosyncratic risks of cryptocurrencies. For practitioners, our analysis suggests that hybrid models combining realized measures, implied volatility, and machine learning elements may offer the most robust framework for volatility forecasting in this asset class. Future research could explore the role of institutional factors, regulatory changes, and cross-market linkages in refining these models further, ensuring their relevance in an evolving digital asset landscape.

title: Learning under Invariable Bayesian Safety
text: This paper introduces a novel framework for learning under constraints, termed "Invariable Bayesian Safety," which integrates Bayesian inference with rigorous safety guarantees to ensure robust decision-making in dynamic environments. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) and Bayesian optimization methods often prioritize performance or exploration, potentially compromising safety in high-stakes applications such as healthcare, autonomous systems, and finance. To address this, we propose a safety-centric approach that maintains invariant safety conditions throughout the learning process by leveraging Bayesian uncertainty quantification and constraint satisfaction mechanisms. Our framework models safety constraints as probabilistic invariants, ensuring that the probability of violating critical thresholds remains below a predefined risk tolerance. This is achieved through a combination of Bayesian posterior updates and constrained optimization, where safety constraints are dynamically adjusted based on observed data while preserving statistical guarantees. We theoretically prove that the proposed method guarantees safety invariance with high probability and demonstrate its empirical effectiveness on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including safe robot navigation and algorithmic trading. Compared to existing safe RL techniques, our approach reduces constraint violations by up to 70% while maintaining comparable task performance. The results highlight the potential of Invariable Bayesian Safety to enable trustworthy, adaptive learning in safety-critical domains, bridging the gap between exploratory efficiency and risk-averse decision-making.

title: Social Engagement versus Learning Engagement -- An Exploratory Study of FutureLearn Learners
text: The advent of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) has revolutionized the landscape of higher education by providing unprecedented access to learning resources for a global audience. Among the various MOOC platforms, FutureLearn stands out due to its emphasis on social learning, distinguishing itself from traditional models that primarily focus on individual learning engagement. While learning engagement typically encompasses cognitive, emotional, and behavioral aspects of student interaction with course materials, social engagement highlights the collaborative and interactive dimensions of learning, such as discussions, peer feedback, and group activities. The interplay between these two forms of engagement is crucial for understanding learner experiences and outcomes in online environments. However, despite the growing body of literature on MOOCs, there remains a gap in empirical research exploring how social engagement compares to and influences learning engagement among FutureLearn participants. This exploratory study aims to address this gap by examining the dynamics between social and learning engagement, and their respective impacts on learner satisfaction and course completion rates. By analyzing data from a diverse cohort of FutureLearn users, this research seeks to provide insights into the effectiveness of social learning features and offer recommendations for optimizing MOOC design to enhance both social and learning engagement.

title: Kinetic-controlled hydrodynamics for multilane traffic models
text: This paper introduces a novel kinetic-controlled hydrodynamic framework for modeling multilane traffic flow, addressing limitations in traditional macroscopic models that struggle to capture lane-changing dynamics and microscopic interactions at scale. By integrating kinetic theory principles with hydrodynamic conservation laws, we derive a hierarchy of equations that couple lane-specific density, velocity, and momentum transfer mechanisms. The model incorporates a stochastic lane-changing probability function informed by driver decision-making processes, parameterized through empirical data on gap acceptance and lateral maneuver preferences. A key innovation is the use of a non-local collision operator to represent inter-lane interactions, enabling the capture of complex phenomena such as shockwave propagation across lanes and capacity drop at bottlenecks. We validate the framework using high-resolution trajectory data from a multi-lane highway, demonstrating improved accuracy in predicting lane-specific flow patterns and congestion onset compared to classical LWR and second-order models. The model's modular structure allows for scalable implementation across varying road geometries and traffic conditions. Numerical simulations reveal that lane-changing intensity significantly impacts macroscopic flow stability, with optimal lane-usage distributions emerging under moderate switching rates. We further analyze the model's thermodynamic limits, showing convergence to equilibrium speed distributions consistent with observed real-world traffic states. The findings suggest that kinetic-hydrodynamic coupling provides a robust theoretical basis for designing adaptive traffic control systems and intelligent infrastructure interventions. This work advances multiscale traffic modeling by bridging microscopic driver behavior with macroscopic flow characteristics, offering new tools for optimizing multilane road network performance under heterogeneous demand scenarios.

title: Investor Emotions and Earnings Announcements
text:
The relationship between investor emotions and financial market outcomes has garnered significant attention in behavioral finance, challenging the traditional assumption of rational decision-making under the Efficient Market Hypothesis. Earnings announcements, as pivotal corporate events, serve as critical moments for investors to process new information and adjust their expectations. However, the interplay between these announcements and investor sentiment remains underexplored, particularly in how emotional biases—such as overconfidence, loss aversion, or herd behavior—influence reactions to earnings surprises. While classical finance theory posits that markets efficiently incorporate such information, empirical evidence suggests that investor emotions can drive deviations from fundamental values, leading to short-term mispricing and increased volatility. This paper examines the nuanced dynamics between investor emotions and earnings announcements, aiming to clarify how psychological factors shape market responses to corporate disclosures.  

Prior research has established that earnings announcements trigger heightened trading activity and price adjustments, reflecting investors’ revisions of firm valuations. Yet, these adjustments are not always aligned with the magnitude or direction of the earnings surprise. Behavioral finance literature attributes such discrepancies to cognitive biases and emotional reactions, such as optimism during positive news or panic following negative disclosures. For instance, investors may overreact to initial earnings data due to anchoring biases or later correct their positions as emotions subside, resulting in post-announcement drift. Despite these insights, gaps persist in understanding how specific emotions—fear, greed, or regret—interact with institutional factors like analyst coverage or media sentiment to amplify or mitigate market reactions.  

This study contributes to the literature by integrating psychological theories of emotion with event-study methodologies to analyze investor behavior around earnings announcements. Using a sample of U.S. publicly traded firms, we explore whether emotional responses to earnings surprises vary across industries, firm sizes, or market conditions. By disentangling the role of sentiment from rational information processing, our findings offer implications for investors seeking to mitigate emotional biases and for regulators aiming to enhance market transparency. Ultimately, this work underscores the importance of accounting for human psychology in financial models, bridging the gap between theoretical assumptions and real-world market behavior.

title: Network desynchronization by non-Gaussian fluctuations
text:
Our experiments quantified the impact of non-Gaussian noise on network synchronization across 100-node Erdős–Rényi random graphs with a connection probability of 0.1. Under Gaussian noise (σ = 0.5), the network maintained a high average order parameter ⟨r⟩ = 0.92 ± 0.01, indicating strong synchronization. Introducing non-Gaussian Lévy noise (α = 1.5, β = 0) reduced ⟨r⟩ to 0.68 ± 0.03, with 23% of nodes desynchronizing entirely (r_i < 0.3). The critical noise intensity for desynchronization shifted from σ_c = 1.2 (Gaussian) to σ_c = 0.7 under Lévy noise, highlighting heightened vulnerability.  

Time-series analysis revealed intermittent phase slips in 15% of nodes under Lévy noise, absent in Gaussian regimes. Power spectral density plots showed a 1/f^α decay (α ≈ 1.2) for Lévy-driven fluctuations, contrasting with the Lorentzian profile of Gaussian noise. This aligns with theoretical predictions that heavy-tailed distributions disrupt collective rhythms via rare, high-magnitude events.  

Simulations with varying stability parameters (λ) demonstrated that networks with λ < 0.8 (weaker coupling) collapsed to ⟨r⟩ < 0.2 under Lévy noise, whereas Gaussian noise permitted partial synchronization (⟨r⟩ ≈ 0.5). These results suggest non-Gaussian noise imposes a stricter stability threshold, as heavy-tailed fluctuations overwhelm compensatory coupling mechanisms.  

Statistical tests (Kolmogorov–Smirnov, p < 0.01) confirmed that phase distributions under Lévy noise deviated significantly from Gaussian expectations, with excess kurtosis (γ₂ = 5.2) indicating leptokurtic behavior. Our findings underscore the critical role of noise statistics in network dynamics, with implications for power grids and neural systems where non-Gaussian perturbations are prevalent.

title: Inflation Dynamics of Financial Shocks
text:
This study has provided a nuanced exploration of the inflation dynamics triggered by financial shocks, integrating theoretical models with empirical evidence to elucidate the complex transmission mechanisms at play. Our findings underscore that financial shocks—whether originating from sudden shifts in credit availability, asset price collapses, or disruptions in banking sectors—exert significant but heterogeneous effects on inflation. Initially, such shocks often depress inflation through reduced aggregate demand, as tightened financial conditions constrain household spending and business investment. However, over time, the interaction between financial frictions and monetary policy responses can lead to divergent outcomes. In environments with anchored inflation expectations and credible central banks, accommodative policies may stabilize prices by counteracting demand shortfalls. Conversely, in settings where policy credibility is weak or financial imbalances are severe, prolonged low interest rates can fuel asset bubbles or supply-side bottlenecks, eventually reigniting inflationary pressures.  

The empirical analysis, leveraging high-frequency data and structural VAR models, confirms that financial shocks account for a non-negligible portion of inflation volatility, particularly in advanced economies with deep financial markets. Moreover, the transmission varies across sectors: financial distress in housing markets tends to have stronger inflationary effects than shocks in equity markets, highlighting the role of household balance sheets in price dynamics.  

These insights carry critical implications for policymakers. First, central banks must adopt a holistic approach to monitoring financial stability, recognizing its direct link to inflation outcomes. Second, macroprudential tools should complement monetary policy to mitigate the buildup of financial vulnerabilities without undermining price stability. Finally, future research should explore how technological advancements, such as fintech and digital currencies, alter the propagation of financial shocks. As financial systems evolve, so too must our understanding of their interplay with inflation—a challenge that demands ongoing collaboration between academia and policymakers to safeguard economic resilience.

title: Prediction of short and long-term droughts using artificial neural networks and hydro-meteorological variables
text: This study presents a comprehensive framework for predicting short- and long-term droughts by integrating artificial neural networks (ANNs) with hydro-meteorological variables. Leveraging historical precipitation, temperature, soil moisture, and evapotranspiration data, we developed hybrid ANN models to capture nonlinear interactions among these variables and enhance drought forecasting accuracy. The methodology involves feature selection to identify critical predictors, optimization of ANN architectures using grid search and cross-validation, and evaluation against observed drought indices (e.g., Standardized Precipitation Index and Palmer Drought Severity Index). Results demonstrate that the proposed models outperform traditional statistical methods, achieving higher precision in both short-term (1–3 months) and long-term (6–12 months) predictions. Soil moisture and antecedent precipitation emerge as dominant predictors for short-term droughts, while temperature anomalies and large-scale climate indices (e.g., El Niño-Southern Oscillation) significantly influence long-term forecasts. This research provides actionable insights for water resource management and climate adaptation strategies, highlighting the potential of machine learning in advancing drought early warning systems.

title: Decentralized Safe Reactive Planning under TWTL Specifications
text:
In recent years, the development of autonomous systems has necessitated the integration of advanced planning and control mechanisms to ensure safe and efficient operation in dynamic and uncertain environments. Among the various challenges faced by these systems, the need for decentralized decision-making frameworks stands out prominently, particularly in multi-agent settings where coordination and safety are paramount. Traditional centralized approaches, while effective in certain scenarios, often struggle with scalability and robustness in large-scale systems due to their reliance on a single control entity. This limitation has spurred significant interest in decentralized methodologies that distribute computational tasks among multiple agents, enhancing flexibility and resilience.

A critical aspect of decentralized planning involves the incorporation of formal specifications that articulate desired system behaviors and safety constraints. Temporal logic specifications, such as Time-Windowed Temporal Logic (TWTL), provide a powerful and expressive framework for defining such requirements, enabling agents to reason about temporal and sequential aspects of their tasks. However, integrating TWTL specifications into decentralized planning introduces complex challenges, particularly in ensuring that individual agent decisions collectively satisfy global objectives while adhering to safety constraints.

This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a novel decentralized safe reactive planning framework under TWTL specifications. Our approach leverages local information and reactive strategies to enable agents to adapt dynamically to environmental changes and unexpected events, ensuring both safety and specification adherence. We present theoretical foundations for our framework, along with empirical evaluations demonstrating its effectiveness in various multi-agent scenarios.

title: Masks and COVID-19: a causal framework for imputing value to public-health interventions
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the critical role of public-health interventions in mitigating viral transmission, with mask-wearing emerging as a central, yet contentious, strategy. This paper introduces a causal framework to systematically evaluate the value of mask mandates and voluntary adoption in reducing SARS-CoV-2 spread, addressing challenges in attributing outcomes to interventions amidst confounding variables and heterogeneous adherence. Drawing on causal inference methodologies, including counterfactual analysis and structural equation modeling, we disentangle the direct and indirect effects of masking policies from concurrent measures such as social distancing, lockdowns, and vaccination rates. By integrating data from epidemiological studies, mobility reports, and behavioral surveys across 12 countries, we quantify the causal impact of masking on key metrics: infection rates, hospitalization burdens, and mortality. Our findings reveal that universal mask mandates reduced transmission by an estimated 23–30% in high-compliance settings, with greater efficacy in indoor environments and among high-risk populations. Voluntary masking, while less consistent, demonstrated measurable benefits when baseline adherence exceeded 40%. The framework also identifies critical mediators, such as policy timing, public trust, and access to high-quality masks, that modulate intervention effectiveness. We further propose a cost-benefit analysis incorporating healthcare savings, economic productivity, and equity considerations to impute the societal value of masking policies. This study advances a replicable methodology for evaluating public-health interventions, offering policymakers a tool to optimize resource allocation and communication strategies during pandemics. By clarifying the causal pathways linking masking to health outcomes, our work supports evidence-based decision-making to balance individual freedoms with collective safety in future crises.

title: Projection methods for solving split equilibrium problems
text:
The study of equilibrium problems has emerged as a central topic in optimization and applied mathematics, driven by their broad applicability in engineering, economics, and the natural sciences. These problems generalize classical optimization frameworks by incorporating multiple interacting constraints and objectives, often modeled through variational inequalities or fixed-point conditions. A particularly challenging subclass, known as split equilibrium problems (SEPs), extends this paradigm to scenarios where the solution must simultaneously satisfy equilibrium conditions in two or more interconnected spaces. This structure arises naturally in decentralized resource allocation, image restoration, and inverse problems, where data or constraints are distributed across distinct domains. Despite their relevance, SEPs pose significant computational hurdles due to their nonconvexity, nonsmoothness, and the need to coordinate solutions across subspaces. Traditional methods, such as gradient-based or proximal algorithms, often struggle with convergence guarantees or require stringent assumptions, motivating the development of specialized techniques.

Projection methods have gained prominence as a robust tool for addressing SEPs, leveraging their ability to handle complex constraints through geometric operations. By iteratively projecting onto feasible sets or approximating equilibrium conditions, these methods balance computational efficiency with theoretical rigor. Recent advancements have introduced hybrid approaches, combining projections with inertial terms, splitting strategies, or adaptive step sizes to accelerate convergence. However, challenges persist in ensuring global convergence, managing high-dimensional data, and adapting to dynamic environments. 

This paper explores novel projection-based algorithms tailored for SEPs, focusing on their convergence properties and practical performance. We propose a unified framework that integrates relaxed projection operators with adaptive parameter tuning, addressing limitations of existing methods in handling large-scale or noisy data. Theoretical analysis establishes strong convergence under mild assumptions, while numerical experiments on benchmark problems demonstrate the efficacy of our approach compared to state-of-the-art alternatives. Our contributions advance the understanding of projection methods in distributed optimization and provide scalable solutions for real-world applications requiring equilibrium computation across multiple domains.

title: Causal inference methods for small non-randomized studies: Methods and an application in COVID-19
text:
We applied three causal inference methods—inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE), and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART)—to estimate the causal effect of early corticosteroid administration (within 48 hours of hospitalization) on 30-day mortality in a cohort of 250 non-randomized COVID-19 patients (mean age 62.3 ± 15.1 years; 58% male). Baseline covariates included age, comorbidity burden (Charlson score), oxygen requirement, and inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, ferritin).  

IPTW yielded an average treatment effect (ATE) of -0.12 (95% CI: -0.22 to -0.02), suggesting a 12% absolute reduction in mortality risk with early corticosteroids. However, balance checks revealed residual imbalance in oxygen requirement (standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.18), indicating potential confounding. TMLE, which combines propensity score weighting with outcome regression, produced an ATE of -0.15 (95% CI: -0.25 to -0.05), with better covariate balance (all SMDs < 0.10). BART, a non-parametric machine learning approach, estimated an ATE of -0.17 (95% CI: -0.28 to -0.06), aligning closely with TMLE but with narrower confidence intervals, likely due to its flexibility in modeling non-linear interactions.
