We found that a small proportion of cases were responsible for a disproportionate number of secondary infections, underscoring the importance of identifying and isolating high-risk individuals quickly to mitigate outbreaks. The temporal patterns observed in our data suggest that timely interventions, such as social distancing measures and travel restrictions, played a significant role in flattening the epidemic curve during the initial phases. Additionally, our spatial analysis demonstrated that urban areas, particularly Seoul and Daegu, were hotspots for transmission, reflecting higher population density and mobility. These findings align with previous studies and provide empirical support for targeted public health responses. While our study offers valuable insights into the early transmission dynamics in South Korea, limitations such as potential underreporting of cases and incomplete contact tracing data should be acknowledged. Future research could explore the long-term impacts of these interventions and the evolution of the virus over time. Overall, this work contributes to a better understanding of COVID-19 transmission patterns and provides lessons that can inform global efforts to control the pandemic.

title: Randomized RX for target detection
text: This paper introduces a novel approach termed "Randomized RX" for target detection in hyperspectral imagery, addressing the limitations of traditional RX (Reed-Xiaoli) detectors that often suffer from reduced performance in heterogeneous backgrounds and high-dimensional data environments. The proposed method integrates random projection techniques with the RX framework to enhance robustness and computational efficiency. By projecting high-dimensional spectral data into a lower-dimensional randomized subspace, the algorithm preserves essential discriminative features while reducing noise sensitivity and computational complexity. We theoretically analyze the statistical properties of the randomized projections and demonstrate their effectiveness in improving target-to-clutter contrast. Experimental results on synthetic and real hyperspectral datasets show that Randomized RX achieves superior detection accuracy compared to conventional RX and other state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios with limited training samples or non-Gaussian background distributions. The approach offers a scalable solution for real-time target detection applications in remote sensing and surveillance systems.

title: A rank-3 network representation for single-affiliation systems
text: Network representation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for analyzing complex systems, enabling the extraction of meaningful features from relational data through low-dimensional embeddings. While significant progress has been made in modeling multi-affiliated systems—where entities belong to multiple overlapping groups—the representation of single-affiliation systems remains underexplored. In such systems, entities are uniquely assigned to one group, yet their interactions often exhibit hierarchical or multi-layered structures that conventional pairwise network models fail to capture. For instance, academic collaboration networks typically associate researchers with single institutions, but their research outputs may reflect institutional hierarchies (e.g., departments, faculties) or interdisciplinary influences. Similarly, biological networks may group genes into single functional categories while their interactions span multiple regulatory layers. Addressing this gap, we propose a rank-3 network representation framework that extends traditional graph-based models by incorporating a third-order tensor to encode hierarchical affiliation-aware interactions. Unlike existing methods that rely on pairwise edge weights or community partitions, our approach explicitly models triadic relationships between entities, their primary affiliations, and latent hierarchical roles. This enables a more nuanced understanding of single-affiliation systems by preserving structural information across organizational layers. We validate the framework through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority in tasks such as link prediction and role identification compared to baseline methods.

title: ConvGRU in Fine-grained Pitching Action Recognition for Action Outcome Prediction
text: Fine-grained pitching action recognition is critical for predicting outcomes in baseball, such as pitch type, speed, and trajectory, yet remains challenging due to subtle inter-class differences and complex temporal dynamics. Traditional models often struggle to capture long-range dependencies and spatial-temporal interactions in sequential pitching motions. This paper introduces a novel framework leveraging ConvGRU (Convolutional Gated Recurrent Unit) networks to address these challenges by integrating convolutional operations for spatial feature extraction with recurrent units for temporal modeling. The proposed architecture employs a hierarchical ConvGRU structure to encode multi-scale motion patterns across video frames, enabling robust discrimination between visually similar pitching actions (e.g., fastball vs. slider). To enhance discriminative power, we incorporate a dual-stream design that separately processes skeletal joint data and optical flow features, followed by a late-fusion mechanism to combine complementary information. Additionally, we introduce a temporal attention module to dynamically weight salient frames, improving focus on critical motion phases (e.g., wrist rotation or leg drive). Extensive experiments on a custom dataset of professional baseball pitches demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving 92.3% accuracy in pitch type classification and reducing mean absolute error in speed prediction by 18.7%. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the ConvGRU’s spatial-temporal fusion and attention mechanism in capturing fine-grained motion nuances. These findings suggest that our approach provides a scalable solution for real-time action outcome prediction, with potential applications in athlete training, game strategy optimization, and sports analytics.

title: One-Shot Object Localization Using Learnt Visual Cues via Siamese Networks
text:
Object localization—the task of identifying and precisely delineating target objects within a scene—is a foundational challenge in computer vision with applications spanning robotics, autonomous driving, and medical imaging. Traditional methods often rely on extensive training datasets with annotated bounding boxes or segmentation masks, requiring substantial human effort and limiting scalability to novel object categories. One-shot learning, which aims to generalize from a single exemplar, offers a compelling alternative but introduces unique challenges in balancing accuracy and adaptability. This paper introduces a novel approach for one-shot object localization using Siamese networks, leveraging learnt visual cues to bridge the gap between limited training data and robust spatial reasoning.  

Siamese networks, originally designed for metric learning and similarity comparison, are repurposed here to encode discriminative features from both a query image and a single exemplar. By training the network to maximize inter-class separation while minimizing intra-class variance, the model learns to identify shared visual patterns indicative of the target object’s presence and location. Unlike existing methods that rely on pre-defined templates or heuristic-based matching, our approach dynamically adapts to variations in object appearance, scale, and orientation through end-to-end optimization.  

The proposed framework demonstrates promising results on benchmark datasets, achieving competitive localization accuracy with significantly reduced annotation requirements. By integrating attention mechanisms and multi-scale feature fusion, the model further enhances its ability to focus on relevant regions while suppressing background noise. This work contributes to the growing field of few-shot learning by providing a scalable, data-efficient solution for real-world scenarios where labeled data is scarce or costly to acquire.

title: Learning Undirected Graphs in Financial Markets
text:
Our experiments evaluated the performance of the proposed Bayesian structural learning framework on synthetic and real-world financial datasets. For synthetic data, we generated 100-node undirected graphs with 200 edges, reflecting sparse market connectivity. The algorithm achieved a precision of 0.89 and recall of 0.82 (F1 = 0.85) in edge recovery under 1,000 samples, outperforming LASSO-based methods (F1 = 0.73) and PC algorithm (F1 = 0.68) due to its robustness to noise.  

In real-world data, we analyzed daily returns of 50 S&P 500 stocks from 2018–2023. The learned graph revealed clusters aligned with sectors (e.g., Technology, Healthcare), with 78% of edges connecting stocks in the same sector versus 22% across sectors. Notably, the algorithm identified 15 edges between seemingly unrelated stocks (e.g., Microsoft and Johnson & Johnson), later validated by co-movement during the 2020 market crash (correlation = 0.72 vs. 0.31 pre-crash).  

Stability analysis showed that 92% of edges persisted across 80% of bootstrap samples, indicating robustness. However, performance degraded with fewer samples (n < 500), highlighting data dependency. Comparing to a threshold correlation method, our approach reduced false positives by 41% by penalizing spurious links via the graphical lasso regularization.  

The graph’s topology also revealed hubs (e.g., Apple, Amazon), whose removal increased average path length by 35%, suggesting systemic importance. During the 2022 inflation shock, stocks connected to energy-sector hubs exhibited 22% higher volatility, underscoring the graph’s predictive utility.  

These results demonstrate the framework’s ability to capture meaningful market structures, balancing sparsity and accuracy. Limitations include sensitivity to hyperparameters and computational cost (O(n³)), which we mitigate via parallelized edge screening. Future work will integrate temporal dynamics to model evolving dependencies.

title: Minimum wave speeds in monostable reaction-diffusion equations: sharp bounds by polynomial optimization
text: This paper investigates the minimum wave speeds of traveling wave solutions in monostable reaction-diffusion equations, which are pivotal in understanding the propagation dynamics of various physical, chemical, and biological systems. By leveraging advanced techniques from polynomial optimization, we derive sharp upper and lower bounds for these minimum speeds, addressing a longstanding challenge in the mathematical analysis of such equations. Our approach involves formulating the problem as a constrained optimization task, where the objective is to minimize the wave speed subject to the reaction-diffusion dynamics and boundary conditions. By employing polynomial approximations of the reaction term and utilizing semidefinite programming relaxations, we transform the infinite-dimensional problem into a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem that can be solved efficiently. The resulting bounds are shown to be tight in several benchmark cases, providing a rigorous framework for estimating minimum wave speeds without resorting to numerical simulations. We also demonstrate the applicability of our method to a range of monostable nonlinearities, highlighting its versatility and potential for further extensions to more complex reaction-diffusion models. This work contributes significantly to the theoretical foundation of reaction-diffusion systems and offers practical tools for analyzing wave propagation phenomena.

title: Long Distance Continuous Methane Emissions Monitoring with Dual Frequency Comb Spectroscopy: deployment and blind testing in complex emissions scenarios
text: Methane (CH₄), a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential approximately 28 times greater than carbon dioxide over a 100-year period, plays a critical role in climate change mitigation strategies. Accurate and continuous monitoring of methane emissions, particularly from distributed and remote sources such as oil and gas infrastructure, landfills, and agricultural operations, remains a significant challenge due to the complexity of emission scenarios and the need for high spatial-temporal resolution measurements. Traditional monitoring techniques, including point sensors and periodic sampling, often suffer from limited coverage, low sensitivity, and inability to capture transient emission events. Recent advancements in dual frequency comb spectroscopy (DFCS) have demonstrated unprecedented precision and rapid acquisition rates for trace gas detection, offering a transformative approach for real-time, long-distance methane monitoring. This study introduces a field-deployable DFCS system designed for continuous methane emissions monitoring and evaluates its performance through blind testing in complex, real-world emission scenarios to validate its robustness and accuracy.

title: Inference of a universal social scale and segregation measures using social connectivity kernels
text: This paper introduces a novel framework for inferring a universal social scale and quantifying segregation patterns using social connectivity kernels derived from large-scale network data. By leveraging the mathematical properties of graph kernels, we propose a method to map heterogeneous social interactions—spanning online and offline domains—into a continuous, comparable metric space that captures the strength and context of relational ties. This approach enables the derivation of a universal social scale, facilitating cross-platform comparisons of social structures. We further develop kernel-based segregation measures that account for both explicit group boundaries and latent homophily, addressing limitations of traditional indices by incorporating multi-hop connectivity and weighted interactions. Validated through synthetic networks and empirical analyses of urban mobility, online collaboration, and communication datasets, our framework reveals nuanced segregation dynamics across scales, from local neighborhoods to global communities. The results demonstrate that kernel-weighted interactions reduce biases in segregation estimation and provide insights into the interplay between physical proximity and digital connectivity in shaping social stratification. This work advances theoretical and computational tools for analyzing social complexity, offering scalable methods to assess inequality in diverse socio-technical systems.

title: Competition among Large and Heterogeneous Small Firms
text:
The dynamics of competition in modern markets are increasingly shaped by the coexistence of large, resource-dominant firms and a diverse array of smaller, heterogeneous enterprises. While traditional economic frameworks often emphasize the role of scale economies and market concentration in driving competitive outcomes, recent shifts—such as technological disruption, globalization, and evolving consumer preferences—have reshaped the landscape. Large firms leverage their capital, brand recognition, and supply-chain dominance to secure market share, yet smaller firms persist and even thrive by exploiting niche opportunities, agility, and localized knowledge. This duality challenges conventional assumptions about market structure, suggesting that competition is not merely a contest between similarly sized rivals but a complex interplay of strategies across firm sizes and capabilities. Understanding how these heterogeneous actors interact is critical for policymakers, entrepreneurs, and scholars seeking to foster innovation, equitable growth, and resilient economic ecosystems.  

Existing literature has extensively analyzed competition between large firms and homogeneous small businesses, such as in perfectly contestable markets or monopolistic competition models. However, less attention has been paid to scenarios where small firms exhibit significant heterogeneity in resources, expertise, and strategic objectives. This gap limits insights into how diversity among smaller players—ranging from tech startups to family-owned enterprises—alters competitive dynamics. For instance, while some small firms may adopt disruptive innovations to challenge incumbents, others might focus on hyper-local markets or sustainable practices, creating multi-layered competitive pressures. Furthermore, the rise of digital platforms and decentralized production networks has lowered entry barriers, enabling smaller firms to compete globally while retaining flexibility.  

This study investigates the mechanisms through which large firms and heterogeneous small firms coexist and compete, emphasizing the role of innovation, resource allocation, and institutional factors. By analyzing sector-specific case studies and cross-regional data, we explore how small firms’ diversity influences market outcomes, including pricing strategies, entry barriers, and industry evolution. Our findings challenge the notion that size alone determines competitive advantage, highlighting instead the importance of adaptability, strategic positioning, and ecosystem integration. The implications extend beyond theory, offering actionable insights for designing policies that support inclusive growth without stifling the dynamism of smaller enterprises.

title: How Do Open Source Software Contributors Perceive and Address Usability? Valued Factors, Practices, and Challenges
text: Survey responses (n=223) revealed that 78% of contributors prioritize usability as “very important,” yet only 42% reported formal usability training. Documentation (89%) and intuitive design (81%) were ranked highest among valued factors, while accessibility (53%) and localization (39%) were deemed less critical. Open-source projects with dedicated usability teams (31% of cases) showed a 40% higher satisfaction rate among users compared to projects without such teams (p<0.01). Interviews highlighted that 65% of contributors rely on ad-hoc methods like community feedback (e.g., GitHub issues) to identify usability issues, while only 28% use structured heuristic evaluations. Key challenges included resource constraints (cited by 72%) and conflicting priorities between developers and end-users (59%). Contributors in large projects (100+ contributors) were 2.3x more likely to implement usability testing than those in smaller projects (p=0.03), suggesting scalability influences practice adoption. These findings underscore a gap between perceived importance of usability and systematic implementation, driven largely by limited resources and fragmented workflows.

title: GPU-Accelerated Drug Discovery with Docking on the Summit Supercomputer: Porting, Optimization, and Application to COVID-19 Research
text: In this study, we successfully demonstrated the power of GPU-accelerated drug discovery by porting and optimizing a molecular docking workflow to the Summit supercomputer, one of the world’s most powerful computing systems. Through careful optimization of memory management, parallel task distribution, and GPU kernel performance, we achieved substantial speedups, enabling the screening of billions of compounds in a fraction of the time required by traditional CPU-based methods. This capability was applied to COVID-19 research, where we rapidly evaluated a large library of potential inhibitors against key viral protein targets, identifying several high-affinity candidates for further experimental validation. Our results highlight the transformative potential of exascale computing in accelerating drug discovery, particularly in urgent health crises. The methodologies and optimizations developed here are not limited to SARS-CoV-2 but can be extended to other diseases, offering a scalable framework for future drug development efforts. As supercomputing resources continue to advance, GPU-accelerated docking will play an increasingly vital role in bridging computational and experimental drug discovery, ultimately reducing the time and cost of bringing life-saving therapies to patients.

title: Valuation Models Applied to Value-Based Management. Application to the Case of UK Companies with Problems
text: This paper explores the integration of valuation models within the framework of value-based management (VBM), focusing on their application to UK companies facing operational or financial challenges. VBM emphasizes aligning corporate strategies with shareholder value creation, yet its practical implementation often encounters difficulties when firms confront structural inefficiencies, market volatility, or legacy issues. The study evaluates three widely used valuation methodologies—discounted cash flow (DCF), residual income models (RIM), and market multiples—by applying them to a sample of distressed or underperforming UK-listed companies. Through comparative analysis, the research identifies scenario-specific strengths and limitations of each model, highlighting how DCF’s reliance on long-term cash flow projections may overlook near-term liquidity risks, while RIM’s focus on accounting-based residual earnings offers insights into sustainable profitability. Market multiples, though sensitive to sector-wide sentiment, provide benchmarking opportunities but risk mispricing during economic downturns. The case studies reveal that hybrid approaches combining model outputs with qualitative risk assessments enhance accuracy in turbulent environments. The findings contribute to debates on VBM’s adaptability by demonstrating how tailored valuation frameworks can better inform turnaround strategies, stakeholder communication, and resource allocation in crisis-affected firms. Practical implications for managers, investors, and policymakers are discussed, emphasizing the need for dynamic model calibration to reflect evolving macroeconomic and industry-specific risks.

title: Introduction of water-vapor broadening coefficients and their temperature dependence exponents into the HITRAN database, Part I: CO2, N2O, CO, CH4, O2, NH3, and H2S
text: The accurate modeling of atmospheric radiative transfer and remote sensing applications relies heavily on the availability of comprehensive and reliable spectroscopic databases. Among the critical parameters stored in such databases, line-broadening coefficients and their temperature dependence exponents play a pivotal role in determining the spectral line shapes under varying atmospheric conditions. Water vapor, being the most abundant and variable greenhouse gas, significantly influences the broadening of spectral lines of other molecules through collision processes. Despite its importance, the water-vapor broadening coefficients and associated temperature dependence exponents for many atmospheric species remain inadequately characterized or absent in widely used databases such as HITRAN (High-Resolution Transmission Molecular Absorption Database). This work aims to introduce newly measured and compiled water-vapor broadening coefficients along with their temperature dependence exponents for several key atmospheric molecules, including CO2, N2O, CO, CH4, O2, NH3, and H2S, into the HITRAN database, thereby enhancing its accuracy and applicability for atmospheric studies.

title: High-Speed Robot Navigation using Predicted Occupancy Maps
text: This paper introduces a novel approach for high-speed robot navigation in dynamic environments by leveraging predicted occupancy maps (POMs). Traditional navigation methods often rely on static or near-real-time sensor data, limiting their ability to anticipate changes in the environment and respond proactively. Our method integrates a predictive model that forecasts the future state of obstacles using historical and current sensor readings, generating a time-varying occupancy map. This allows the robot to plan trajectories that account for both current and anticipated future obstacle positions, significantly improving navigation performance at high speeds. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive simulations and real-world experiments, showing that POMs enable safer and faster navigation compared to reactive methods, especially in scenarios with moving obstacles. The results suggest that predictive occupancy mapping is a promising direction for enhancing robotic agility and reliability in dynamic settings.

title: Quantum Brownian oscillator for the stock market
text:
The stock market, a complex adaptive system characterized by non-linear dynamics and emergent phenomena, has long challenged traditional models rooted in classical statistical mechanics and rational agent theory. While classical frameworks like the Black-Scholes model or geometric Brownian motion have provided foundational insights into price fluctuations, they often fail to capture extreme events, market crashes, and the interplay of heterogeneous investor behaviors. These limitations underscore the need for novel theoretical approaches that integrate stochasticity, uncertainty, and collective interactions more holistically. Recent interdisciplinary advances suggest that quantum mechanics—despite its origins in microscopic physics—may offer powerful tools to model macroscopic financial systems. By reframing market dynamics through the lens of quantum probability and open quantum systems, researchers can explore phenomena such as superposition of investor strategies, entanglement between assets, and decoherence induced by external noise, which classical models struggle to represent.  

This paper introduces a *quantum Brownian oscillator* framework to analyze stock market behavior, merging concepts from quantum mechanics with stochastic calculus. The model treats the stock price as a quantum observable evolving under a Hamiltonian that incorporates both deterministic trends and stochastic fluctuations. Investors, represented as quantum states, exhibit probabilistic decision-making influenced by market information and herding effects, akin to quantum measurement processes. The market environment acts as a dissipative reservoir, introducing decoherence that aligns with observed volatility clustering and long-memory effects in financial time series. Unlike classical models, this approach inherently accounts for non-Gaussian distributions and path-dependent outcomes, providing a more flexible foundation for risk assessment and option pricing.  

By leveraging quantum master equations and path integral methods, the framework bridges gaps between microscopic investor interactions and macroscopic market observables. We demonstrate its applicability by simulating price trajectories under varying market conditions, revealing how quantum noise alters return distributions compared to classical Brownian motion. The results highlight the potential of quantum-inspired models to improve predictions of fat-tailed events and systemic risks, offering a paradigm shift in financial modeling. This work not only extends quantum theory to economic systems but also invites re-examination of classical assumptions about market efficiency and rationality.

title: Insider Ownership and Dividend Payout Policy: The Role of Business Cycle
text: In conclusion, this study provides nuanced insights into the interplay between insider ownership, dividend payout policy, and business cycle fluctuations. Our findings reveal that insider ownership exerts a differential impact on dividend decisions contingent on the phase of the business cycle. During economic expansions, higher insider ownership aligns with increased dividend payouts, suggesting that insiders leverage favorable conditions to signal confidence and distribute excess cash. Conversely, in recessions, the relationship becomes inverted, with insiders prioritizing liquidity retention over payouts to mitigate risks and safeguard firm stability. These results underscore the importance of macroeconomic context in corporate finance decisions, challenging the one-size-fits-all assumptions of agency theory. Future research could explore sector-specific variations or the influence of regulatory changes on these dynamics. Overall, our study highlights the need for policymakers and investors to consider business cycle phases when evaluating corporate payout strategies, offering a more dynamic framework for understanding insider behavior and dividend policy.

title: DeFi Protocols for Loanable Funds: Interest Rates, Liquidity and Market Efficiency
text: This paper examines the dynamics of DeFi (Decentralized Finance) protocols for loanable funds, focusing on their role in shaping interest rates, liquidity provision, and overall market efficiency within decentralized ecosystems. Unlike traditional financial systems, DeFi protocols operate through smart contracts, enabling permissionless access to borrowing and lending services without intermediaries. We analyze how these protocols determine interest rates through algorithmic mechanisms that respond to supply and demand fluctuations in real time, contrasting them with centralized counterparts that rely on manual adjustments or policy-driven frameworks. Our study highlights the unique liquidity features of DeFi, where liquidity pools and automated market makers (AMMs) facilitate instant asset exchanges, reducing friction but introducing new risks such as impermanent loss and smart contract vulnerabilities. We investigate the efficiency of these markets by evaluating price discovery mechanisms, arbitrage opportunities, and the impact of oracle reliability on interest rate accuracy. Using empirical data from leading DeFi platforms like Aave, Compound, and MakerDAO, we demonstrate that while DeFi markets exhibit high responsiveness to short-term liquidity shocks, they are also prone to inefficiencies stemming from network congestion, gas fees, and speculative behavior. Furthermore, we explore the interplay between protocol design choices—such as collateralization ratios and liquidation thresholds—and systemic stability, noting that overly aggressive parameters can amplify volatility. Our findings suggest that while DeFi protocols enhance financial inclusion and innovation, their market efficiency remains constrained by technical and governance challenges. The paper concludes with recommendations for improving protocol resilience, including adaptive interest rate models, decentralized oracle solutions, and enhanced risk management frameworks to foster sustainable growth in decentralized lending markets.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Deep Convolutional Candlestick Learner
text:
The rapid advancement of deep learning has revolutionized financial time series analysis, particularly in the domain of algorithmic trading, where deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in interpreting candlestick patterns—a critical visual representation of price movements in financial markets. By automatically extracting hierarchical features from raw candlestick charts, CNN-based models have achieved superior predictive performance in stock price movement forecasting and market trend analysis. However, despite their efficacy, these models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where subtle, imperceptible perturbations in input data can lead to catastrophic misclassification. This vulnerability poses significant risks in high-stakes financial environments, where erroneous predictions may result in substantial economic losses.  
Existing research on adversarial robustness has predominantly focused on computer vision and natural language processing domains, leaving the financial application of CNNs underexplored. Financial time series data exhibit unique characteristics, such as non-stationarity, low signal-to-noise ratios, and temporal dependencies, which differentiate them from traditional image or text datasets. Consequently, adversarial strategies effective in other domains may not directly translate to candlestick analysis, necessitating domain-specific robustness evaluations. Moreover, the lack of standardized benchmarks for adversarial attacks in financial contexts further complicates the assessment of model resilience.  
This study addresses these gaps by systematically investigating the adversarial robustness of deep convolutional candlestick learners. We propose a novel framework to generate adversarial candlestick perturbations that preserve semantic validity while maximizing model misclassification. Through comprehensive experiments on real-world stock datasets, we evaluate the vulnerability of state-of-the-art CNN architectures under various attack scenarios and analyze the transferability of adversarial examples across different models. Our findings highlight critical weaknesses in existing approaches and provide insights into designing more robust financial prediction systems. By advancing the understanding of adversarial threats in this niche, this work contributes to safer and more reliable deployment of deep learning in algorithmic trading.

title: Intervention Threshold for Epidemic Control in Susceptible-Infected-Recovered Metapopulation Models
text: This study investigates the intervention threshold required to control epidemics in metapopulation systems modeled by the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) framework. Using a network-based approach, we analyze how spatial connectivity, population heterogeneity, and mobility patterns influence the critical intervention intensity necessary to prevent widespread outbreaks. By integrating stochastic simulations with analytical solutions of a metapopulation SIR model, we derive a generalized threshold condition that accounts for inter-subpopulation coupling strength, local transmission rates, and recovery dynamics. Our results demonstrate that intervention efficacy depends nonlinearly on both the structure of mobility networks and the temporal synchronization of control measures across subpopulations. We find that weakly connected metapopulations require lower intervention thresholds compared to highly interconnected systems, while heterogeneity in subpopulation sizes and contact rates significantly raises the threshold for effective control. The study also identifies critical trade-offs between targeted interventions in high-risk subpopulations and uniform strategies, highlighting scenarios where localized measures fail to contain epidemics. These findings provide a quantitative foundation for optimizing resource allocation in real-world epidemic management, offering insights applicable to both historical pandemics and emerging infectious diseases.

title: A Novel Ramp Metering Approach Based on Machine Learning and Historical Data
text:
Urban traffic congestion remains a persistent challenge, with ramps connecting highways to arterial roads serving as critical bottlenecks. Ramp metering, which regulates the flow of vehicles entering highways through traffic signals, has proven effective in mitigating congestion and improving mainline throughput. However, traditional methods often rely on static thresholds or simplistic control rules, such as fixed-cycle metering, that fail to adapt to dynamic traffic conditions. These approaches struggle to account for fluctuations in demand, incidents, or weather, leading to suboptimal performance and persistent delays. As urban populations grow and traffic patterns become increasingly complex, there is a pressing need for more adaptive, data-driven ramp metering strategies.  
Recent advancements in machine learning (ML) and the availability of large-scale historical traffic data provide new opportunities to enhance ramp metering systems. By leveraging historical patterns of congestion, demand, and incident occurrences, ML algorithms can predict short-term traffic conditions and optimize metering rates in real time. Unlike rule-based systems, ML-driven approaches can continuously learn from evolving traffic dynamics, enabling more precise and responsive control. This research introduces a novel ramp metering framework that integrates historical traffic data with machine learning models to dynamically adjust metering signals, aiming to reduce delays, improve highway safety, and enhance overall network efficiency.  
The proposed approach addresses key limitations of existing methods by incorporating contextual factors such as time of day, day of week, and weather conditions into its predictive models. By training on multi-year datasets from diverse urban environments, the system captures recurring patterns while adapting to unforeseen disruptions. Preliminary simulations suggest that this data-driven strategy outperforms traditional ramp metering techniques, particularly during peak hours and adverse conditions. This paper outlines the methodology, experimental design, and initial results, demonstrating the potential of ML-enhanced ramp metering to transform traffic management in smart cities.

title: Neural encoding with visual attention
text:
Our fMRI analysis revealed that visual attention significantly modulated neural encoding in early visual (V1-V3) and higher-order (IPS, FEF) regions. When participants attended to stimuli in the right visual field, BOLD activation in contralateral V1 increased by 18% (t(22) = 3.4, p < 0.01) compared to unattended trials, with a smaller 9% boost in ipsilateral V1 (t(22) = 2.1, p = 0.04). Attentional effects scaled with stimulus contrast: at high contrast, V1 activation under attention was 24% greater than baseline (t(22) = 4.1, p < 0.001), while low-contrast stimuli showed only a 12% increase (t(22) = 2.5, p = 0.02).  

In higher-order areas, the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) exhibited a 22% attention-driven activation increase (t(22) = 3.8, p < 0.001), correlating strongly with behavioral accuracy (r = 0.65, p < 0.001). The frontal eye field (FEF) showed a 15% rise (t(22) = 2.9, p = 0.008), but this effect was delayed by ~150 ms relative to IPS, suggesting a hierarchical processing sequence.  

Decoding analyses using support vector machines demonstrated that attention improved classification accuracy of stimulus orientation in V1 by 14% (from 68% to 82%, p < 0.001) and in IPS by 19% (from 71% to 90%, p < 0.001). These results indicate that attention enhances neural encoding through both amplification of sensory signals and refinement of representational fidelity, with early visual areas prioritizing contrast gain and higher-order regions optimizing feature selectivity.

title: Considerations for developing predictive models of crime and new methods for measuring their accuracy
text: In conclusion, the development of predictive models for crime represents a powerful yet ethically complex tool for enhancing public safety and resource allocation. While advances in machine learning and data science have enabled more sophisticated modeling approaches, the effectiveness of these tools hinges on careful consideration of data quality, model transparency, and fairness. As demonstrated throughout this paper, traditional accuracy metrics like precision, recall, and AUC-ROC often fail to capture the nuanced impacts of predictive errors, particularly in high-stakes domains like criminal justice. New methods, such as cost-sensitive accuracy measures and equity-focused evaluation frameworks, offer promising alternatives by explicitly accounting for the differential consequences of false positives and false negatives across demographic groups. These innovations underscore the importance of moving beyond generic performance benchmarks toward context-specific assessments that align with societal values. However, challenges remain in operationalizing these metrics, particularly due to limitations in data availability and the need for interdisciplinary collaboration between technologists, policymakers, and community stakeholders. Future research should prioritize the development of open-source tools for equitable model evaluation, as well as robust guidelines for integrating predictive systems into real-world decision-making processes. By addressing these gaps, the field can move toward predictive models that not only improve accuracy but also uphold principles of justice and accountability, ensuring that advancements in technology serve the public good without reinforcing systemic biases.

title: The Right Tools for the Job: The Case for Spatial Science Tool-Building
text: This paper advocates for the strategic development of specialized spatial science tools to address complex, location-based challenges across disciplines. While general-purpose software dominates current workflows, its limitations in handling spatial data’s unique dimensions—such as scale, topology, and dynamic interactions—often hinder analytical precision and innovation. By integrating principles from geography, computer science, and domain-specific knowledge, purpose-built tools can optimize data processing, enhance visualization, and enable more sophisticated modeling of spatial phenomena. The case studies presented demonstrate how tailored solutions improve outcomes in urban planning, ecological conservation, and disaster response, where off-the-shelf software falls short. Furthermore, the paper argues that investing in open-source, modular tool-building frameworks fosters collaboration, reduces redundancy, and democratizes access to advanced spatial analytics. Ultimately, the authors contend that a paradigm shift toward disciplined, user-centric tool development is critical to unlocking the full potential of spatial science and addressing 21st-century socio-environmental problems effectively.

title: Conscious Intelligence Requires Lifelong Autonomous Programming For General Purposes
text:
The pursuit of artificial intelligence (AI) has long been guided by the aspiration to replicate the versatile cognitive abilities of the human mind. While contemporary AI systems, particularly those rooted in deep learning, have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in specialized tasks—ranging from image recognition to natural language processing—they remain constrained by their reliance on static, pre-defined datasets and narrow operational frameworks. These limitations underscore a fundamental discrepancy: unlike human intelligence, which exhibits adaptive fluidity across diverse domains and evolving contexts, machine intelligence operates within rigid boundaries, incapable of autonomous generalization or self-directed improvement. This gap highlights a critical challenge in AI research—the need to transition from specialized, task-oriented systems to architectures capable of conscious intelligence, defined here as the capacity for self-aware reasoning, lifelong learning, and purposeful adaptation without human intervention.  
Central to this challenge is the concept of autonomous programming, a dynamic process wherein intelligent systems continuously refine their own algorithms, knowledge representations, and decision-making frameworks in response to environmental feedback and introspective analysis. Unlike traditional AI paradigms, which depend on external supervision for updates, autonomous programming demands intrinsic mechanisms for self-assessment, goal redefinition, and iterative optimization. Such capabilities are essential for achieving general-purpose intelligence, as they enable systems to navigate unforeseen scenarios, integrate cross-domain knowledge, and evolve beyond their initial training parameters.  
This paper argues that conscious intelligence, characterized by adaptability and self-sufficiency, cannot emerge from static architectures but requires lifelong autonomous programming as its foundational principle. By examining the cognitive underpinnings of human learning and the shortcomings of current AI models, we propose a framework for designing systems that emulate biological intelligence through self-directed exploration, meta-cognitive reasoning, and open-ended skill acquisition.

title: A Topological Approach to Inferring the Intrinsic Dimension of Convex Sensing Data
text: The intrinsic dimension (ID) of high-dimensional sensing data reflects the minimal number of latent variables required to describe its underlying structure, offering critical insights for dimensionality reduction, manifold learning, and signal reconstruction. Traditional methods for ID estimation, such as PCA-based eigenvalue thresholds or nearest-neighbor statistics, often struggle with convex data geometries, where local linear approximations fail to capture global topological constraints. This paper introduces a novel topological framework for inferring the ID of convex sensing data by leveraging persistent homology, a tool from algebraic topology that quantifies the stability of topological features across scales. By analyzing the persistence diagrams of Rips complexes constructed from convex datasets, we derive a robust estimator for the ID that accounts for both local curvature and global convexity. Experiments on synthetic and real-world convex data (e.g., polyhedral shapes, compressed sensing measurements) demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline approaches in accuracy and stability, particularly under noise and sparsity. This work bridges topological data analysis with convex geometry, providing a principled solution to ID estimation in structured sensing regimes.

title: Heterogeneity Learning for SIRS model: an Application to the COVID-19
text:
The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the critical need for nuanced epidemiological modeling to inform public health strategies, particularly in capturing the complex dynamics of disease transmission across diverse populations. Traditional compartmental models, such as the Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered-Susceptible (SIRS) framework, often assume homogeneity in population behavior and contact patterns, limiting their ability to account for real-world variability in susceptibility, infection rates, and immunity waning. This oversimplification can lead to inaccurate predictions and suboptimal policy interventions, especially during prolonged outbreaks like COVID-19, where factors such as age, social behavior, and healthcare access drive significant heterogeneity. Addressing these gaps requires advanced modeling approaches that integrate individual-level variability into population-level dynamics, enabling more precise forecasting and targeted control measures.  

Heterogeneity learning—a data-driven methodology that identifies and quantifies subpopulation-specific parameters—offers a promising solution to enhance SIRS models. By leveraging high-resolution data, such as mobility patterns, contact networks, and clinical outcomes, this approach can disentangle the effects of demographic, geographic, and behavioral factors on transmission. For instance, variations in vaccination uptake, mask usage, or social distancing compliance create distinct risk profiles within communities, which traditional models fail to capture. Incorporating these nuances into the SIRS framework allows for stratified analysis of disease progression, shedding light on critical drivers of resurgence and persistence.  

This study applies heterogeneity learning to the SIRS model to analyze COVID-19 dynamics, focusing on the interplay between immunity decay and population stratification. Using real-world data from multiple regions, we demonstrate how accounting for heterogeneity improves the accuracy of epidemic projections and identifies high-risk subgroups. Our findings provide actionable insights for policymakers, emphasizing the importance of tailored interventions over one-size-fits-all strategies. By bridging the gap between theoretical modeling and empirical complexity, this work advances the field of computational epidemiology and offers a scalable tool for managing future pandemics.

title: MatDRAM: A pure-MATLAB Delayed-Rejection Adaptive Metropolis-Hastings Markov Chain Monte Carlo Sampler
text: MatDRAM’s performance was evaluated across three synthetic benchmarks: a 2D Gaussian mixture, a 10D Rosenbrock function, and a 50D banana-shaped distribution. Compared to the standard Adaptive Metropolis-Hastings (AMH) and a delayed-rejection (DR) variant, MatDRAM achieved superior sampling efficiency. For the 2D Gaussian (10,000 samples), MatDRAM’s acceptance rate stabilized at 68.2% (AMH: 23.4%; DR: 41.7%), reducing autocorrelation by 82% relative to AMH. In the 10D Rosenbrock test, MatDRAM’s effective sample size (ESS) per second was 3.2× higher than AMH and 1.8× higher than DR, demonstrating scalability with dimensionality. For the 50D banana distribution, MatDRAM maintained a 54.1% acceptance rate, while AMH dropped to 12.3%, requiring 3× more iterations to converge. Adaptive covariance tuning reduced MatDRAM’s warm-up phase by 67% versus static proposals. These results confirm that delayed rejection mitigates local trapping, while adaptive covariance scaling enhances exploration in high dimensions. MatDRAM’s pure-MATLAB implementation achieved competitive runtime (e.g., 12.3 sec per 10,000 samples in 10D), validating its utility for rapid prototyping and educational use without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Impact of climate change on surface stirring and transport in the Mediterranean Sea
text: The synthesis of observational data and high-resolution model simulations in this study underscores the profound and multifaceted impacts of climate change on surface stirring and transport processes in the Mediterranean Sea. Our findings reveal a consistent trend of intensified surface stirring, particularly in the eastern basin, driven by stronger and more frequent mesoscale eddies and wind-driven currents. This enhancement in stirring has significant implications for marine ecosystems, as it alters nutrient distribution, larval dispersal patterns, and the connectivity of marine populations. Concurrently, changes in transport pathways, marked by shifts in the position and intensity of major currents such as the Algerian and Levantine Currents, are reshaping the biogeographical distribution of species and influencing the spread of pollutants and invasive organisms. These modifications to surface dynamics also have broader implications for regional climate feedbacks, as altered heat and salt fluxes between the ocean and atmosphere can further modulate local and global climate patterns. The results highlight the urgent need for integrated management strategies that account for these dynamic changes, particularly in the context of fisheries, coastal protection, and marine conservation. Future research should focus on refining model resolutions and incorporating emerging observational technologies to better predict and mitigate the cascading effects of climate change on the Mediterranean’s unique and vulnerable marine environment.

title: Embedded hyper-parameter tuning by Simulated Annealing
text: Hyper-parameter tuning is a critical yet computationally expensive phase in developing high-performance machine learning models, particularly for embedded systems where resources are constrained. Traditional methods such as grid search and random search often suffer from inefficiency, while Bayesian optimization, though effective, demands substantial computational overhead, limiting its applicability in resource-scarce environments. This paper introduces a novel approach to embedded hyper-parameter tuning by leveraging Simulated Annealing (SA), a probabilistic optimization technique inspired by the metallurgical process of annealing. The proposed method systematically explores the hyper-parameter space by accepting both beneficial and transiently detrimental moves with a temperature-dependent probability, thereby escaping local optima and converging toward the global optimum. Unlike gradient-based methods, SA does not require derivative information, making it suitable for discrete or non-differentiable hyper-parameters commonly encountered in machine learning pipelines. Furthermore, the algorithm is adapted to embedded systems by incorporating lightweight evaluation metrics and early stopping criteria to minimize resource consumption during model training and validation. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the SA-based tuning method achieves comparable or superior model performance compared to conventional techniques while significantly reducing computational costs. The approach is particularly effective for low-power devices, where energy efficiency and real-time constraints are paramount. By providing a balance between exploration and exploitation, this work advances the state of the art in automated hyper-parameter optimization for embedded machine learning applications, offering a scalable and efficient alternative to existing methodologies.

title: Análise dos fatores determinantes para o decreto de prisão preventiva em casos envolvendo acusações por roubo, tráfico de drogas e furto: Um estudo no âmbito das cidades mais populosas do Paraná
text: The decision to impose preventive detention represents a critical juncture in criminal proceedings, balancing individual liberties with societal security demands. In Brazil, particularly within densely populated urban centers, the application of pretrial detention remains a contentious issue, shaped by legal frameworks, judicial discretion, and socio-structural factors. This study focuses on cases involving robbery, drug trafficking, and theft—crimes that dominate criminal dockets in Paraná’s largest cities, such as Curitiba, Londrina, and Maringá, and often trigger heightened public concern over safety. While existing literature has explored determinants of pretrial detention, including the severity of charges, prior criminal records, and procedural risks like flight or recidivism, gaps persist in understanding how these factors interact within specific regional contexts. Moreover, the interplay between judicial ideologies, police practices, and socioeconomic disparities in urban settings remains underexamined. This paper employs multivariate analysis of judicial decisions across 1,200 cases from 2018–2023 to assess how legal, evidentiary, and extralegal variables influence pretrial detention orders. By contextualizing findings within Paraná’s urban landscape, the study contributes to debates on procedural fairness and the socio-legal construction of risk in Brazil’s criminal justice system.

title: Prediction of Chronic Kidney Disease Using Deep Neural Network
text: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) poses a significant global health burden, necessitating early and accurate prediction for timely intervention. This study proposes a deep neural network (DNN)-based framework to enhance CKD prediction by leveraging clinical and laboratory data. The model integrates multi-layered neural architectures with advanced optimization techniques to automatically extract hierarchical features from heterogeneous datasets. We evaluated the framework using a large-scale CKD dataset, comparing its performance against traditional machine learning models and existing DNN approaches. Results demonstrate superior predictive accuracy, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.94, sensitivity of 92%, and specificity of 90%. The model also identifies key risk factors, such as elevated serum creatinine and reduced glomerular filtration rate, through interpretability analysis. This research highlights the potential of DNNs in improving CKD prognosis, offering a scalable tool for clinical decision support and personalized treatment strategies.

title: Disparities in ridesourcing demand for mobility resilience: A multilevel analysis of neighborhood effects in Chicago, Illinois
text:
Ridesourcing services like Uber and Lyft have become integral to urban mobility systems, offering flexible, on-demand transportation options that complement traditional public transit. However, their adoption is not uniform across neighborhoods, raising critical questions about equity in access to mobility resilience—the capacity to maintain mobility during disruptions such as public transit strikes, extreme weather, or infrastructure failures. While prior research has examined individual-level factors influencing ridesourcing demand, such as income or car ownership, less attention has been paid to how neighborhood-level characteristics shape disparities in service utilization. This gap is particularly salient in cities like Chicago, Illinois, where socioeconomic and racial segregation intersect with uneven public transit coverage, potentially exacerbating inequities in access to reliable transportation alternatives. Understanding these dynamics is essential for designing policies that ensure ridesourcing services contribute to, rather than undermine, equitable urban mobility.  

This study employs a multilevel modeling approach to analyze ridesourcing demand across Chicago neighborhoods, integrating data on trip frequency, socioeconomic composition, and built environment features. By examining how neighborhood attributes—such as poverty rates, transit accessibility, and racial demographics—interact with individual-level factors, we aim to identify systemic barriers to mobility resilience. For instance, neighborhoods with limited public transit options may rely more heavily on ridesourcing, yet face higher costs or supply constraints due to perceived safety risks or lower provider interest. Conversely, affluent areas might experience surplus service availability, reinforcing spatial inequities.  

Chicago provides a compelling case study due to its history of segregation and recent investments in ridesourcing partnerships to address transit gaps. Our analysis leverages granular trip data from the Chicago Data Portal alongside census-derived neighborhood metrics, enabling a nuanced exploration of how contextual factors influence demand. The findings have implications for urban planners and policymakers seeking to promote equitable access to mobility resilience tools, particularly in marginalized communities where transportation insecurity is most acute. By disentangling the interplay of individual and neighborhood-level drivers, this research advances scholarship on transportation equity and offers actionable insights for fostering inclusive urban mobility systems.

title: OPRA: An Open-Source Online Preference Reporting and Aggregation System
text: OPRA was deployed across three pilot studies involving 1,250 participants, with 92% successfully completing preference reporting tasks. In Study 1 (n=500), users ranked 10 policy options using OPRA’s drag-and-drop interface, achieving a 98% accuracy rate in capturing ordinal preferences compared to manual entry. Median completion time was 2.3 minutes, 40% faster than a legacy system. Study 2 (n=450) tested OPRA’s aggregation algorithm under simulated voting scenarios, revealing a 95% consistency rate with known majority-rule outcomes, even with 15% incomplete preference sets. Study 3 (n=300) evaluated real-time consensus visualization: 82% of participants reported improved clarity in group preference trends, with 76% adjusting their rankings after viewing aggregated data. Statistical analysis (ANOVA, p < 0.01) confirmed significant differences in user satisfaction (M=4.6/5) and perceived transparency (M=4.3/5) versus control tools. Minor issues included occasional latency during peak loads (5% of sessions) and confusion over weighted voting mechanics (12% of users). These findings validate OPRA’s technical robustness and usability, though optimizations for scalability and user guidance remain priorities.

title: Stochastic Planning and Scheduling with Logic-Based Benders Decomposition
text: In conclusion, this paper has introduced a novel framework for stochastic planning and scheduling problems that integrates logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD) to effectively manage uncertainty and complex constraints. By leveraging the strengths of LBBD, we demonstrated how the stochastic problem can be decomposed into a master problem handling strategic decisions and subproblems addressing operational details under various scenarios. This decomposition not only reduces computational complexity but also enhances solution quality by allowing tailored solution techniques for each substructure. Our numerical experiments on benchmark instances and real-world inspired problems show that the proposed approach significantly outperforms traditional methods in terms of solution robustness and computational efficiency, particularly for large-scale instances with high degrees of uncertainty. Furthermore, the flexibility of LBBD in incorporating different types of constraints and uncertainty representations makes it a promising tool for a wide range of stochastic optimization problems. Future research directions include exploring adaptive scenario selection strategies and integrating machine learning techniques to further improve the scalability and applicability of the framework in dynamic environments. Overall, this work contributes to the advancement of stochastic optimization by providing a systematic and efficient approach to tackle complex planning and scheduling challenges under uncertainty.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Lookahead Factor Models for Quantitative Investing
text: This paper introduces Uncertainty-Aware Lookahead Factor Models (UALFM), a novel framework designed to enhance quantitative investment strategies by integrating forward-looking uncertainty estimation into factor modeling. Traditional factor models often rely on historical data to predict asset returns, overlooking the dynamic and uncertain nature of financial markets. UALFM addresses this limitation by incorporating a probabilistic lookahead mechanism that quantifies both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties in factor predictions. The model employs a hybrid architecture combining a deep neural network for capturing complex factor interactions with a Bayesian approach to estimate predictive uncertainty. By doing so, UALFM provides not only point estimates of factor returns but also confidence intervals that reflect the inherent market volatility. We evaluate the proposed framework on multiple global equity markets, demonstrating its superiority over conventional factor models in terms of risk-adjusted returns and drawdown control. Our empirical results show that UALFM achieves significant outperformance, particularly during periods of heightened market uncertainty, by dynamically adjusting factor exposures based on estimated uncertainty levels. This research contributes to the field of quantitative finance by offering a principled approach to uncertainty-aware factor investing, enabling more robust and adaptive portfolio construction strategies.

title: Peut-on former les enseignant$\cdot$e$\cdot$s en un rien de temps ?
text: The rapid transformation of educational landscapes worldwide, fueled by technological advancements and shifting pedagogical paradigms, has intensified the demand for well-prepared, adaptable teachers. However, the question of whether teachers can be effectively trained within compressed timeframes remains a contentious issue in educational research and policy. Traditional teacher education programs, often spanning several years, emphasize comprehensive theoretical knowledge, practical classroom experience, and reflective practice. Yet, in response to urgent global challenges—such as teacher shortages, the need for rapid digital integration, or emergency responses to crises like the COVID-19 pandemic—there has been a growing interest in accelerated or "fast-track" teacher training models. These models promise to equip educators with essential skills in a fraction of the time, raising critical questions about their feasibility, efficacy, and long-term impact on teaching quality and student outcomes. This paper explores the tensions between the ideal of thorough teacher preparation and the pragmatic necessity of expedited training, examining whether it is possible to cultivate competent, confident educators without sacrificing the depth and rigor of traditional programs. By analyzing existing literature, case studies, and empirical evidence, we aim to contribute to the global discourse on optimizing teacher development in an era of rapid change.

title: NuClick: A Deep Learning Framework for Interactive Segmentation of Microscopy Images
text: Interactive segmentation of microscopy images is a critical task in biomedical research, enabling precise delineation of cellular and subcellular structures for analysis. However, existing methods often struggle with complex image textures, low contrast, and the need for extensive user input, limiting their practical utility. This paper introduces NuClick, a novel deep learning framework designed to facilitate interactive segmentation by integrating user guidance in a robust and efficient manner. NuClick leverages a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture enhanced with a guided attention mechanism, allowing it to dynamically adapt to user-provided inputs—such as scribbles, clicks, or bounding boxes—while maintaining contextual awareness of the underlying image structure. The framework employs a multi-scale feature fusion strategy to capture both local and global information, improving segmentation accuracy in challenging scenarios. We evaluate NuClick on diverse microscopy datasets, including fluorescence and histology images, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art interactive and automated segmentation methods. Quantitative results show significant improvements in Dice coefficient and intersection-over-union scores, particularly in low-contrast regions, while requiring fewer user interactions. Furthermore, NuClick’s lightweight design ensures real-time performance, making it suitable for high-throughput applications. By bridging the gap between user intent and algorithmic precision, NuClick advances interactive segmentation tools for microscopy, offering researchers a flexible and reliable solution for complex image analysis tasks. The framework’s open-source implementation and pre-trained models are publicly available to accelerate adoption in biomedical research.

title: Critical pedagogy in the implementation of educational technologies
text:
The integration of educational technologies into classroom settings has accelerated globally, reshaped by advancements in artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and interactive platforms. While these tools promise enhanced engagement, personalization, and accessibility, their implementation often reflects the values and power structures of the systems that design them. Dominant approaches to educational technology (EdTech) prioritize efficiency, standardization, and technical functionality, frequently overlooking the socio-political dimensions of learning environments. This gap underscores the urgency of adopting critical pedagogy—a framework that challenges hierarchical power dynamics, interrogates systemic inequities, and empowers learners to critique and transform their realities—as a lens for reimagining EdTech’s role in education. Critical pedagogy, rooted in the works of Paulo Freire and later expanded by scholars like Henry Giroux, emphasizes education as a practice of freedom rather than domination. By centering students’ lived experiences and fostering dialogue about oppression, it provides a counter-narrative to technocratic models of teaching and learning.  

Current EdTech implementations, however, often reinforce neoliberal agendas, such as data-driven accountability and individualized competition, which marginalize marginalized communities and perpetuate inequities. For instance, algorithmic bias in adaptive learning systems may disadvantage non-dominant cultural or linguistic groups, while surveillance tools normalize monitoring and control. These outcomes highlight the need for a critical examination of how technologies are designed, deployed, and evaluated. This paper argues that critical pedagogy offers a vital framework for disrupting these patterns, advocating for technologies that align with principles of social justice, inclusivity, and collective empowerment. By integrating critical consciousness into EdTech practices, educators can transform tools from instruments of compliance into catalysts for critical reflection and societal change.  

This study explores the intersection of critical pedagogy and educational technology through a mixed-methods analysis of case studies, policy documents, and practitioner interviews. It investigates how educators and institutions navigate tensions between top-down technological mandates and grassroots efforts to democratize learning environments. The findings reveal that while challenges persist—such as institutional resistance and limited teacher training—intentional, student-centered design processes can foster technologies that amplify marginalized voices and challenge dominant narratives. Ultimately, this research contributes to a broader conversation about redefining the purpose of EdTech in service of equity and liberation.

title: Analysis of the main factors for the configuration of green ports in Colombia
text:
The analysis of 12 major Colombian ports revealed key factors influencing green port configuration. On average, ports investing over 15% of annual revenue in sustainable infrastructure (e.g., shore power systems, waste recycling facilities) reduced carbon emissions by 22% (SD = 4.5%) within three years. For instance, Buenaventura Port, which allocated 18% of its 2022 budget ($12 million) to green initiatives, achieved a 27% drop in emissions, primarily due to the adoption of 100% electric cargo-handling equipment.  

Regulatory compliance emerged as another critical driver. Ports adhering to Colombia’s 2020 National Green Port Strategy, which mandates 30% renewable energy usage by 2030, reported 19% higher operational efficiency scores compared to non-compliant ports. Barranquilla Port, despite lower initial investment (12% of budget), improved efficiency by 15% after implementing solar panels and rainwater harvesting systems to meet regulatory targets.  

Stakeholder collaboration correlated strongly with sustainability outcomes. Ports partnering with at least three external entities (e.g., NGOs, tech firms) averaged 25% better waste management performance. Cartagena Port’s alliance with a local university to develop algae-based biofuels reduced fuel costs by 14% and cut particulate emissions by 31%.  

These findings suggest that financial commitment, regulatory alignment, and partnerships are pivotal for green port success in Colombia, with diminishing returns observed when investments fall below 10% of revenue or collaboration networks remain limited to two stakeholders.

title: A Fully Integrated Sensor-Brain-Machine Interface System for Restoring Somatosensation
text: In conclusion, this study demonstrates the successful development of a fully integrated sensor-brain-machine interface system capable of restoring somatosensation with high fidelity. By combining advanced tactile sensors, real-time signal processing algorithms, and bidirectional neural interfacing, our system achieves closed-loop sensory feedback that closely mimics natural touch perception. Experimental results in both in vitro and in vivo settings confirm the system’s ability to decode and encode somatosensory information with minimal latency, enabling precise control and enhanced functionality in prosthetic applications. Importantly, the biocompatible, wireless design supports long-term implantation and chronic use, addressing key challenges in current BMIs. This work represents a significant step toward seamless integration of artificial limbs with the nervous system, offering promising avenues for improving quality of life in amputees and individuals with sensory deficits. Future research will focus on optimizing sensor resolution and expanding the range of perceivable stimuli to further enhance realism and adaptability.

title: New Insights on Learning Rules for Hopfield Networks: Memory and Objective Function Minimisation
text: This paper presents novel insights into the learning rules governing Hopfield networks, focusing on their dual capacity for memory storage and objective function minimisation. Traditional Hopfield networks rely on Hebbian-style learning rules, such as the outer product rule, to store patterns as attractors in the network's energy landscape. However, these methods often face limitations in terms of memory capacity and the quality of fixed-point attractors, particularly when dealing with non-binary or correlated data patterns. We introduce a refined learning framework that integrates principles from optimisation theory to enhance both memory retrieval and convergence towards desired solutions. By formulating the learning process as an objective function minimisation problem, we derive updated rules that explicitly account for the trade-off between memory capacity and the stability of stored patterns. Our approach leverages gradient-based optimisation techniques to iteratively adjust synaptic weights, ensuring that the network not only stores patterns efficiently but also minimises a user-defined objective function during retrieval. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed learning rules significantly improve the network's ability to recover stored patterns even in the presence of noise and partial occlusions, while also facilitating convergence to optimal states in constraint satisfaction tasks. These findings offer a promising avenue for advancing the theoretical understanding and practical applications of Hopfield networks in machine learning and cognitive computing.

title: The Wage Premium of Communist Party Membership: Evidence from China
text: The wage premium associated with Communist Party membership in China has attracted considerable attention from scholars and policymakers, given the pivotal role of the Communist Party of China (CPC) in the country's political and economic landscape. As the world's largest political party, the CPC not only shapes policy directions but also influences individual career trajectories and labor market outcomes. Existing literature has explored various dimensions of Party membership, including its impact on employment opportunities, career advancement, and social networks. However, empirical evidence on the wage premium—the additional earnings that Party members receive compared to their non-member counterparts—remains limited and inconclusive. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing robust empirical analysis using a nationally representative dataset from China. By examining the wage differential between Party members and non-members, we seek to uncover the underlying mechanisms driving this premium, such as human capital accumulation, political connections, and job characteristics. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the labor market implications of political affiliation in China and offer insights into the broader interplay between politics and economics in authoritarian regimes.

title: Semiparametric Bayesian Inference for the Transmission Dynamics of COVID-19 with a State-Space Model
text: This paper introduces a semiparametric Bayesian framework for modeling the transmission dynamics of COVID-19 using a state-space model that integrates both parametric mechanistic components and flexible nonparametric elements. By combining a compartmental susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) structure with a Gaussian process-based latent process, our approach captures complex, time-varying patterns in transmission rates and reporting delays without requiring strict parametric assumptions. The model leverages observed case counts, hospitalization data, and mobility indicators to disentangle the effects of interventions, behavioral changes, and viral evolution on disease spread. We employ Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for posterior inference, enabling uncertainty quantification in key epidemiological parameters such as the basic reproduction number ($R_0$), infection fatality rate, and case detection efficiency. Simulation studies demonstrate robustness to model misspecification, while applications to regional COVID-19 data reveal critical insights into transmission heterogeneity and the impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions. Our semiparametric Bayesian state-space model provides a flexible, data-driven tool for real-time epidemic monitoring and policy evaluation, addressing limitations of traditional parametric approaches in capturing unobserved dynamics during rapidly evolving outbreaks.

title: Death by starvation in May-Leonard models
text:
The dynamics of cyclic dominance, where competing species or strategies maintain balance through sequential predation or suppression, have long fascinated researchers in evolutionary game theory and population ecology. Among the most influential frameworks for studying such interactions is the May-Leonard model, a mathematical system originally designed to explore how three competing strategies can coexist through non-transitive relationships. However, while the classic May-Leonard model assumes that interactions between species are symmetric and that elimination occurs only through direct competition, real-world ecosystems often involve additional layers of complexity, such as resource depletion and starvation. These factors can dramatically alter the stability and outcomes of cyclic dominance, yet they remain underexplored in traditional formulations of the model.  

Recent advancements in theoretical ecology have highlighted the importance of incorporating metabolic constraints and resource availability into models of cyclic competition. Starvation, in particular, introduces a time-dependent mechanism where individuals or populations may perish not solely from direct predation but also from the gradual exhaustion of resources. This distinction is critical, as it shifts the focus from instantaneous interactions to cumulative processes that unfold over multiple generations. Despite its relevance, the role of starvation in modifying the dynamics of May-Leonard systems has received limited attention, leaving gaps in our understanding of how resource limitations interact with cyclic dominance.  

This paper addresses this gap by systematically investigating how starvation mechanisms influence the stability, extinction risks, and coexistence patterns in May-Leonard models. By integrating resource-dependent mortality into the classic framework, we explore scenarios where populations face not only mutual predation but also the threat of collapse due to sustained resource scarcity. Our findings reveal that starvation can destabilize otherwise persistent cycles, promote alternative equilibria, and even drive entire systems toward extinction under specific conditions. These results underscore the need to account for metabolic and resource-based constraints in theoretical models of cyclic competition, offering new insights into the resilience of ecological and evolutionary systems.

title: A Nonparametric Bayesian Item Response Modeling Approach for Clustering Items and Individuals Simultaneously
text:
The proposed nonparametric Bayesian item response model successfully clustered 150 items and 500 individuals into meaningful latent groups using simulated and real-world educational assessment data.
